A DNA analysis has confirmed that a Nazca infant who lived in southern Peru 1,600 years ago had a rare congenital condition called trisomy 13.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Peru have discovered the skeleton of an infant with a rare birth defect that left only one central eye socket in the child's skull. DNA analysis of the remains confirmed a chromosomal abnormality caused the deadly condition in the infant over 1,600 years ago, according to a new study.

"We cannot really say how long this individual survived," study co-author Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Live Science in an email. But "the burial of this infant suggests that the Nasca treated this individual in death like most other infants."

The skeleton of this female infant was discovered alongside a second one inside a ceramic urn at the archaeological site of Jauranga in Peru's Palpa Valley, where numerous geoglyphs known as the Nazca Lines have been found. Archaeologists uncovered several dozen other burials dated to the Middle Nazca (also spelled Nasca) period (A.D. 325 to 440) at the site, but one of the co-buried infants had an extremely rare condition, researchers wrote in a study published Monday (Nov. 9) in the journal PNAS.

The infant had a very small skull and a single eye socket in the middle of her face, along with other developmental issues of the cranial bones. These traits match modern clinical descriptions of cyclopia, a lethal condition that occurs when the front part of a fetus's brain fails to divide into left and right hemispheres.

This condition can also cause alterations in the nasal structures, resulting in a missing nose or a tube-like nose above the single eye.

A medical illustration from 1891 of two infants with cyclopia.

"The cause of the malformation was present at fertilization, but manifestation occurs around the fourth to fifth week in utero [in the womb], when the frontal lobe of the brain has to divide," study first author Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao, an archaeologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told Live Science in an email.

Cyclopia is a rare condition, occurring in about 1 out of every 100,000 births. To learn more about the infant's short life, the researchers sequenced her genome. (DNA suggested the infant carried two X chromosomes, typical of a female.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team detected an extra copy of chromosome 13, meaning the infant had a genetic condition called trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome. It's known to be a major chromosomal cause of cyclopia; that said, only a small percentage of trisomy 13 cases involve cyclopia.

While trisomy 13 is associated with advanced maternal age, it is not clear whether that was the case for this infant, Fehren-Schmitz said.

"This condition has been documented in historic and modern anatomical collections, but to my knowledge this is the first archaeological example of this developmental abnormality," Siân Halcrow, a bioarchaeologist at Durham University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers' estimate of the infant's age at death suggests she may have survived for several weeks or months after birth, Halcrow pointed out. "This raises important questions about how infants with profound congenital differences were cared for and treated in past societies," she said.

The infant was buried in a ceramic urn, the researchers noted in the study, which was a common burial method in the Nazca period, along with a second female infant who had no skeletal abnormalities. "The baby with cyclopia was at the bottom of the jar, while the other baby was on top. Nevertheless, it appears that they were interred in a single event," Tomasto-Cagigao said. The genetic analysis showed that the two infants did not have the same mother.

A burial of two infants in one urn is unusual for this culture, the researchers said, but there is not enough archaeological evidence to conclude that the infant with cyclopia was given a different type of burial.

"The fact that the individual was buried with a 'healthy' individual in a regular cemetery, without any special grave goods, suggests that, to some extent, the individual was not treated differently in death, even though it had such a rare condition," Fehren-Schmitz said. "It was neither 'excluded' because of it nor treated in a 'special' way."

In ancient Andean societies, some people with disabilities took on special societal roles, such as ones associated with religious practices. "If that reflects Nasca society as a whole, we can't say based on one case," Fehren-Schmitz said, "but it does reflect the community this infant was part of, even if only briefly."

Tomasto-Cagigao, E., Reindel, M., Isla Cuadrado, J., Lund Valle, M., Kassadjikova, K., Harkins, K., Fehren-Schmitz, L. (2026). A Nasca-period perinatal burial reveals cyclopia associated with trisomy 13 in southern Peru. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2625042123

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6378. The 7 Best Portable Jump Starters to Bring Your Vehicle Back to Life

The days of needing jumper cables and another motorist to revive your vehicle are over.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

Like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also important to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

There are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In short, each device in this roundup can quickly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

My recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

With 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

This device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts

The GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—important so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

Protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

The interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review

This is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

It has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

Like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

The Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.)

I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so users need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

For motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

This device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

With 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

For years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

With 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

This portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

The Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

Portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

The two most important specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

Most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

If you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

Look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

Yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two important. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

Definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will issue a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

Yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That said, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

#6377. Blood Vessel Function Improved Just 60 Minutes After Taking This Anti-Aging Supplement

Blood vessel function improved within an hour of a supplement’s first dose in a small human trial, though lasting protection against cardiovascular disease remains unproven.

What if protecting the heart and blood vessels requires more than treating traditional risk factors such as high blood pressure and cholesterol?

Cardiovascular disease remains the world’s leading cause of death, and researchers at the University of Surrey are exploring whether targeting the biology of aging could help protect the heart and blood vessels. In a small trial, they tested a nutritional supplement designed to address several aging-related processes at once, finding improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure over six months.

The randomized controlled trial enrolled 61 participants, with 33 taking NOVOS Core and 28 receiving a placebo once daily for six months. Researchers investigated whether combining these substances could improve cardiovascular health by influencing multiple aging-related pathways simultaneously.

The supplement combines 12 ingredients selected to target biological processes associated with aging. These include glycine, magnesium malate, calcium alpha-ketoglutarate, glucosamine sulfate, vitamin C, L-theanine, hyaluronic acid, and small amounts of lithium, along with plant-derived compounds such as fisetin, pterostilbene, Rhodiola rosea extract, and ginger extract.

Professor Christian Heiss, Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Surrey, said: “Biological aging is not driven by one pathway, but by a number of interacting molecular and cellular processes. The idea behind this study was to ask whether addressing several of these processes at the same time via a nutritional supplement could produce measurable effects on cardiovascular health biomarkers.

“As a first step, we looked at established biomarkers of vascular health, such as blood pressure and cholesterol levels, rather than clinical outcomes. We found favorable changes in endothelial function, arterial stiffness, and systolic blood pressure after six months. These findings are encouraging. We now need larger studies to understand the mechanisms involved and, importantly, whether these changes translate into longer-term health benefits.”

Researchers measured flow-mediated dilation, or how readily an artery widens as blood flow increases. This reveals how well its inner lining, the endothelium, works to regulate vessel width and blood clotting. Dilation improved in the supplement group compared with the placebo group after six months. An improvement also appeared just one hour after the first dose, while placebo readings remained largely unchanged.

Arteries were also less stiff in the supplement group. Researchers assessed this using pulse wave velocity, the speed at which a pressure wave travels through arteries. Slower waves indicate more flexible arteries, and the adjusted difference between groups was 1.18 meters per second after six months.

Systolic blood pressure, the pressure when the heart contracts, was an adjusted 6.1 mmHg lower in the supplement group than in the placebo group at six months. A difference was also observed one hour after the first dose. Estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk decreased modestly, largely reflecting the blood pressure difference.

Previous large studies have associated a sustained 5 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure with approximately 10 percent fewer major cardiovascular events. The Surrey trial measured markers associated with risk and was not designed to determine whether participants experienced fewer such events.

Diogo Barardo, PhD, Director of R&D at NOVOS and a geroscientist, a scientist specializing in the biology of aging, said:

“When we began developing NOVOS Core in 2019, our hypothesis was that simultaneously targeting all the hallmarks of aging, the fundamental biological processes underlying aging and age-related diseases, could produce measurable improvements in the organs and systems affected by aging.

“The STAMINA results provide encouraging clinical evidence consistent with that hypothesis, demonstrating improvements across three measures of cardiovascular function, particularly meaningful given that cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide.”

Blood tests showed no significant changes in cholesterol or other blood lipids, suggesting that lipid lowering did not explain the improvements in blood vessel measures.

Professor Juliet Wright, Founding Dean of the School of Medicine at the University of Surrey, said:

“This study is a good example of how ideas emerging from the biology of aging can be tested rigorously in people. The findings provide an interesting proof of concept, but the important next step is to understand the underlying biology and establish whether changes in cardiovascular biomarkers translate into meaningful longer-term health benefits.”

Reference: “Acute and 6-month vascular effects of a multi-component nutritional supplement: a randomized controlled trial” by Charles Piercy, Jenny Harris, Kenza Sackho, Paola Campagnolo, Diogo Barardo, Ben Creagh-Brown and Christian Heiss, 4 November 2026, European Heart Journal Open. DOI: 10.1093/ehjopen/oeag157

The investigator-initiated study was supported by NOVOS Labs through provision of the study supplement known as NOVOS Core and matching control and an unrestricted contribution towards research costs. NOVOS Labs had no role in study design, collection, or primary interpretation of the data, or the decision to publish.

#6376. ALMA Reveals a Jet of Cool Gas from a Microquasar

There's a strange gamma-ray emitter in the Large Magellanic Cloud that has astronomers stumped about its source. It lies within the ashes left behind by a supernova that created a compact object that's part of the system. The supernova remnant provides a piece of evidence to explain the emissions, but not the whole story.

So, a research team from two Japanese universities decided to give the object, called LMC P3, a closer look. Instead of tracking the gamma rays, they looked at the object with the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile. This is a series of radio telescopes that provide highly detailed radio views of objects in the sky. ALMA focused on radio emissions from carbon monoxide (CO) molecules in proximity to the cold cloud in the area around LMC P3. It's one of the few such objects found outside the Milky Way, and astronomers have dubbed it a microquasar. It consists of a giant O-type star and a compact object that could be explained by the existence of a black hole or a neutron star.

According to astronomer Yasuo Fukui of Nagoya University, who worked with team leader Bhuvana Gadikere Rajendra of Gifu University, what they detected at LMC P3 is unusual. âWe discovered a gigantic molecular jet,â said Fukui. The jet consists of molecular gas that stretches out across 26 light-years of space. For reference, the bright star Vega lies 25 light-years away from us, so the jet would connect us and that star quite easily.

The strange thing is, the molecular jet itself is cold (by our standards), but astrophysically "heated" to a temperature of about 35 to 60 Kelvin. By comparison, that's warmer than the 15 Kelvin surrounding gas but still very cold. That temperature difference means that the gas is interacting with another jet— this one a high-energy stream of particles coming from the nearby compact object with enough energy to power gamma-ray emissions. The object turns out to be a micro-quasar, which would have the energy to do the job.

Micro-quasars are interesting objects. They actually consist of two objects: a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star coupled with a companion star. The black hole constantly sucks material from the star, and that creates a swirling accretion disk around the black hole. It's a fairly energetic interaction that leads to X-ray and gamma-ray emissions. It also creates high-speed jets that travel out at nearly light-speed velocities. They're called micro-quasars because they're a smaller type of quasar, which is a highly active region around a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy.

Fukui said the relatively high temperature observed over a large fraction of the molecular cloud makes it a very strong case that the gas is interacting with a high-energy jet coming from the compact object â precisely the kind of jet that can also power LMC P3âs gamma rays. This also provides a boost to the idea that the object is a black hole, leftover from the collapse of a supermassive star in a supernova explosion.

Prior to this discovery, scientists had two competing theories about what could be powering the emissions. One is that pulsar winds could have been causing the emissions. That means the object has to be a pulsar, which would send out streams of energetic particles in pulsations as the object spins. Neutron stars are created when a supermassive star collapses, but a stellar remnant remains behind consisting solely of neutrons packed tightly together in a space about the size of a city.

The other theory is that the object is indeed a microquasar. The discovery of the newly found "cold" jet strongly suggests that the compact object could be a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star that draws in material from its companion to form an accretion disk. Since black holes drive more powerful jets than neutron stars, the fact that LMC P3âs gamma-ray emission is particularly high is a smoking gun pointing toward the micro-quasar origin of the signals found by ALMA. âIt provides very strong support for the possibility that its central object is a black hole," said Fukui.

Object LMC P3 was first discovered in 2016 thanks to its very strong gamma-ray emissions. It was also the first one found outside the Milky Way. From the beginning, astronomers suspected it was an X-ray binary, and Chandra X-ray Observatory studies seemed to confirm that. Then, the FERMI telescope observed it and found a 10.3-day period in gamma-ray emissions from the object. That suggested a number of ideas, including jets.

Detailed observations with ALMA focused on the surrounding gas clouds and found the "cold" jet streaming away. That raised questions about the "launch mechanism" for such a jet. In the paper the team published about their observations, they wrote: "We interpret that the high temperatures are due to shock heating of a microquasar jet driven by the gamma-ray binary, where the compact object has an accretion disk fed by the O-star winds. The CO jet matches existing predictions from magnetohydrodynamical simulations, which show that a CO jet can form from the interaction of the microquasar jet and an ambient interstellar medium (ISM) cloud. These results provide strong evidence that CO jets are a signature sculpted by microquasar jets, lending support for mass accretion in LMC P3 as the gamma-ray origin.

This discovery has important astrophysical implications for the study of high-energy emissions and the objects that provide them. Coupled with ongoing studies of such objects as SS 433, which is the first microquasar ever found, discoveries such as LMC P3 give new insight into the actions of compact objects and their interactions with surrounding objects.

Has a Mysterious Gamma-ray Powerhouse Revealed its Smoking Gun?

ALMA Observations of DEM L241/LMC P3 in the Large Magellanic Cloud: Evidence for the Formation of Cool Molecular Jets Driven by a Microquasar

#6375. The Restaurants Already on Eater Editors’ Radar for 2027

These restaurants are already creating buzz

Editors’ scouting for the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, wrapped up at the end of August — just as fall restaurant-opening season was heating up. That means several notable restaurants that debuted in 2026 didn’t quite make the cut, either because they didn’t open in time or had only been open a matter of weeks and were still finding their footing as of our deadline. But that just gives us a place to start on next year’s research. Here are some early contenders on our radar — places we’re thrilled to have in the conversation no matter how the scene shakes up as 2026 wraps and we continue into 2027.

Our New York team is excited to see the full spectrum of what pastry chef Camari Mick has in store with her own new venture, Afro-Caribbean brasserie and bakery Calabash, which opened in the West Village in early October.

Also in the West Village, the Taqueria Ramírez team debuted this Mexican-seafood-focused wine bar, which translates to “the hairy shrimp.” The tiny convivial space opened in mid-September.

Alex McCoy’s resurrected Thai restaurant, which opened in early September, is dishing up some of the spiciest Thai food the D.C. area has seen since the much-lamented closure of Little Serow. The alleyway hot spot in Georgetown is drawing crowds for its monkfish curry, khao soi, and natural wine list. Thanks to its moody, candlelit atmosphere, it’s also becoming a favorite tucked-away date spot.

Chicago’s tavern-style pizza has been having a moment outside of the Midwest; in D.C., it’s a menu centerpiece of La Merna, which has been one of the city’s tough-to-get tables since its August opening. Co-owner Bradley Shorten used to run a few tavern-style pizzerias in Chicago, and his wife and partner Meg Schmitt, who has a background in cheese distribution, is topping pastas with cheeses she makes fresh. The wood-paneled dining room with red leather-covered booths resembles a Midwest supper club with its laid-back, old-school atmosphere.

We had high hopes that this coastal Italian Pittsburgh restaurant — from the team behind Lilith, Jamilka Borges and Dianne DeStefano — would open in time for 2026 Eater Awards consideration, but the opening date kept continually getting pushed back. The most recent estimate is “late fall.”

Atlanta already knows the team behind Lucian can combine a fantastic wine list with thoughtful food and a carefully curated retail experience; they’ve started doing it again at Sargent, the combination bistro and bookstore that hadn’t yet opened when our scouts hit the city in early August. The classic menu and gorgeous space are already catching attention in the city; we’re also keeping our eyes on the upcoming opening of Thai-style bar Some Luck from the Talat Market team, slated to open any day now.

This new modern Mexican restaurant was only a few days old when our correspondent Matthew Kang stopped by in early September. Our LA team has high standards for tacos, and Kang says the top-notch Chihuahuan food here could already hold its own even when competing with standout California options. Kang appreciated Chiwas’s delicious seafood and short ribs, and approachable, homey vibe; we’ll be back to see how the restaurant matures.

October brought the debut of this ambitious restaurant from chef Jonathan Granada, and editor Dianne de Guzman is ready to try the tableside duck, laminated brioche, and a gougeres-like Parmesan tart — all set inside an Art Deco-style former post office.

We thought this long-in-the-works, highly anticipated Filipino cocktail bar might open in time for us to visit Detroit and check it out this year, but the project from Tyler Olivier and Marcee Sobredilla is still wrapping up construction.

This Evanston, Illinois, project is the first full-service restaurant from Chicago barbecue royalty D’Andre Carter and Heather Bublick. The restaurant is a true celebration of their community, decked out with local art and paired with a steakhouse-esque menu. It opened just outside our 2026 cutoff, and it’s looking like an exciting time for barbecue in the Windy City in general, as Chicago also awaits the opening of Sanders BBQ Prime in Hyde Park.

Lielle was a hit with the Eater LA team when it opened this year, and our team might even be more enamored with follow-up Marée, which just missed our window with its early September opening. At a recent visit, Matthew Kang noted the creamy mussels au gratin and Instagram-worthy squab, and says the au poivre burger earns its $42 price tag.

#6374. Scientists Warn of a Disturbing Rise in Vitamin K Deficiency Among American Newborns

Only about one in five infants diagnosed with vitamin K-related bleeding had received the shot, U.S. health records show.

Babies are born with little vitamin K, leaving them vulnerable to bleeding that can cause permanent brain damage or death. A single shot helps protect against that danger. The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended one dose injected into a muscle for newborns since 1961, and a growing number of American parents are choosing to skip it.

That trend has coincided with a sharp rise in diagnoses of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). A nationwide study found that their rates increased by 216% and 347%, respectively, between 2017 and 2025, while the percentage of newborns receiving injectable vitamin K fell from 97.7% to 95.0%. The findings were published on November 5, 2026, in JAMA Pediatrics.

Vitamin K activates specialized proteins needed for normal blood clotting. Newborns receive too little through the placenta, absorb it poorly through their digestive systems, and get little from breast milk. The injection addresses a deficiency at a time when its consequences can be severe.

Classical VKD occurs between 2 days and 1 week after birth and causes bruising and bleeding from the umbilicus, or belly button. Late VKD, which occurs between 1 week and 6 months of age, carries a 30% to 60% risk of intracranial hemorrhage, or bleeding inside the skull. That bleeding can lead to seizures, permanent brain damage, or death.

Refusal of the shot has increased over the past decade. Previous studies found that the proportion of newborns who did not receive intramuscular vitamin K rose from 2.9% in 2017 to 5.2% in 2024.

To investigate the consequences of that trend, Elizabeth Wolf, M.D., MPH, led the new nationwide study. Wolf is a pediatrician at Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU and an associate professor in the Department of Pediatrics at Virginia Commonwealth University School of Medicine.

The researchers analyzed de-identified electronic health records from a large national database covering health systems across the United States. Their analysis included more than 11 million infants aged 0 to 6 months who were born at 35 weeks’ gestation or later and received care between 2017 and 2025.

Only 40% of infants diagnosed with VKD and about 19% of those diagnosed with VKDB had received vitamin K shots. About 7% of infants with VKD and 2% of those with VKDB also had a diagnosis of intracranial or intracerebral hemorrhage, meaning bleeding inside the skull or within the brain tissue itself.

“We knew from prior studies that vitamin K refusal had been increasing in the U.S., and we wanted to learn if there were any real-life consequences of this trend,” Wolf said. “We found that the answer is undeniably yes, with the rates of VKD and VKDB multiplying over the course of our study.”

The researchers caution that the simultaneous decline in injections and increase in diagnoses does not prove causation. Wolf considers other explanations unlikely, however, because behaviors and diseases that increase the risk of VKD remained constant or decreased during the study period.

The study’s co-authors included Steven Woolf, M.D., director emeritus of the VCU Center on Society and Health and a professor in VCU School of Medicine’s Department of Family Medicine, Evan French, MS, of VCU’s C. Kenneth and Dianne Wright Center for Clinical and Translational Research, and Darya Shokouhi Niaki, Pharm.D., of the VCU School of Public Health’s Department of Biostatistics.

Wolf connected the findings to growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals.

“Similar to the recent measles outbreaks, we are seeing the real-world implications of growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals. We need clear messaging from all levels of public health about the benefits of vitamin K administration for newborns.”

Like childhood vaccines, the researchers say, vitamin K has been “a victim of its own success,” with many parents unaware that refusing the shot can have serious lifelong consequences. Wolf says more research is needed to determine how best to communicate the seriousness of vitamin K deficiency and encourage use of the medication in newborns.

“We should continue to follow these trends moving forward since the rates of vitamin K deficiency and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding may continue to rise if vitamin K refusal keeps increasing. We need to better understand why parents are refusing vitamin K and what can be done to improve the uptake of this important medication,” Wolf said.

Reference: “Vitamin K Deficiency and Associated Bleeding in Infants” by Elizabeth R. Wolf, Evan French, Darya Shokouhi Niaki and Steven H. Woolf, 5 November 2026, JAMA Pediatrics. DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.5794

#6373. Automated Assembly in Space is the Future and NOM4D is Showing the Way

If we want big things in space, we'll have to build and assemble them there. Rocket fairings are not large enough to accommodate the large things we want to have in space. Not only that, but the stubborn rocket equation refuses to bend itself to our desires.

Telescopes like the JWST feature ingenious folding designs that unfold in space like insects metamorphosizing. That was a very impressive way to bypass the restrictions imposed by rocket fairings. But that's not practical in every case.

What's far more feasible is sending smaller components into space inside fairings and then assembling them into a larger structure once there. That's what NOM4D, the Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials and Mass-efficient Design program is demonstrating. NOM4D reached an important milestone recently when it successfully demonstrated automated in-space assembly for the first time.

The demonstration involved a gantry robot, also known as a linear robot, building a typical truss structure. Gantry robots move in straight lines along x, y, and z axes. The payload came from Caltech and consisted of individual components with custom joints put together to form the structure. The individual components were not only assembled, but a thin reflective mesh that mimics what a space-based antenna might have was also simultaneously applied.

âNOM4Dâs objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space,â said Andrew Detor, NOM4D program manager. âBy âvery large,â I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today.â

This concept image shows a space-based antenna autonomously assembled by a NOM4D-type device. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

There is no shortage of ideas of how space-based manufacturing and construction could be used, but it all starts with programs like NOM4D. NOM4D is fairly simple at this point, like a child's construction toy, but that's its strength.

âYou can think of the Caltech approach as similar to Tinkertoys or Kânex construction toys: individual truss members are joined at nodes, one section at a time, to create a larger structure,â Detor said. âWithin the automated assembly box, each section is built piece by piece, a reflective mesh is attached, and the assembled sections are deployed as they are complete. There are no complicated robotics or advanced algorithms; itâs just solid engineering from the Caltech team to combine operations in a way that scales.â

Decades ago, thinkers proposed different types of rotating space stations that could be homes for thousands of people. The O'Neill Cylinder is probably the most well-known one of these, and space-heads and sci-fi dreamers of a certain age may have carried around a dog-eared copy of Gerard K. O'Neill's "The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space."

"More important than material issues, I think there is reason to hope that the opening of a new, high frontier will challenge the best that is in us, that the new lands waiting to be built in space will give us new freedom to search for better governments, social systems, and ways of life, and that our children may thereby find a world richer in opportunity by our efforts during the decades ahead," O'Neill wrote.

The O'Neill Cylinder lies in the realm of science fiction or the distant future for now, as do O'Neill's hopes for humanity. But that was 50 years ago, and technology has advanced considerably, even if how humans conduct themselves hasn't advanced at the same pace.

But there are other proposed space structures that are closer to reality, and they may be stages towards O'Neill's hopeful vision that can be built by NOM4D or its successor.

It may begin with Low-Earth Orbit transfer stations and lunar orbit stations that would expand our presence in space. The proposed Lunar Gateway was one of these, and was envisioned as a modular design built in space from pre-made components. It would be a docking station and communications relay facility for trips to the lunar surface and operations there. These types of orbital facilities could be hybrids of pre-made components and structural frameworks made by NOM4D or something like it.

This concept image shows how a NOM4D-inspired device might autonomously construct a circular truss structure in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

Another future use for scalable construction concerns lunar lava tubes. The Moon has what appear to be networks of subsurface lava tubes that provide natural protection from hazards. Robotic assembly could feasibly be used to reinforce these natural tubes and turn them into habitats.

Another idea is liquid mirror telescopes. Building a huge telescope mirror and sending it into space would be near impossible, but a liquid mirror telescope could be built in a lunar crater out of components shipped individually into space. And NASA's Lunar Crater Radio Telescope (LCRT) is a concept for a crater-based telescope on the lunar far side, isolated from Earth's radio pollution. These ideas are waiting for the engineering to catch up.

âIn a future space economy, weâre going to need large things,â Detor said. âThink large space depots or habitats, large solar arrays to collect power, or large radio antennas to explore the edges of the universe. Those things require size, and NOM4D gives us a path to accelerate creation of new capabilities.â

The rapid advancement of the NOM4D program surprised even NOM4D personnel themselves. This successful on-orbit demonstration wasn't expected to happen so soon.

Back in February 2025, NOM4D changed its timeline. What was expected to be a third phase of more laboratory tests was instead changed to on-orbit tests, and SpaceX launched Caltech's NOM4D payload into space in March 2026.

âCaltech [California Institute of Technology] and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have demonstrated tremendous advances in the first two phases and have now partnered in Phase 3 with space-launch companies to conduct in-space testing of their novel assembly processes and materials,â Detor said at the time. âOriginally, Phase 3 was going to be about making things more precisely in the lab than we did in Phase 2. But we said, âYou know, the maturity is there, and there would be more impact if we took the capabilities we have now and actually go demonstrate them in space to show that it can be done,â"Detor said.

Now, way ahead of its original schedule, NOM4D has demonstrated its capabilities and is maturing rapidly. As Detor makes clear, leaping from the laboratory to space is a huge jump.

âItâs the speed and the scale that made this a DARPA project. We went from the idea of an on-orbit demo to launching a working prototype into space in 15 months,â Detor said. âOperating in space is much harder than operating on the ground â thereâs virtually no margin to address issues that may arise. Testing in the operational environment is instrumental to rapidly maturing the technology.â

There's still another test upcoming for NOM4D now that it's demonstrated successful on-orbit assembly. Next, the NOM4D team from University of Illinois Urbana-Champagne will launch a test project to the ISS. This will be more than just assembly; it will demonstrate composite material processing. A monomer resin will be used to build a high-strength structure in space. It will use an energy-efficient method to heat the resin and create a strong polymer. This is similar to how resins are used in Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) manufacturing to build things like aerospace components, where strength and light weight are critical.

If that test is successful, then it really will be time to start thinking big, according to Detor.

This concept image shows what the future of NOM4D-like construction might look like. Large space structures like these could be built entirely in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

âThe NOM4D Caltech demonstration is not an endpoint; itâs a beginning,â Detor said. âNow that weâve demonstrated a process that can scale to large structures, what do we go make? What wild ideas get assembled thousands of miles above us and what new capabilities do those structures enable?â

Is it time to open Gerard K. O'Neill's seminal book again?

The O'Neill Cylinder, the OG of space habitats. Maybe one day. Image Credit: By NASA/Rick Guidice - https://space.nss.org/settlement/nasa/70sArtHiRes/70sArt/art.html (image link), Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=675434

Five U.S. chefs making waves in their communities with compelling menus

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Each of the chefs featured in our new national Chef of the Year category made news in a major way. But their most recent projects are just one part of their story.

This year we celebrate five chefs who are making an impact both on the city where they cook and on the larger culinary conversation. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

San Francisco diners became acquainted with powerhouse couple Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their championing of Eastern Mediterranean cuisine at Dalida. That restaurant told the story of Sayat’s upbringing and influences in Istanbul, Turkey, opening in 2023 inside a historic building within the lush environs of the Presidio and earning critical acclaim for the duo’s cooking.

In the years since, diners came to know Laura outside of Dalida. She completed an impressive run on Top Chef in 2024, where viewers saw her deftly plant one foot in Mediterranean food and another in Mexican cuisine, showcasing her skill in both fields throughout the season. With the 2026 debut of the Ozyilmazes’ restaurant Maria Isabel, the food feels like an even fuller expression of Laura’s heritage and personal history.

Named after Laura’s sister (Maria) and her mother (Isabel), the restaurant steeps in Mexican matriarchy, highlighting female winemakers, ceramics made by Mexican producers, and indigenous Mexican ingredients. The menu channels Laura’s upbringing in Guerrero and her family’s Sinaloan roots, as recounted through mariscos and maiz, moles and salsa macha. The ceviche Acapulqueño reimagines the Fanta- and ketchup-laden version instead with marigold flowers and preserved Seville oranges dressing tender shrimp and raw scallop; petals — and three fried shrimp heads — adorn the top. Duck enmoladas showcase the power of mole negro against a seasonal mole (sometimes a peach manchamanteles, other times a rhubarb rendition, but always compelling). Chochoyotes, a lesser-seen dish in San Francisco, demonstrates the restaurant’s ability to apply masa in different ways — in this case, dumplings — while harnessing the earthy flavor of huitlacoche. Maria Isabel is both a conduit for diners to connect with complex Mexican flavors and a view into Laura’s vision of the Mexico of her past and future. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

Chef Carlos Delgado’s meteoric rise in D.C. began in 2022 with the opening of tiny tasting room Causa, located in Shaw, where he sends diners on a seafaring voyage along the Peruvian coastline and into the Andes he grew up around, and its accompanying upstairs pisco destination Bar Amazonia. His meticulous sourcing and culinary skills quickly drew critical acclaim.

2026 might be the Lima native’s biggest year yet: His breakout project, Maru San, commanded instant Capitol Hill buzz upon opening in February for its orchestra of Nikkei-style hand rolls, sashimi, and other polished seafood plates he and fellow José Andrés alum Simon Lam pass across a 25-seat black marble counter under a big pink octopus mural, as his favorite tropical house blasts in the background. A rare few get to sample the restaurant’s elaborate tasting menu full of ingredients like high-end uni and dry-aged fish; reservations for the 15-course feast are nearly impossible to get.

The ambitious chef, at 36, isn’t afraid to stretch in many directions. He linked up with the Eaternity Group last year to give the Mediterranean-themed La Vie a needed menu makeover at D.C.’s Wharf development — meanwhile, at least one more Maru San is in the works elsewhere in D.C.

Sounds a lot like his former mentor: Before Causa, Delgado honed his craft under José Andrés as the longtime executive chef at Penn Quarter’s Peruvian mainstay China Chilcano. They still text frequently. — Tierney Plumb, Northeast editor

While Amir Hajimaleki has had American-leaning restaurants in Austin for well over a decade, he hasn’t had the opportunity to fully express himself as an Iranian-born, Texas-raised chef. That is until he opened Roya, his most personal restaurant and a project that has been in the works for more than eight years. Here, he manifests the depth and diversity of Persian cuisine, a bold feat for the middle of Texas. The space, designed with his brother Ali Hajimaleki, feels transportive with intricate tile mosaics, burnished gold and dark blue hues, and delicate chandeliers.

There’s been an electric energy to the Philly restaurant scene in recent years. The city, ever the underdog, has long punched above its weight; now, the rest of the world has come to the same realization. Amid this buzz, two newer restaurants have outrun the shadow cast by the city’s big names: Cambodian noodle house Mawn, which opened in 2023, and Southeast Asian oyster house and raw bar Sao, which opened last September.

At their helm is the slick, stylish Phila Lorn. The restaurants he runs with his wife Rachel feel singular, blending the influences of his Philadelphia upbringing with his Cambodian background in food that feels playfully free and emboldened by a lack of boundaries between cuisines. At Mawn, funnel cake meets coconut macaroons, and vinegar peppers enhance scallops in red curry. At Sao, the crispy rice in the nam khao salad, which features Italian sausage, feels analogous to arancini. Tuna carpaccio is served with crispy shallots and jalapeños, then cured in lime until it picks up the aura of the bowls of beef pho on Washington Avenue.

Hear Lorn talk, with his South Philly-bred bravado (and requisite uses of “jawn”) giving him a commanding presence, and it’s clear that the city’s culinary community is listening, rallying, and getting stoked to eat more of his food. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tucson-based chef Aaron Lopez had a vision that started in his small California city of El Centro, an agricultural city near the U.S.-Mexico border. There, he hatched a plan to create a menu imbued with the techniques and flavors of the Sonoran Desert that spans northern Mexico, Arizona, and southeastern California. Trained at top kitchens in Los Angeles and beyond, Lopez researched by going deep into the desert, armed with a camera and his wits. A year later, he and his wife June Chee carried the project to Tucson, a larger venue still deeply embedded in the desert, but with a new audience.

Inside the high-ceilinged, brick-walled downtown space, Ursa serves as a hushed gallery for Lopez and his team’s $150 tasting menu, which merges Indigenous cooking techniques with foraged and locally farmed ingredients. Barrel fruit (a yellow cactus) topped with the tang of pickled chiltepin leaves is the first bite, a luscious treat you may never see on a European plate. Quail breast arrives on a metal skewer dressed in pickled yucca, hovering over a jujube broth like a quiet offering. Goat roasted in agave, pit barbacoa-style, is unveiled tableside and served over softened tepary beans.

At every turn, with no extraneous adornments, the kitchen lets the produce and meats boast their innate nature. Lopez eschews conventional comfort, reimagining a meal of cactus, corn, sunflower tea, and beans as true luxuries, and the results are evocative and powerful. His message — seeing the value and beauty of this landscape, its people, its ingredients, and the way it all comes through the cooking — is the luscious pith of the cactus you find beneath the surface of the American Southwest. — Matthew Kang, correspondent

#6371. The 9 Best Gaming Keyboards for Next-Level Play

Get speedy response times, greater accuracy, and advanced customization options.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

As much as we’d like to believe the old adage about a carpenter and their tools, better equipment is a necessity if you want to take your gameplay to the next level. Just as a great gaming mouse ensures rocksteady aim, a proper gaming keyboard has quick, responsive keys to execute your movements precisely.

From strafing to crouching to placing items, not just any old keyboard will do. Dedicated gaming keyboards offer more comfort, precise control, and added functionality over our favorite ergonomic keyboards, making it easy to streamline abilities in MMOs, dodge bullets in online shooters, or move players around in strategy games.

The keyboards we recommend are highly rated by both reviewers and consumers, delivering top gaming performance with responsive touch and high customizability so you can dial in the perfect profile for each game.

For more great keyboards, check out our picks for the best gaming speakers, best gaming monitors, best gaming chairs, and best gaming desktops.

As Popular Mechanics’ resident consumer tech expert and a lifetime gaming enthusiast, I’ve tested some of the most popular gaming keyboards over the years. I prefer the snappiness of mechanical switches, but I’ve come around to membrane options for their quiet and fast keys.

This article reflects my own list of the best gaming keyboards that I created to narrow down my next keyboard purchase. Beyond our consumer tech experts' personal experience, we also researched reliable sources such as TechRadar, PC Mag, and PC Gamer, and read consumer reviews to select the top gaming keyboards. We’ve included a range of options to meet different budgets and preferences so you can find the one that’s right for you.

The Apex Pro has long led the pack thanks to its tunable actuation, and the third generation goes further. Its OmniPoint 3.0 magnetic switches give you 40 actuation levels per key, from a hair-trigger 0.1 mm to a deliberate 4.0 mm. You can set it shallow for fast play or deeper to cut down on typos.

The Gen 3 also adds three competitive features. Rapid Trigger resets a key the moment you let go. Rapid Tap snaps to your most recent key press so you can strafe and dodge faster. Protection Mode reduces accidental presses of neighboring keys. SteelSeries' QuickSet presets load pro-level settings automatically when your game launches, and the OLED screen lets you change actuation and profiles on the fly without opening software.

The tenkeyless layout leaves more room for your mouse. Quantum 2.0 Dual Wireless connects over lag-free 2.4GHz for gaming or Bluetooth for your other devices. Some owners say the battery life is only middling, and at about $300 it's a real investment. Still, few keyboards can match its speed and customization.

For an entry-level mechanical keyboard that won't break the bank, the Logitech G413 SE is a great pick. You won't get all the bells and whistles of more expensive models, but its tactile mechanical switches give each keystroke a satisfying bump. Six-key rollover anti-ghosting means even your most frantic key combinations register.

The SE also upgrades to PBT keycaps, which resist heat, wear, and the shiny fade that cheaper keycaps develop over time. Twelve function keys handle volume, play/pause, track skipping, lighting, and Windows lock. A brushed aluminum-magnesium alloy top case keeps flex to a minimum and gives the board a sleek look. If you'd rather have more desk space, Logitech also makes a tenkeyless version, the G413 TKL SE.

The G915 X TKL takes everything we loved about the original G915 TKL and refines it. At just 0.9 inches tall, it's one of the slimmest mechanical gaming keyboards around. Its brushed aluminum alloy plate also keeps flex to a minimum, so it's tougher than its size suggests.

Lightspeed wireless delivers lag-free play, and Bluetooth and wired modes let you switch between your gaming rig and your other devices. The tenkeyless layout drops the number pad, so your mouse has more room, while dedicated media and volume controls stay within reach. If you're heading to a tournament or just moving your setup to another room, the G915 X TKL is still the portable powerhouse to beat.

The ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless gives you nearly everything a full-size keyboard does, number pad included, in a body only about 1 cm wider than a typical 80 percent board. That leaves you more room for your mouse without giving up the keys you use for work.

Low-latency 2.4GHz wireless keeps gameplay lag-free. Bluetooth lets you pair up to three other devices, and you can plug in over USB-C when you need to. Battery life is the standout, with Asus rating it at up to 1,500 hours with the lighting off and about 90 hours with RGB on.

An aluminum alloy top plate, sound-dampening foam, and double-shot PBT keycaps give it a solid, refined feel. The hot-swappable board lets you swap in different switches whenever you want. A multifunction key and clickable roller handle volume, media, and lighting, and a padded magnetic wrist rest comes in the box for marathon sessions.

If you play MMOs or want shortcuts for streaming and editing, the BlackWidow V4 Pro has more programmable controls than almost any keyboard around. It has five dedicated macro keys down the left side, three more macro buttons along the edge of the chassis, and a multifunction Command Dial that can hold up to 100 custom modes. Razer's HyperShift adds a second layer to nearly every key, and the keyboard can save up to five profiles.

It's no slouch in-game, either. Full N-key rollover means every key registers even when you're mashing several at once, and an 8,000 Hz polling rate helps cut input delay. You can choose loud, satisfying Razer Green clicky switches or smooth Razer Yellow linear switches. Machined metal media keys and a volume roller sit in the top right corner, and an aluminum alloy top plate keeps the board sturdy.

The padded leatherette wrist rest snaps on magnetically and extends the keyboard's underglow, so the whole setup glows as one. It's big, so make sure you have the desk space, but if you want every command a single keypress away, the BlackWidow V4 Pro is the one to get.

If desk space is tight, or you want as much room as possible for your mouse, a 60 percent keyboard is the way to go. The Huntsman V3 Pro Mini trims the keyboard to the essentials without sacrificing features. Its analog optical switches let you set how far each key travels before it registers, so you can set it to shallow for hair-trigger movement or deeper to avoid accidental presses.

Rapid Trigger resets each key the moment you start to let go, so you can repeat inputs faster. Snap Tap prioritizes whichever direction you pressed most recently, making strafing quicker in shooters. The keyboard also has dual-purpose modifier keys that let one key do two jobs, which helps make up for the missing keys. Doubleshot PBT keycaps resist the shine that cheaper keycaps get over time.

The trade-off is that arrow keys, F-keys, and the number pad all move to a secondary layer, so expect a short adjustment period. For competitive players who want a small, fast keyboard, it's an excellent pick.

If you grew up with an original Xbox, this keyboard will feel instantly familiar. Its design is based on the console's Transparent Green Edition. RGB lighting glows through the jade-like translucent shell and double-layered keycaps, and the arrow keys are made of crystal-clear plastic. Taller, retro-style keycaps and a top-mount design finish the throwback look. It's officially licensed by Xbox, and the dedicated Xbox button opens the Windows Game Bar.

It also comes with 8BitDo's Dual Super Buttons, a pair of giant arcade-style buttons that plug into the keyboard. You can map them to a macro or any key without installing software, and up to four sets can connect at once. An aluminum plate keeps the 87-key layout sturdy, and the hot-swappable board lets you swap out the Kailh Jellyfish X switches later. A control panel at the top handles volume, connection mode, and button mapping with a simple turn and click.

It connects over 2.4GHz wireless, Bluetooth 5.0, or USB. The 4,000 mAh battery lasts up to 280 hours over 2.4GHz and 300 hours over Bluetooth. Despite the branding, it works only with Windows PCs and Android devices, not Xbox consoles. If you want a PC keyboard that stands out in your setup, though, it's hard to beat.

Most keyboards will plug into a console, but they won’t always work. HyperX lists the Alloy Origins 65 as compatible with PlayStation 5, PlayStation 4, Xbox Series X|S, and Xbox One. It's a wired keyboard, so there's no Bluetooth pairing or wireless receiver to troubleshoot.

The 65 percent layout is small enough to sit on your lap, but it keeps dedicated arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, Home, and Delete for moving through menus and stores. The full aluminum body is sturdy, and the double-shot PBT keycaps have secondary functions printed on their sides, so the shortcuts are easy to find.

HyperX's switches come in linear Red or tactile Aqua, are rated for 80 million keypresses, and actuate at 1.8 mm. N-key rollover registers every keypress, and per-key RGB lighting shines through the exposed switches. The NGENUITY software only runs on PC, so set up your macros and lighting there, then save them to one of the keyboard's three onboard profiles.

Most gaming keyboards clack loudly enough to bother everyone in the room. The K65 Plus Wireless is much quieter, with Corsair putting a layer of foam and a silicone pad inside the case to absorb vibration. Combined with factory-lubed MLX Red linear switches, that turns each keystroke into a low, muted thock instead of a sharp clack. It's quiet enough for late-night sessions in a shared apartment or for typing during voice calls without your coworkers hearing every key.

The switches are light and smooth, and the hot-swappable board lets you swap in silent switches if you want to make it even quieter. The 75 percent layout keeps dedicated arrow keys and a function row in a compact frame, and a knurled metal knob in the corner can be programmed for volume or other controls.

Connect over 2.4GHz wireless for gaming, Bluetooth for a work laptop, or USB-C for charging. Battery life reaches up to 266 hours with the lighting off. The plastic case and plain keycaps give it a less premium feel, and the RGB lighting doesn't shine through the legends. Still, if you want a quieter keyboard without giving up gaming performance, it's an excellent choice.

Short of building a mechanical keyboard with your own layout design and keycaps, purchasing a factory gaming keyboard gives you plenty of advanced customization options.

Beyond aesthetic choices like lighting, you can program key bindings to perform menu shortcuts with a single press. These streamlined commands help you better focus on the in-game action.

Outside of gaming, macro keys (programmable keys) can help you create productivity shortcuts in all your programs. If you often use video editing software to edit gameplay clips, you can assign actions to macro buttons to create content faster. This is especially handy if you plan to use your gaming keyboard for everyday tasks, too.

Beyond individual key settings, some gaming keyboards include keyboard profiles with specific key functions and lighting tailored to each game you play. For example, a Cyberpunk-themed profile might set your keyboard to a neon yellow glow with the Q button bound to a quick attack.

Most first-person shooters map the Q button to a special ability or cover, but with individualized profile bindings, you can program each button to do what you want. Some titles, such as Diablo III, can even use your keyboard’s RGB lighting to indicate when you cast a spell or when your character is low on health, increasing immersion.

With tons of keys and lighting options, your keyboard’s body size determines just how many extra buttons or light sections can fit.

Bigger, longer, and uncut, full-sized keyboards include every single key you'll see on a typical keyboard (and more) for access to extra action buttons, a number pad, and dedicated media keys. There's more room to spread out, but full keyboards are less portable—well worth the compromise if you'll use your keyboard to type for work or if you need plenty of command keys for RTS or MOBAs.

Tenkeyless boards axe the right-hand number pad for a tighter shape. The result is a compact keyboard (at least 20 percent smaller than a full-size model) that’s easy to move and leaves you with more space on your desk to operate your mouse. If you don’t have to work with data entry and don't mind losing extra inputs, a tenkeyless board transports with ease and offers an organic typing experience.

Ditching the number pad and F-keys, compact keyboards are limited to the alphanumeric zone. They’re still capable of comfortable typing, but if you often use F commands, you’ll have to assign a number key to use with the function key. Once you have your compact keyboard configured, it’s by far the easiest keyboard to wield, albeit with extra steps for pulling up shortcuts.

Streamlined for command efficiency, one-handed keyboards trim the fat of all characters on the right half of your keyboard. With dead keys gone and game inputs in reach of your left hand, you have more precision than any other keyboard type. You’re still going to need a daily keyboard, however, as this style is meant to supplement your main keyboard, not replace it.

Mechanical keyboards use three switch types for feedback: tactile (usually brown), clicky (usually blue), and linear (usually red).

Tactile switches provide a small bump and subdued clack to confirm registered keystrokes. They are the most popular because they offer the feedback of clicky switches with speed similar to linear switches.

Clicky switches have a higher actuation pressure requirement to reduce typos while writing, a big bump for validation, and a signature loud click that’s music to any typist’s ears but a bane to coworkers’ and housemates’.

Linear speed switches are great for gaming because they’re smooth, offer minimal resistance, and have none of the noise of a brown or blue switch. People often bottom out on these red or silver keys since there’s no clear indication you’ve triggered their actuation point. Linear keys fire off on all cylinders, but they’re not so great for typing because their zippiness can cause typos.

Membrane keys aren’t mechanical and rely on a single mechanism under the keys to register presses. Some people complain that membrane inputs feel mushy, but they last longer than mechanical keys and cost much less because they don’t have an intricate system of moving parts.

It can be tempting to go for a cheap gaming keyboard and save the extra cash for a better gaming PC or monitor, but higher-quality mechanical switches—along with more durable materials like aluminum—can improve performance, provide a sturdier base, and increase reaction speed.
