#6336. Highly Specific Observations While Scouting for the 2026 Eater Awards

The great dishes, gorgeous restaurants, and quirky cocktails that commanded our attention, even if they didn’t make the big list

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The past year has been one of “Great Chickenings” and fine dining flips, British food invasions and restaurants whose dining rooms feel like living rooms, vibrant global steakhouses and unserious Y2K food. Among the slate of our 2026 Eater Award winners — which also brought undeniable new chef talent, core-memory-forming dishes, and groundbreaking bakeries and bars — are the places we could not stop thinking about for highly specific reasons. While this crop of restaurants and bars did not make the ultimate cut for the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, they commanded enough attention during our expansive scouting and research months to deserve acknowledgment. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

Cabbage is having its moment. From a star turn on the Sandy Liang runway as a ruffled bag to a hand-painted Bordallo Pinheiro dinner set and a declaration from Vogue that the leafy green has gone “chic,” the cruciferous vegetable is 2026’s “it” girl. The cult of the cabbage has made its way to Monte’s in Montecito, a cozy Korean American bistro where cone cabbage gets coal-roasted and kissed with salty smoked shiitake XO, an umami-heavy spin on the Hong Kong-born sauce. The fall-apart-tender cabbage beds on creamy tofu puree, the whole thing studded with hazelnuts that bring out the vegetable’s innate sweetness. Preparations like the one at Monte’s make it feel as though cabbage isn’t just this year’s distinguished vegetable — its dominance is here to stay. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

Maybe it was the Negroni, the Old Fashioned, and the gingery mezcal-laced Missed Opportunity. Perhaps it was the jetlag (who can say for sure?), but the bathroom at Bobo — the Filipino bar attached to Muhajir in Chicago’s Lincoln Park — left a lasting impression on me. In a world that’s fully embraced the bathroom selfie, Bobo has answered the call with refractory horizontal-mirrored panel walls and colored light that shifts from reds to greens, turning this lavatory into a mesmerizing disco ball. It’s a fitting touch that matches chef Jacob Dela Cruz’s vision for a red-light district-esque tropical hideaway. — Brenna Houck, Eater editorial manager

In a world of outrageous martinis, the one at Greenpoint Malaysian restaurant Kelang earns its playful name. The Dirty Fish riffs on a Vesper with gin, vodka, dry vermouth, and, saliently, fish sauce, which levels up the drink’s savoriness in every way. The pungent condiment mimics olive brine, delivering a salty taste of the sea to the already strong drink, which then gets garnished with wavy scallions and a long sliver of aromatic ginger. The cocktail showcases owner Chris Low’s background as a Malaysian kid who grew up in New York. It’s simply presented — a cloudy drink in a stemmed coupe glass with those gloating garnishes — and pairs best with that fluffy paratha served over creamy and spicy dal. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

Gone may be the days of business power lunches at Wolfgang Puck’s Spago or Grill on the Alley that required a suit and tie. In their place, a new arrangement has emerged — the low-key power lunch. There may be no better place for the midday meal masquerading as a meeting right now than at Little Fish in Melrose Hill, the first full-service restaurant from the former pop-up-turned-fish sandwich window. The light-filled dining room hums during daytime with flexibly scheduled creatives and well-dressed parents toting young children, all adults in the room sipping wine picked by sommelier Kae Whalen. On the menu, a tuna melt from maverick chefs and owners Anna Sonenshein and Niki Vahle will convert even nonbelievers, especially when paired with peppery fries dunked in horseradish aioli. Of course, there is the calling card fried fish sandwich, but smarter diners go for the beach sandwich layered with guindilla peppers and soy-cured mussels and a bay leaf chip stracciatella flecked with chocolate chips. Melrose Hill and its confluence of independent restaurants has morphed into a miniature walkable neighborhood — the perfect place to see and be seen. And what’s more low-key power lunch than that? — RR

Historically, California is a gold mine of kitsch restaurants, from Clifton’s Republic to the pillowy pink dining room at the Madonna Inn. Night Hawk is the next jewel in that camp crown; the Greek-influenced San Diego restaurant is an anchor of Coronado Island’s hypermaximalist new Baby Grand hotel and beckons diners into a lush, faux-rock-filled outdoor dining room with pink clamshell chairs, waterfalls, and cocktails that have names like the Adonis in Bloom and Spanakopita Punch. In short: Tony Duquette by way of an acid tab. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

British food hit a fever pitch nationally this year as Americans awakened to the allure of meat pies and mushy peas. But if any restaurant truly dispelled notions of the country’s cuisine as dull or bland, it was Ambassadors Clubhouse, with its extensive menu of Punjabi showstoppers such as seven-layer, aloo-filed, Amritsari-style samosas; butter chicken in the form of lollipop-like chops with a heady char; and matka Beliram lamb, its crimson oil heralding intense flavor. In opulent, velvet-adorned surroundings that feel like a hideaway from the city, this luxe London import deliciously makes the case that Indian food is as essential to British cuisine as fish and chips. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

The most beautiful new restaurant in California is tucked into a shopping center in Montecito’s tony upper village. Little Mountain, which opened in November 2025 under chef Diego Moya, gives more to the scene than just a locavore menu that leans into live-fire cooking — it brings a bona fide, Architectural Digest-worthy destination that I would get married (and remarried) in. It may be hard to decide which room to sit in should you land a reservation in time: the comfortable dining room with gold-veil natural lighting and plush caramel booths and banquettes; the larger-party table that foregrounds an open kitchen and its centerpiece hearth; the dim, dark bar that may be the sexiest sliver of drinking den on the Central Coast; the covered patio that leads into a monarchial private dining area; or the outdoor patio that evokes dining in a home garden. Anywhere you sit, you can’t go wrong, especially as the food starts landing in front of you. — NF

Chef Theo Adley opened Heretík last spring, and it has brought a breath of fresh, San Sebastián-esque sea breeze air into the Denver dining scene. The French- and Basque-leaning restaurant serves an endless summer menu of dishes like Santa Barbara uni, a playful pan con tomate martini, and scallops à la plancha with bearnaise and seaweed. The menu’s coastal Euro allure gets amplified by its interior design choices, which sprinkle in vintage furniture and tapered, wax drip-laden candles — but with a name like Heretík, you know that all of that romance is going to come with a healthy dose of cheek. — FK

Chickens, you can’t take credit for this one: The British-inspired pub Dean’s proved that bigger is not always better with its take on a Scotch egg, which employs quail eggs instead of the typical chicken ones. In larger Scotch eggs, what appears in each bite can be inconsistent. But the result of the shrunken-down approach here is a reliably favorable ratio of meat to egg, in which each bite at once encompasses crunchy breading, tender meat filling, runny yolk, and just enough still-bouncy egg white. It’s as nonnegotiable at Dean’s as a pint of Guinness. — BM

Ladyfish in Portland, Maine, has been clear about one thing since the beginning: “A summer fling,” the restaurant declared when it announced its May 2026 arrival. Jordan and Marisa Rubin of Portland sushi spot Mr. Tuna convinced chef Christine Lau to relocate from New York City to helm the seasonal seafood pop-up. Lau, whose resume includes Japanese-Italian and Chino Latino restaurants, brings her distinctive flair to classic Maine ingredients for dishes like scallops in a blanket with fried milk bread and the showstopping twin lobster mountain served with fries, rice cakes, and dan dan au poivre sauce. True to its word, the restaurant closed at the end of October. Here’s hoping the return of next year’s summertime crowds also brings back this match made in seafood heaven. — Stephanie Wu, editor in chief

Los Angeles-born chef Ray Garcia opened Broken Spanish Comedor in Culver City in late 2025, years after his groundbreaking Mexican fine dining restaurant, Broken Spanish, and more casual B.S. Taqueria closed in Downtown Los Angeles. Garcia’s contribution to Alta California cuisine, rooted in Mexican cooking told through a California lens, remains one of the most distinct of this generation of restaurants. Still, he manages to surprise both longtime fans and newcomers to his work: The Comedor, whose name nods to the Indigenous homestyle restaurant tradition in Mexico, feels fresh in its A-frame home. It’s not uncommon for locals and those working in Los Angeles hospitality to stop in for a meal of crispy, crown-whorled chicharron or quesillo-threaded refried lentils; a classics-leaning drinks menu (cócteles, cervezas, vino) keeps the room humming happily. In a year brimming with big restaurant comebacks (see also: Venice’s resurrected Tasting Kitchen and Keith Corbin’s reframed Alta Adams), it feels good to have an Angeleno chef like Ray Garcia capture our collective imagination again. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

If ever there was a destination in need of effective hangover cures, it’s New Orleans. While I was totally ready to rally after a two-bar, two-restaurant evening the night before (I am, of course, a professional), I also wasn’t mad about consuming something fortifying at Casimiro, the charming all-day cafe from award-winning Acamaya chef Ana Castro, the next morning. The restaurant delivered: textbook chilaquiles, impossibly fluffy conchas, crispy pescaditos, and one of the best tortas I’ve ever had. If hair of the dog is in your future in the City That Always Drinks, go with the well-balanced Cynar daiquiri to finish. — Missy Frederick, dining editorial director

The weirdest thing I ate on a pastry this year was “lettuce cream” lacquered onto the BLT Danish at Dahlia in Minneapolis. The chartreuse-colored cream anchored a slice of late-August tomato and dollops of bacon jam atop persistently crisp laminated dough. One bite was enough to make me think, This should be more of a thing. You wouldn’t know at first glance that this bakery, tucked into an office complex, turns out treats of this caliber: jam-filled croissants with speculoos crumble, unassumingly perfect English muffins, plush milk bread and fluffy focaccia for sandwiches. This kind of out-of-the-box baking makes eating pastries right now so fun. — BM

#6335. Archaeologists Uncover 3,800-Year-Old Burial Mystery on Spain’s Coast

A burial ground on Spain’s southern coast suggests ancient communities may have continued building massive shared tombs during the Bronze Age, rather than simply reusing older monuments.

A 3,800-year-old burial mystery on Spain’s southern coast is challenging what archaeologists thought they knew about prehistoric burial traditions.

At a time when communities across the Iberian Peninsula were abandoning massive communal tombs in favor of smaller, individual graves, people near the Strait of Gibraltar appear to have continued burying their dead together. Even more puzzling, the stone monuments they used may have been newly constructed rather than inherited from earlier generations.

The discovery comes from the Trafalgar necropolis, where archaeologists investigated two collective tombs containing the remains of multiple individuals.

Radiocarbon dating of 16 individuals places the use of these tombs between 1875 and 1625 BC, making them among the latest known examples of collective megalithic burial in Iberia.

But the age of the human remains is only part of the mystery. Archaeologists also found no evidence of earlier occupation at the site, raising the possibility that the monuments themselves were constructed during the Bronze Age, when such building traditions were thought to be fading.

The study, published November 11, 2026, in the open-access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz in Spain and colleagues.

Determining when a tomb was used is not the same as establishing when it was built. Elsewhere in Iberia, Bronze Age communities sometimes buried their dead inside monuments dating back to the Copper Age, making it difficult to distinguish new construction from the reuse of older structures.

Trafalgar may represent an important exception. The absence of evidence for an earlier burial ground suggests the cemetery could have been established in the early second millennium BC. However, additional dating methods are needed to determine when the monuments were originally constructed.

The authors explain, “The Trafalgar megalithic necropolis has revealed a highly significant finding. During the Bronze Age, an entirely new funerary space was constructed in a landscape dominated by the sea. We propose this hypothesis based on the absence of archaeological evidence for earlier occupation in the surrounding area. Until now, the evidence available for this period has primarily pointed to the reuse of megalithic monuments built during the Copper Age. This discovery offers a new perspective on funerary practices during this period and would demonstrate that new monumental burial spaces continued to be constructed.”

The excavations also uncovered grave goods, including gold and copper earrings, silver beads, and an ivory comb, offering additional clues about the people buried at the site.

If further research confirms that the monuments were newly built during the Bronze Age, Trafalgar would provide rare evidence that monumental communal burial traditions survived longer than previously recognized.

Researchers believe additional tombs may remain undiscovered, potentially offering further insight into ancient Iberian burial traditions. However, strong coastal winds and shifting sands threaten to bury the site beneath the dunes again, making continued preservation essential for future excavations.

Reference: “The last builders of megaliths in the South of the Iberian peninsula? The Bronze Age necropolis of Trafalgar (Barbate, Cádiz, Spain)” by Eduardo Vijande-Vila, Serafín Becerra-Martín, Berta Morell-Rovira, Marta Díaz-Zorita Bonilla, Eduardo Molina-Piernas, Alejandro Muñoz-Muñoz, Adolfo Moreno-Márquez, Pablo González-Fernández, Salvador Domínguez-Bella, María Leticia Gómez-Sánchez, Diego Salvador Fernández-Sánchez, José Luis Ramírez-Amador, José María Corona-Borrego, María Carmona-Gil, Jesús Corrales Díaz and Juan Jesús Cantillo-Duarte, 11 November 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0359220

This research was supported by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the Regional Government of Andalusia, the European Union’s Complementary Marine Sciences Plan (MEDUSA project), and CEIMAR’s 2021 and 2022 Young Researchers Research Projects programs.

A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a new theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

Built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

Magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?"

"Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso said. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself."

Comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the new study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso said. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study shows that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require new physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso said.

"Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still new insights to be gained from those same equations."

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso said. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically."

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate."

Comisso, L., & Asenjo, F. A. (2026). Reconnection of gravitational fields. Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

#6333. Dense Galaxy Clusters Foster Mechanisms That Throttle Star Formation

Star-forming regions are plentiful in the Milky Way, and they're some of the most visually glorious sights in the galaxy. In these regions, the powerful light from massive young stars shapes and energizes gas into glowing arrangements of filaments and billowing clouds. Astronomers study these intently, and astrophotographers share their enthusiasm.

One of the most well-known star forming regions is the stunning Orion Nebula, captured in all its glory by space telescopes like the Hubble and the JWST, and by astrophotographers on the ground. Most of us have seen some of these images, even if only in passing.

Despite the presence of so many star-forming regions, the Milky Way only forms about 6 or 7 new stars every year. This pales in comparison with the cosmos' peak star formation rate about 10 billion years ago. That period of time is called the Cosmic Noon, and during that epoch, star formation was as much as 30 times greater than it is today, all across the Universe, including in the Milky Way.

The star formation rate has slowed precipitously, and today it's dropped by about 97%. What caused this drop in star formation? Stars form from cold, dense gas, so something must have happened to the gas.

Astronomers know that environmental effects play a leading role in diminishing gas supplies and slowing star formation, both inside galaxies and between galaxies in galaxy groups. Stellar winds can blow gas away, and astrophysical jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can heat gas and disperse it. There are other types of disruptions, like gas stripping via galaxy mergers, and galaxy deformations from the same mergers. Sometimes galaxies can merge and gas can be spread out into space in tidal tails. In other cases, galactic star-forming gas is heated through interactions with the much hotter intergalactic medium, or even stripped away by these encounters.

Since most galaxies exist in galaxy groups, researchers try to understand the drop in star formation in these environments. But measurements of the gas supply in galaxy groups are rare.

New research to be published in Astronomy and Astrophysics measured how the supply of molecular gas, the raw material of star formation, is shaped by a galaxy's wider environment in dense galaxy clusters. It's titled "Probing the molecular gas content of galaxies in an over-dense group at z~0.7: A test case for environmental quenching," and the lead author is Jonathan Freundlich. Freundlich is an astrophysicist at the University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory (ObAS). The work is focused on a distant galaxy group called COSMOS-Gr30.

This image shows a dense region of the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group about 6.5 billion light-years away from Earth. The observations were made using the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope. The image was the ESO's Picture of the Week on the 13th of November 2017. Image Credit: ESO/T. Contini (IRAP, Toulouse), B. Epinat (LAM, Marseille)

When astronomers want to probe molecular hydrogen (H2), the raw stuff of star formation, they face an obstacle. Despite being by far the most abundant molecule in the interstellar medium and the primary ingredient in the giant molecular clouds (GMCs) where stars form, H2 is virtually undetectable in radio observations. Since star formation needs cold gas, radio is the way to observe it. Astronomers make us of the fact that carbon monoxide (CO) is the second most abundant component of GMCs, and observe it as a proxy for H2. In particular, they measure what are called CO(2-1) emissions, which appear when CO drops its energy state and releases a photon with radio levels of energy. Then they rely on a standard conversion factor between H2 and CO to turn CO observations into H2 observations.

That's what they did in this research that focuses on COSMOS-Gr30, an exceptionally dense group of galaxies.

"We investigated the impact of group environment on molecular gas reservoirs at an intermediate redshift by observing the CO(2-1) emission from the galaxy group COSMOS-Gr30 at zâ¼0.7 with the Institut de Radioastronomie Millimetrique (IRAM) NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) and 30m telescope," the authors write. This is a very dense environment where massive cosmic filaments intersect and host a large structure of ionized gas that's about 100 billion square light years in size.

This is the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group, located about 7 billion light years away, as seen with the JWST. The contours show the structure of diffuse ionized gas in between the group's member galaxies, as observed with the Multi-Unit Spectral Explorer instrument on the ESO's Very Large Telescope. Image Credits: Casey et al. 2023, Epinat et al. 2018, 2024, Freundlich et al. 2026.

The researchers measured the gas in the interstellar medium (ISM) inside of the galaxies as well as the gas in the intergalactic medium (IGM) between the galaxies. These simultaneous measurements generated a more comprehensive look at star-forming gas and its availability in dense galaxy cluster environments. It revealed mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in dense clusters.

"Deep MUSE (Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer) observations reveal a large, massive structure of ionized gas surrounding eight galaxies of the group, including one active galactic nucleus (AGN) host," the authors write. "This gas is not pristine and was likely expelled from the galaxies through both internal processes, such as star formation and AGN outflows, and external processes in the dense environment, such as ram pressure stripping and tidal interactions."

The results also show that less than one-third of the gas displaced from COSMOS-Gr30's member galaxies and moved into the diffuse structure is cold enough to form stars.

The researchers found that galaxies in this dense environment have only about 20% to 40% of the molecular gas found in typical main-sequence galaxies. Main-sequence galaxies are benchmark galaxies that form stars at a steady, typical rate.

Astronomers have studied molecular gas and its availability for star formation inside galaxies before, and they've done it for the intergalactic medium, too. But this work takes it a step further by characterizing gas availability in dense cluster environments. The research "... highlights the importance of simultaneously probing gas reservoirs within galaxies and the surrounding intragroup medium to capture environmental quenching in action," the authors explain.

"In the case of CGr30, the depletion of molecular gas within galaxies, combined with the presence of an extended gas structure, provides a consistent picture of environmental quenching," the researchers write.

This is the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) radio interferometer, located in the Hautes-Alpes at an altitude of 2550m. It has 12x15m radio dishes, and was used in this work to observe CO emissions in the galaxies of the COSMOS-Gr30 group. Image Credit: IRAM-gre via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

They do state a caveat with their results, and that regards some of the uncertainties in their work, including the star-formation rate (SFR) and how accurate the CO observations are as a proxy for molecular hydrogen.

"Although the uncertainties are significant, this suggests that environmental processes efficiently deplete molecular gas reservoirs in the galaxies of this group," the authors write.

More observations of COSMOS-Gr30 will address these uncertainties, and ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, will provide important observations. It's the most powerful radio antenna array in the world, more powerful than NOEMA used in this work. It has 66 high-precision 12 meter antennas that can collectively create a baseline up to 16 km wide. It can zoom into regions like COSMOS-Gr30 to uncover unseen detail.

"Furthermore, more precise SFR measurements are necessary to decrease the uncertainties, and larger samples of target galaxies in groups will allow us to assess group-to-group variance," the authors conclude.

#6332. A Strange Liquid Is Helping Scientists Overcome a Major Barrier in Nanotechnology

By filling the tiny pores of fragile materials with an unusual liquid, scientists have found a way to create intricate patterns without destroying their structures.

Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) contain networks of tiny pores that can trap gases, capture pollutants, and support chemical reactions. These properties make them attractive for advanced sensors and electronic devices, but their fragile structures are easily damaged by the processes used to manufacture such devices. Researchers in Japan have now developed a way to carve precise patterns into these materials at room temperature without causing the extensive structural damage normally associated with the process.

The technique, developed at Tokyo University of Science (TUS), involves filling the pores of MOFs with an ionic liquid before exposing them to a focused ion beam. In experiments, the liquid strengthened a copper-based MOF and substantially reduced damage, allowing researchers to produce intricate features only a few hundred nanometers wide.

The origins of MOFs trace back to 1974, when University of Melbourne chemistry professor Richard Robson began exploring whether molecules and chemical bonds could replace the wooden balls and metal rods used in structural models. His experiments with copper ions connected by four-armed organic molecules helped establish the foundations of a new class of porous materials. Today, approximately 100,000 MOFs are known, with potential applications ranging from gas storage and chemical separation to pollution control.

Turning these materials into functional devices requires precise fabrication, often involving dry etching, which removes material using energetic particles such as ions. Unfortunately, ion beams can disrupt the delicate crystalline frameworks and produce unwanted cavities. Cryogenic etching has offered a way to limit this damage, but it requires specialized cooling equipment and liquid nitrogen.

Led by Assistant Professor Yumeng Zheng and Professor Kentaro Kinoshita from TUS’s Department of Applied Physics, the researchers investigated whether ionic liquids could make MOFs more resistant to ion beam damage. Their approach builds on earlier findings from Kinoshita’s team showing that these liquids can improve the mechanical stability of MOFs. The study was scheduled for publication in Communications Materials.

The team tested four imidazolium-based ionic liquids in Cu3BTC2, a copper-based MOF containing benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid (BTC). Each liquid occupied approximately 50% to 60% of the material’s pore volume. The researchers then used a focused gallium ion beam to etch patterns into the samples at room temperature.

Untreated MOFs suffered substantial structural damage, including the formation of large cavities. Samples containing ionic liquids showed considerably less visible microstructural damage under the same conditions. The researchers successfully etched a square measuring 5 × 5 micrometers (approximately 0.0002 × 0.0002 inches), a pillar, and a Chinese character with lines just 130 to 300 nanometers (about 5 to 12 millionths of an inch) wide.

“In this study, we developed a simple method for room-temperature dry etching of this fragile class of materials. By infiltrating MOFs with ionic liquids, their mechanical stability is greatly improved, and the damage from electron and ion beams is reduced, achieving harmless ion beam etching,” says Dr. Zheng.

The researchers propose that ionic liquids protect MOFs through a combination of thermal and electrical effects. The liquids may absorb heat generated during ion bombardment, reducing local temperature changes, while their mobile ions could help redistribute accumulated electrical charge and screen local electric fields. These mechanisms remain proposed explanations rather than directly established causes of the reduced damage.

Additional measurements confirmed that all four ionic liquid treatments increased the MOF’s hardness without substantially changing its stiffness. Thermal analysis also showed that treated samples decomposed at higher temperatures than untreated material, indicating improved thermal stability.

Although the experiments focused on a single copper-based MOF, the researchers believe the approach could potentially work with other frameworks. If its effectiveness extends to additional materials, room-temperature etching could provide a more accessible route to manufacturing MOF-based devices without the cooling requirements of cryogenic processing.

“We can foresee applications in high-sensitivity sensors, separation and analysis devices, and catalytic devices. This technology has the potential to become a foundational technology for bridging the exceptional material functionalities of MOFs with their use in practical devices,” says Prof. Kinoshita.

Reference: “Ionic-liquid-assisted room-temperature dry etching of metal–organic frameworks” by Yumeng Zheng, Momoka Muraoka, Koki Egawa and Kentaro Kinoshita, 10 November 2026, Communications Materials. DOI: 10.1038/s43246-026-01396-3

This work was partly supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 26K00987.

#6331. LOFAR Takes the Deepest Image of the Low-Frequency Radio Sky to Date

An international team led by researchers from Leiden University has produced the deepest and most detailed view of low-frequency radio galaxies in the Universe. Using the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), the team observed ELAIS-N1 (European Large-Area ISO Survey-North 1), a region of the northern sky that contains very little galactic dust, gas, or stars. This makes the field highly favorable for deep multi-wavelength studies that probe the distant Universe.

For years, astronomers at the LOFAR observatory have been observing ELAIS-N1 to map low-frequency radio sources. The latest image has twenty times the resolution of the previous LOFAR image, which was made possible through advances in modern interferometry - a technique where light from multiple telescopes is combined to produce a single clearer image. The full image features 63,000 radio sources, including quasars and star-forming galaxies.

This new view of the low-frequency radio sky comes from 200 hours of observation and amounts to 400 terabytes of data in an 8-billion-pixel image. A few years ago, processing this amount of data from radio telescopes at such high resolution was impossible. But thanks to the Spider data-processing platform developed by researchers from the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy (ASTRON) and their collaborators, and other improvements in calibration and data-reduction methods, processing times have been reduced by a factor of ten.

The core of the LOFAR radio telescope array near Exloo, Netherlands. Credit: LOFAR/ASTRON

"The entire dataset could be processed on Spider, the high-performance data processing platform hosted at SURF in the Netherlands, in just a few months," said Jurjen de Jong, a postdoctoral researcher at Leiden Observatory and ASTRON (who led the research). LOFAR's high sensitivity also revealed numerous filaments surrounding the radio galaxies, especially near galaxy clusters, as well as their morphology and spectral characteristics. Resolving these structures required combining high-resolution and low-frequency observations made possible by LOFAR.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), also known as quasars, are particularly dominant in the image - the bright centers of galaxies powered by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their accretion disks. AGNs are also known to produce relativistic jets of superheated gas and dust that emanate from the black holes' polar regions and emit considerable radiation themselves. These structures are something LOFAR is especially well suited to observe, given its sensitivity to extended low-frequency radio emissions.

In previous, lower-resolution surveys, these distant galaxies and their relativistic jets would appear as little more than featureless blobs, making it difficult to distinguish individual galaxies from clusters. The high-resolution LOFAR data, in contrast, allow scientists to discern individual radio sources and massive jets, which can be traced in detail. This new view of the cosmos provides scientists with new opportunities to study how these jets interact with their environment and evolve over cosmic time.

The other major population in the image is the small, young galaxies that are still experiencing high rates of star formation. Because radio waves can pass through gas and dust that obscure the visible and infrared light of star formation, radio observatories provide a clear view of the processes taking place within these galaxies. This allows astronomers to study how galaxies that existed in the early Universe evolved into the older, larger spiral and elliptical galaxies we see in the local Universe.

The giant LOFAR radio telescope took this picture of the black holes at the heart of the active galaxy Cygnus A. Credit: J. McKean and M. Wise/ASTRON

According to the research team, this work demonstrates the potential of the upgraded LOFAR2.0 telescope, which ASTRON is currently working on with its European partners. The upgrades will enable wider, higher-resolution images, allowing LOFAR to remain competitive with next-generation radio telescopes like the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), which will combine the MeerKAT array in South Africa and the Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara (Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory) in Australia.

The data will be especially useful when combined with images of the same patch of sky taken by other telescopes at other wavelengths. This includes optical, infrared, and X-ray observations, from which astronomers can determine properties like the distance and mass of each radio source.

#6330. The 9 Best TVs for Next-Level Home Entertainment

We thoroughly scrutinized and reviewed the most impressive TVs available today—and several of our picks are surprisingly affordable.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In 2026, the best TVs deliver a leap forward in picture quality and come packed with convenient extra features like built-in streaming apps, high refresh rates to improve your gaming experience, and compatibility with your go-to virtual assistant, to name a few.

The TV market is chock-full of great models across the entire price spectrum, so whether you're looking for a budget-friendly upgrade or a home alternative to your local movie theater, there are a lot of great options. I've been testing TVs all year, and with the holiday season closer than it would seem, it's a good time to start shopping for your next big screen.

If you know what kind of TV you're looking for, check out our detailed guides on the Best OLED TVs, 4K TVs, and Outdoor TVs.

My journey testing TVs began almost a decade ago, so I’ve experienced the product category’s evolution practically in real time. For this guide, I handpicked sets from leading brands like Hisense, LG, Samsung, and TCL, among others. I zeroed in on futureproof products at various price points that offer amazing picture quality and handy onboard features to sustain you for years after making the big-ticket purchase.

A follow-up to one of my favorite TVs of 2025, the TCL QM8L builds on the successful design of the QM8K with a new, super-bright super quantum-dot (SQD) mini-LED panel. I was hesitant to recommend the 2026 at launch because of its price tag, but with prices now well below $2,000 for both the 65-inch and 75-inch models, it’s a lot easier to say that this set is the best bang for your buck if you’re looking for a mini-LED that’s bright enough to maintain its best image quality in dynamic lighting.

In addition to the new tech enhancing both brightness and color reproduction, upgraded local dimming leads to better HDR with less haloing, for a sharper picture in high-contrast scenes. You get a beautiful picture with vivid-yet-accurate colors and deep contrast.

The TCL QM8L also offers excellent viewing angles, so long as direct light reflections literally aren’t in the picture. When the TV is facing a window or a lamp, its picture quality diminishes, especially when displaying dark scenes. This isn’t a dealbreaker, though I’d be super mindful about light sources when placing the set.

On the audio front, the TCL QM8L delivers an impressively powerful experience via a sophisticated speaker setup tuned by the luxury audio experts at Bang & Olufsen. The bespoke B&O audio customization interface is as impressive as its sound output.

LG has long been synonymous with top-tier OLED TVs, and the C6 Series is a great upgrade, especially now that its price has dropped significantly since its debut a few months ago. With millions of individually backlit pixels, its OLED display panel produces vivid colors, infinite contrast, and, thanks to LG’s proprietary evo technology, strong brightness. As a cinema buff, I also appreciated the TV's Filmmaker Mode, which removed picture-quality enhancements to deliver a viewing experience as the movie director intended.

The brightness-boosting display technology lets the LG C6 deliver an even more immersive HDR viewing experience in any setting, even in rooms with bright ambient light. Curiously, the larger 77-inch and 83-inch versions pack an upgraded Tandem OLED display, which boosts brightness to dramatically improve performance in brightly lit spaces.

Another significant reason to consider the LG C6 Series is that it is a gaming powerhouse, thanks in part to support for both Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium variable refresh rate standards, which will help games run smoothly on both consoles and PC.

What’s more, the TV’s feature-rich webOS platform offers access to Nvidia GeForce NOW and Xbox cloud gaming, so all you need is an external controller to enjoy high-resolution gameplay with smooth refresh rates.

The LG C6 also has a beautiful design, a capable speaker system for its form factor, and support for all leading smart home connectivity standards. Unlike its competition, this 4K TV comes in multiple screen sizes, from compact 42- and 48-inch models to larger 77- and 83-inch options.

This more budget-friendly cousin of the QM8L features many of my top mini-LED picks’ best new features, including SQD display technology, but costs much less, dropping below $1,000 in many sizes. While it does not have the tools to produce quite as bright or sharp a picture as my top pick, it’s easily the best TV I’ve seen for less than $1,000.

Like many of TCL’s best TVs, the QM7L has an elegant design with ultra-slim screen bezels and a Bang & Olufsen-tuned speaker system. The TV is available with a screen up to 98 inches. The latter currently costs less than $3,000, which is an incredible bargain given its size and picture quality.

The TCL QM6K 4K TV is the best for upgraders on a tight budget. Priced below $500 for a version with a 55-inch screen, this TV offers a no-nonsense design with a slim display bezel, impressive picture quality for the money, and a feature-packed platform with seamless smart home integration.

Experiencing the TCL QM6K genuinely made me feel like I was viewing a 4K TV from a higher price tier. Its bright QD-Mini LED display easily bests similarly priced big-name competitors by producing stellar peak brightness, rich colors, and deep contrast via hundreds of local dimming zones. The introduction of a mini-LED panel made the newcomer's picture quality a massive leap forward over its predecessor's.

Because its display has a 144-Hz native refresh rate, the TCL QM6K can deliver a high-quality gaming experience with a PS5 or Xbox Series X. Equipped with HDMI 2.1, the TV supports variable refresh rate gameplay at up to a brisk 288 Hz.

The Hisense UR9 is among the first TVs in a large 2026 wave of RGB mini- and micro-LED TVs, and the best one we’ve tested to date for the average TV watcher. RGB TVs use separate red, green, and blue light diodes rather than a uniform light source, which generates deep contrast and vivid colors that are comparable to an OLED TV, while maintaining a higher peak brightness. Combined with a legion of local dimming zones to maximize high-dynamic range, and the UR9 feels like a do-it-all option, and doesn’t cost quite as much as the alternatives out there from brands like Samsung and Sony.That brightness, combined with Hisense’s “obsidian” anti-glare coating, makes the UR9 vastly better at managing exposure to direct light sources (e.g., windows, lamps) than a standard mini-LED TV. That’s great if you plan to put this TV in a living room with lots of windows, and might have to contend with sunlight washing out the screen from time to time.In a manner befitting its premium price category, the Hisense UR9 also features a rich set of wired and wireless connectivity features, as well as a capable Dolby Atmos speaker system. The latter has been tuned by experts from the luxury French audio brand Devialet. The U9 series took a year off in 2025, but it’s been a favorite of mine in the past. I’m happy to see this colorful glow-up bring it back to top form.

The TCL X11L is the first major TV launch of 2026 and creates a new apex for high fidelity among the largest of at-home screens. It boasts a luxurious design, exceptional picture quality, and immersive sound tuned by Bang & Olufsen. It's incredibly expensive, starting at nearly $7,000 for a 75-inch screen, but you're getting a genuinely cutting-edge set that sets a new benchmark for the entire product category.

What's new and exciting here is the X11L's SQD mini-LED panel, which combines the quantum dot layer found in QLED and QD-OLED TVs with Mini-LED technology to create dynamic lighting across the TV. Combined with incredible brightness—up to 10,000 nits—the so-called "Super Quantum Dot" achieves contrast and color depth that, at least to my eye, looks on par or possibly even better than an OLED screen.

It has small flaws, like a lack of anti-glare coating, but this is a remarkable TV and the model I would recommend if you're looking for a technological centerpiece to put at the center of a large home theater. And I emphasize large, because it only comes in three "XXL" sizes: 75 inches, 85 inches, and 98 inches.

Developed in-house by Roku, the 2025 Pro Series TV is unsurprisingly the best to run the platform and an equally excellent upgrade for first-time users and longtime faithful. It is capable of delivering excellent picture quality and top-notch sound for its form factor. And since it runs a platform that has been a longtime favorite among consumers, it's easy to use, even for first-time smart TV users.

The mini-LED display panel of the Roku Pro Series TV produces vibrant colors and deep contrast, courtesy of multiple local dimming zones. I like that the product has a setting dubbed Roku Smart Picture Max, which can optimize any content for its screen, saving time digging through settings menus.

Another significant reason to consider this TV is its refined design and clever cable management setup, featuring integrated Velcro straps. The handy bits make it ideal for wall mounting. Another thing that impressed me was the option to adjust the height of its stand without the need to use a screwdriver.

Roku’s backlit remote with rechargeable battery is another major product draw, as it’s intuitive and easy to locate if lost. The TV has a button for locating the essential accessory, and I reckon it’ll be a lifesaver for many.

You can choose from 55-, 65-, and 75-inch versions of the Roku Pro Series. Similarly priced rivals from Hisense and TCL offer higher peak brightness and deeper contrast, but the refined design and intuitive platform make Roku’s product worth considering.

The Samsung S95H OLED TV is the brand’s flagship OLED TV, and the best high-end model I’ve tested this year. It delivers a consistently beautiful viewing experience, with high peak brightness, vibrant colors, and infinite contrast. Its AI-powered upscaling tech even elevates low-resolution content, raising the bar on everything you watch.

The S95H stands out compared to many of the top OLEDs right now because of its high brightness, which makes colors pop and allows it to function well in brightly lit spaces. With Samsung’s anti-reflective coating on the display, it even looks good in direct sunlight. That’s a rare feat for any TV, but especially remarkable for an OLED panel.

And while it’s a secondary concern, I love how the physical TV looks. Its metal frame stands out in a room (in a good way). This set looks like a piece of art and is worth showing off in your living room.

The device's Tizen OS platform, along with a wide selection of apps and cloud-based gaming services, offers seamless integration with Samsung Galaxy phones, tablets, and laptops. If it weren’t for its lack of Dolby Vision support, the S95H would have been my top OLED pick.

Samsung offers the S95H in various screen sizes, ranging from 55 to 83 inches. Opt for the Samsung S90H if you are looking for a great Samsung TV on a tighter budget.

The Sony Bravia 7 II is Sony’s very impressive second-from-top-of-the-line flagship RGB TV, which emphasizes precise color reproduction for folks who care deeply about seeing films (or TV shows, or video games) the way their creators intended for them to be seen. It uses the TV’s Studio Calibrated mode, which optimizes color and contrast for accuracy, rather than brightness or contrast. It isn’t about enhancing performance, but optimizing for accuracy. And, given Sony’s position as both a maker of hardware and content, there’s already a rich selection of content that supports it.

On the gaming front, Sony maintains its tradition of offering a few PlayStation-focused tricks. It seamlessly optimizes HDR settings in some games, ensuring you get the best possible picture. (It’s especially helpful if you have a PlayStation 5 Pro, which unlocks additional graphics options.)

I also like the TV’s design, headlined by a magnetic semi-transparent panel that attaches to its metal stand. It makes the TV look like it’s floating above the surface it’s placed on. Unlike most rivals, the Bravia 7 II is also available in smaller sizes, down to 50 inches. The largest version has a massive 98-inch screen, but at $9,000 before discounts, it’s a tougher sell than the smaller options.

Some mainstream TVs are available in multiple screen sizes, ranging from 43 inches to a head-spinning 98 inches. TVs with 65-inch screens are deservedly popular and the best for most consumers, offering a good balance between immersive viewing, easy home integration (I’ve experienced many in a one-bedroom New York City apartment), and price. Until not too long ago, TV models with screens of 65 inches or more had high price tags, but that's no longer the case. Top-tier TVs with 65-inch screens now cost below $1,500, and larger 75-inch TVs are available for less than $2,000. Believe it or not, you can even get a 98-inch for around $2,000 instead of a five-digit sum.

A TV with a 4K (UHD) screen is the best upgrade option at the moment. Content in this resolution is widely available across all streaming platforms for reasonable price points, so consider it a must. Switching from an older 4K set to one of the latest models is worth it for the picture quality improvements. The difference is even more evident if you are ditching a Full HD TV because its screen has four times fewer pixels than a 4K unit. A Full HD resolution is acceptable only if you are shopping for a small and (very) cheap set. TVs with stunningly sharp 8K screens, like this pricey Samsung, are also widely available. Still, I wouldn’t consider one because native content in this resolution isn’t widely available. You’d be better off spending on a similarly priced 4K TV.

When it comes to refresh rate, avid gamers should look for TVs whose screens support more than the industry-standard 60 hertz. A higher refresh rate—120 Hz, specifically—offers fast and smooth on-screen action.

A high refresh rate can also be beneficial for watching live sports, though that’s a matter of personal preference. I don’t recommend this feature to stream movies and series, as this content has been captured at lower refresh rates.

Unless you are shopping on a tight budget, you should have a TV with an OLED or a mini-LED display on your radar. Featuring individually backlit pixels, OLED TVs give you the best picture quality available, so they are worth the price premium over similarly sized non-OLED models. By producing deep contrast (their pixels switch off to display black color) and vibrant colors, these TVs can make even mundane scenes look amazing. However, mini-LED TVs deserve your attention, as they deliver superior brightness to their OLED counterparts at a lower price tier for the same screen size. Thanks to a sophisticated backlighting setup with thousands of local dimming zones, the latest mini-LED offerings are not too far behind OLEDs in contrast, either. Their viewing angles are narrower than those of an OLED, but the higher peak brightness and the cheaper price can’t be ignored. Commonly referred to as QLED, quantum dot is an important display feature to keep an eye out for, even if you are shopping for a TV on the cheap. Products whose screens have the tech offer more vibrant color and higher brightness than non-QLED rivals.

Peak brightness is a vital display feature to have on your radar when shopping for a TV. The luminosity is measured in nits, and I suggest you look for TVs with peak brightness that exceeds 1,000 nits, even if you are shopping on a tight budget. A higher peak brightness guarantees a better viewing experience with HDR-enhanced content, as well as superior picture quality in brightly lit spaces.

Regarding connectivity features, HDMI 2.1 and WiFi 6 (or higher) are the two most important ones to look for in a spec sheet. The former ensures that your TV can sync perfectly with a top-tier gaming console like a Sony PlayStation 5 or a Microsoft Xbox Series X and treat you to smooth and hiccup-free gameplay. Futureproof WiFi 6 or newer wireless connectivity ensures your TV can stream high-resolution content and reliably link up with other compatible devices on your home network, though not all of our picks below include this feature. Today’s best TVs pack multiple HDMI ports, so you can easily link a soundbar and additional streaming players if you want. USB ports for additional accessories and a coaxial input for basic TV are also available.

Every new TV on this list runs a smart platform with access to all big-name streaming services, so you won’t have to worry about accessing your subscriptions. Support for Apple AirPlay and Google Chromecast for sharing content from a mobile device is also commonly available.

HDR-enhanced content has become common on all streaming services. I suggest you get a TV that supports all leading formats—Dolby Vision, HDR10/10+, and HLG—for movie buffs.

Look for Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant, or Apple HomeKit support if you want to integrate your TV into a smart home setup or control it directly with voice commands. If you don’t own or plan to invest in a soundbar or a surround sound system, be sure to order a TV with a multi-speaker setup and Dolby Atmos support. Thankfully, the functionality is available in many new sets.

With all the above features in mind, find your new home entertainment centerpiece among these TVs we vouch for.

#6329. Powerful New Weight-Loss Drug Could Change How Millions Treat Painful Knee Arthritis

An experimental weight-loss injection may offer more than a way to shed pounds, with clinical trials suggesting it could also ease the burden of painful knee arthritis.

Losing weight can help relieve knee osteoarthritis, yet the condition often makes weight loss difficult in the first place. When walking, climbing stairs, or simply standing up from a chair causes pain, getting enough exercise can become a challenge.

For the roughly 15 million Americans living with painful knee osteoarthritis, treatment options remain limited. Physical therapy, topical medications, anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren, opioids, and corticosteroid injections can help manage symptoms, although steroid injections typically provide only short-term relief.

Previous research has shown that losing just 5% to 10% of body weight through diet and exercise can improve symptoms. Losing more than 10%, however, is difficult through lifestyle changes alone, particularly for people whose knees already limit their movement.

An experimental weight-loss injection called retatrutide may offer another way to address this problem. In two large clinical trials led by Northwestern University, participants who were overweight or had obesity experienced substantial weight loss alongside significant reductions in knee pain.

The phase 3 trials, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, involved more than 1,000 participants combined. Those receiving the highest dose of retatrutide lost approximately 25% of their body weight on average. A pooled analysis found that about two-thirds of participants receiving the drug reported at least a 50% reduction in knee pain, compared with 38% of those given a placebo.

Researchers tracked these changes using the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC), which asks patients to rate their pain from 0 to 10. Participants also recorded their daily pain levels through an app.

“The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you’re going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain,” said corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, a professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. “A major factor is that you’re loading your knees less and therefore, there’s less pain and it allows you to increase your function.”

Developed by Eli Lilly, retatrutide is a once-weekly injection that activates receptors for three naturally occurring hormones involved in metabolism. Existing weight-loss medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide target one or two receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%. Retatrutide produced losses of approximately 20% to 25% in these trials.

“Participants had remarkable responses,” Schnitzer said. “Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more.”

The improvements also extended beyond body weight and joint pain. Participants experienced lower blood pressure, reduced blood lipid levels, and less systemic inflammation, suggesting broader metabolic benefits.

Scientists from Eli Lilly were among the study’s co-authors. Philip Conaghan, professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from the TRIUMPH-4 trial at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were presented separately during a poster session.

Despite the promising results, retatrutide remains experimental and would require approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration before becoming a treatment option. Schnitzer emphasized that diet, exercise, and lifestyle changes should remain the first approach because they are less expensive and avoid potential side effects associated with GLP-1 medications, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss. Preserving muscle is especially important for patients with knee osteoarthritis because it helps stabilize the joint.

The trials also left a crucial question unanswered. Although retatrutide significantly reduced pain, researchers do not yet know whether it slows the underlying progression of osteoarthritis or could help patients avoid knee replacement surgery. People who already needed knee replacements were excluded from the studies.

“That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people’s pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis,” Schnitzer said.

Further research must also determine whether retatrutide could benefit people with knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight, since they were not included in the trials. Scientists are particularly interested in whether the drug’s potential anti-inflammatory effects contribute to pain relief independently of weight loss.

“These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known,” Schnitzer said. “Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also important in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I’ve been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better.”

Reference: “Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity” by Thomas J. Schnitzer, David J. Hunter, Philip G. Conaghan, Arya M. Sharma, Sue D. Pedersen, Kaiyi Chen, So Young Park, Nune Makarova, Kathryn Giblin and Tammy Forrester, 7 November 2026, New England Journal of Medicine. DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoa2610676

Funding for the study was provided by Eli Lilly and Company.

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

#6327. SpaceX Launches Starship But Passes Up Booster Catch for Safety's Sake

SpaceX sent its Starship on a flight that was meant to feature a first-ever retrieval of both rocket stages, but a launch-pad catch of the first-stage booster had to be canceled due to safety concerns.

Instead, the Super Heavy booster was diverted during its descent to make an offshore splashdown. Observers at SpaceX's Starbase on the South Texas coast could hear the sonic boom and see the fiery plunge that took place minutes after launch at 4:47 p.m. CT (2247 GMT) today. "Wow, you could feel the rumble of that splashdown there," launch commentator Jessie Anderson said.

This 15th flight test still has a chance to make history: The mission plan calls for the Starship second stage to spend as much as 22 hours in orbit â ending with a return to the pad for a midair capture by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms. SpaceX has caught Starship's booster during three previous test flights, but this would be a first for a second stage.

Hours after launch, SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice said the booster's control system triggered an abort of the launch-tower catch because the boostback engine burn ended early, apparently due to a low fuel mass alarm. SpaceX's team was still troubleshooting the root cause of the alarm, she said.

Anderson said the offshore splashdown averted the risk of damage or injuries at the launch site. "Safety is always our No. 1 priority," she said. If any further safety concerns arise, SpaceX's mission team has the option of ending the flight early and sending the second stage â known as Ship 42 â down to a controlled ocean splashdown.

After reaching orbit, Ship 42 deployed 26 satellites for SpaceX's Starlink broadband internet network. Three of the satellites were equipped with a suite of cameras to inspect Ship's heatshield after deployment.

Starship ranks as the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, standing 407 feet (124 meters) tall and providing 17 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. The rocket is designed to deploy dozens of Starlink V3 satellites at a time â and eventually send thousands of explorers and settlers to Mars.

NASA is counting on SpaceX to provide a Starship-based system for landing astronauts on the moon by as early as 2028. As a preparatory step, NASA is planning to test Starship as well as Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system in low Earth orbit next year. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman referred to that test mission, known as Artemis III, in a post to X that took note of the video sent down from orbit via the Starlink network.

"Congratulations to the SpaceX team on another spectacular launch," Isaacman wrote. "Very much appreciate how you bring the world along in high resolution. We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III."

This report has been updated with further details about the aborted booster catch.

#6326. Scientists Discover a Surprising New Power of Honey That Could Protect Your Skin

Honey’s medical uses may go beyond healing wounds, as laboratory experiments suggest multifloral honey could strengthen human skin cells’ defenses against damaging UV radiation.

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight can accelerate skin aging and place cells under stress, potentially contributing to damage that precedes skin cancer. As scientists explore ways to better protect the skin, researchers in Italy are investigating whether multifloral honey could help human skin cells withstand UV exposure.

Honey is already valued in medicine and cosmetics for its antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and wound-healing properties. Sterile honey-based dressings, gels, and ointments are used to treat burns and difficult-to-heal wounds.

Dr. Fikiye Fulya Kavak, a member of Professor Margherita Maioli’s research team at the University of Sassari, Italy, drew inspiration from her background in medical biology and interests in beekeeping and cosmetic science.

“I have always been interested in the fact that certain honeys, such as Manuka honey, are used in medical-grade applications,” Kavak said. “This led me to ask whether high-quality multifloral honey could also show measurable protective effects for human skin cells.”

To investigate, the researchers grew human skin stem cells, fibroblasts, and keratinocytes together in a continuously flowing bioreactor designed to simulate conditions in human skin. Some cultures received a 1% multifloral honey treatment for 48 hours before UV exposure, while others remained untreated.

The team then compared how the cells responded to UV-induced stress. Using real-time quantitative PCR, they also measured the activity of selected genes involved in aging, stress responses, tissue renewal, and stemness, the ability of stem cells to reproduce themselves or develop into specialized cells.

The results suggested that honey pretreatment helped skin stem cells and fibroblasts regulate their responses to UV damage. “In skin stem cells, honey increased the expression of stemness-related markers, while reducing the expression of aging-associated genes,” Kavak said.

Honey-treated stem cells also released less nitric oxide and showed greater antioxidant capacity, suggesting improved defenses against UV-induced stress. Genetic analysis further revealed increased expression of stress-protection genes and changes in signals controlling cell proliferation and renewal.

“What was particularly interesting was that honey seemed to help the cells find a healthier balance after UV stress,” Kavak said. “Rather than pushing the cells into an exaggerated repair response, it appeared to support protective mechanisms while keeping renewal-related signals under control.”

The findings offer an early indication that multifloral honey could support skin protection, although the researchers have not established whether these effects occur in people.

“Our study was performed in cell-based experimental models, not in humans, so further laboratory, preclinical, and clinical studies are needed before any practical recommendation can be made,” Kavak said. Honey should therefore not be considered an alternative to sunscreen.

The team is now investigating the molecular mechanisms behind these responses. “We have been working on protein-level validation studies to confirm whether the molecular changes observed at the mRNA level are also reflected at the protein level,” Kavak said.

Researchers are also exploring a nanofiber-based system that could eventually deliver honey’s active compounds in a controlled, skin-compatible form for cosmetic or medical applications.

“These nanofibers have already been characterized, and their biological evaluation is currently ongoing,” Kavak said. “This represents an important next step, as nanofiber-based systems may provide a more advanced platform for studying the potential skin-related applications of natural bioactive compounds such as multifloral honey.”
