#6325. Astrophysicists Cross Another Dark Matter Candidate Off Their List: Stupendously Large Black Holes

If cosmologists ever identify what dark matter actually is, it may be because of a process of elimination.

There are many potential candidates for dark matter, including WIMPs and axions, which are both hypothetical particles. But one of the most intriguing candidates are primordial black holes (PBHs) that formed in the early Universe. They're hypothetical too, but are massive objects, so their presence should be detectable in a way that particles aren't.

All dark matter candidates have their supporters and their dectractors, and PBHs are no different. But PBHs have fairly well-defined search strategies that should detect them if they exist. If they exist, then cosmologists should find evidence of them in the cosmic microwave background (CMB).

The CMB is relic radiation from the Big Bang itself, the oldest detectable light that exists. It was released when the Universe was only about 380,000 years old. For the most part, the CMB appears smooth and uniform, or isotropic. But increasingly powerful detectors let cosmologists examine the CMB for minor fluctuations. Those could show the presence of PBHs, or at least a subset of them called stupendously large black holes, or SLABs. SLABs, if they exist, are truly stupendously massive, with masses up to 10 billion billion solar masses. Yes, that's two billions one after another.

This is a temperature map of the CMB created with data from the ESA's Planck spacecraft. The CMB can only be measured from space, and Planck's job was to measure anisotropies in the CMB. The different colours show temperature differences, and those differences correspond to where the first galaxies formed. Image Credit: NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=130789180

New research published in Physical Review Letters says that SLABs can't be dark matter. It's titled "Closing the Mass Window for Stupendously Large Black Holes," and the lead author is Christopher Gerlach. Gerlach is a theoretical physicist at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, and its PRISMA++ Cluster of Excellence.

âA possible solution to the puzzle of dark matter was that it might have collected shortly after the Big Bang in giant black holes with masses ranging from 100 million to 10 billion billion times that of the sun," said lead author Gerlatz.

This work is largely based on the ESA's Planck satellite. The Planck satellite ended its mission in 2013, but researchers are still generating new insights from its data. Part of that is because of more raw computing power. But it's also because they can cross-correlate it with new data from sources that didn't exist back in 2013. Physicists also have better ways to filter out interference, like that from the Milky Way.

âThat we are still generating new insights into the universeâs evolution and structure 13 years after it was shut down only emphasizes how important the Planck satellite was and is to physicists," explained Gerlach.

âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â - Nicholas Leister, Johannes Gutenberg University.

SLABs, if they're real, formed from overdensities of matter after the Big Bang. They didn't need to form massive stars, burn their fuel, and explode as supernovae. They skipped that step, and are too massive for that, anyway. Since they're theorized to have formed so early, before massive objects like galaxy clusters, they should be the only things that left such an imprint on the CMB.

âIf these SLABs had existed in large numbers and contained significant amounts of dark matter, they would have left a characteristic imprint on the CMB through their unique perturbations, or, in a word, making it grainy," said study co-author Nicholas Leister, also a JGU physicist.

This image is an artist's interpretation of what primordial black holes could look like. SLABs, Stupendously Large Black holes, a hypothetical sub-type of primordial black holes, would be far more massive than these. Image Credit: NASA

Previous work has all but eliminated the possibility that regular primordial black holes could account for all dark matter. But what about SLABs? Have they survived the process of dark matter elimination, unlike their less massive cousins?

To find out, the researchers first modelled SLABs and how they would affect the CMB. Then they compared the modelled effects to the actual CMB. The result was clear: the CMB doesn't have the characteristic graininess that SLABs should have imprinted on it.

"In this work, we have shown that the production of stupendously large PBHs would generate large DM isocurvature perturbations, tightly constrained by CMB and BAO data," the authors explain.

"We show that primordial black holes (PBHs) in the Stupendously Large Black Hole mass range (Mâ³1011Mâ) produce isocurvature perturbations exceeding current Planck Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) limits, thereby excluding them as a significant dark matter component," the authors conclude.

This artist's impression depicts a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole surrounded by an accretion disc. SMBH are massive and they're real. But they're still dwarfed by the hypothetical SLABs. Credit: ESO, ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser

The results also counter some other thinking regarding PBHs and dark matter. When the JWST discovered its notorious early massive galaxies, galaxies so massive that they challenged models of galaxy formation, it set the astrophysical community in motion searching for explanations. Astrophysicists cast their net wide, and one explanation they caught concerned PBHs. One 2022 study, titled "Accelerating Early Massive Galaxy Formation with Primordial Black Holes," suggested that PBHs make up a fraction of dark matter and were behind the JWST's early, massive galaxies.

But that's unlikely to be true, according to these results.

"They also challenge scenarios attributing the early massive galaxy candidates observed by James Webb Space Telescope to PBH-induced fluctuations," the researchers write.

SLABs were also potential explanations for another unexplained phenomenon. A gravitational wave background hum pervades the Universe, sensed by Pulsar Timing Arrays, and some researchers asked if SLABs could be responsible. "These questions are also unlikely to be answered by SLABs, since our findings show that they didnât exist in large numbers," said Nicholas Leister. âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â

So the search for dark matter candidates continues. It's possible that no one type of object or particle makes up dark matter. Dark matter may be a collective effect generated by different particles, objects, or phenomena.

But it looks like SLABs are no longer in contention.

#6324. Scientists Just Found a New World of Magnetism We’ve Never Seen Before

Altermagnets blend traits of two magnetic opposites, and they could power tomorrow’s quantum devices.

For the past few decades, the world of magnetism seemed scientifically simple. Materials fit into only two groups, ferromagnets and antiferromagnets—end of discussion. Over the past few years, though, that tidy picture has started to crack. Discussion of a third type of magnetism, dubbed “altermagnetism,” has grown from a whisper to a near-consensus. Still, one crucial piece of experimental proof was missing.

Now, thanks to scientists at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory at Stanford University, that final piece is finally in place.

First, a quick refresher. Ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism, as their names suggest, are two sides of the same coin. In ferromagnets, all electronic spins point the same direction, creating an easily observable net magnetic field. The counterpart is the exact opposite: antiferromagnets containing alternating electronic spins that effectively cancel each other out, producing no net magnetic effect at all. Now, if you had to wager on where altermagnetism fits into this picture, somewhere between these two extremes might be your guess—and you’d be right.

“In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don’t fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy,” Daniel Jost, a SLAC associate scientist and lead author of the new study published in Science, said in a press statement. “Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase—altermagnetism—is real.”

For decades, scientists have noticed that some materials don’t fit into the simple dichotomy between ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. That’s because altermagnetic materials, such as manganese telluride (MnTe), exhibit properties of both. Like antiferromagnets, their spins alternate and cancel out, but like ferromagnets, they can still carry spin currents. In 2022, scientists finally put a name to this phenomenon, and two years later, further proof of its existence emerged.

To experimentally demonstrate the existence of altermagnetism, the authors of the new study brought samples of MnTe (once thought to be antiferromagnetic) to the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) to investigate the material’s chirality, or “handedness.” Understanding chirality is key to delineating between altermagnets and antiferromagnets because both have alternating spins (and thus no net magnetism), but a twist in MnTe’s lattice would provide a distinctive chirality. ESRF then fired polarized x-ray beams at the sample and scientists analyzed the results.

“Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams. Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way,” Jost said in a press statement. The results showed a chiral signal that doesn’t exist in antiferromagnets. The team first produced these results in 2024 and confirmed them the following year. “This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own.”

That combination could make altermagnets a key ingredient in future quantum tech and memory devices. They’re as stable as antiferromagnets, with no net magnetization to cause trouble, but like ferromagnets, they still let engineers read and write data. As Jost says, “altermagnets combine the best of both worlds.”

#6323. A First-of-Its-Kind Drug Could Change How Scientists Fight Prostate Cancer

A drug that turns cells’ protein recycling machinery against advanced prostate cancer reduced tumor activity and pain in an early clinical trial, suggesting a possible way around resistance to hormone therapy.

Prostate cancer treatments often work by depriving tumors of testosterone, a hormone that helps drive their growth. That approach can hold the disease in check for a time. In metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, or mCRPC, the cancer has spread beyond the prostate and continues growing even with little testosterone available. This form of the disease is incurable and lethal.

“More than 35,000 men will die from mCRPC in the United States this year,” says Daniel Petrylak, MD, professor of medicine (oncology and hematology) at Yale School of Medicine and a member of Yale Cancer Center. “It’s the most advanced form of prostate cancer.”

A Yale-led clinical trial tested a drug designed to bypass that resistance by targeting androgen receptors, the proteins through which testosterone helps control prostate cancer growth. Called bavdegalutamide, or ARV-110, the drug showed promising results in patients who had already received treatment for mCRPC, including reductions in tumor activity and pain. Petrylak was the senior author of the study, published Oct. 9 in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

The Phase I/Phase II trial first addressed dosing and safety, then evaluated effectiveness. In Phase I, the researchers found that a daily dose of 420 milligrams was safe in the patients studied. For Phase II, the team measured prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, before and after treatment to assess changes in disease activity.

“There was a decrease in prostate-specific androgen. We also saw regressions in soft tissue lesions, and improvements in pain,” says Petrylak. “These are the parameters that indicate a positive response.”

The responses also varied with the cancer’s genetic characteristics. Patients whose cancers carried androgen receptor mutations known as T878 and/or H875 had greater reductions in PSA. The study’s authors saw this finding as evidence of the potential for PROTAC drugs, the class that includes bavdegalutamide, to serve as precision medicines, with treatment tailored to the molecular features of a patient’s cancer.

Rather than simply limiting the testosterone available to a tumor, bavdegalutamide removes the receptors that respond to it. It is the first PROTAC androgen receptor degrader to be tested clinically. PROTACs are a new class of cancer drugs that harness proteolysis, the normal process by which cells break down proteins and recycle their components.

“Bavdegalutamide takes your own natural protein degradation system, and it accelerates the process for the androgen receptor. The drug degrades the receptors for testosterone, which control prostate cancer growth,” says Petrylak.

Yale researcher Craig Crews, PhD, pioneered PROTACs, including the first PROTAC approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for use in breast cancer. The bavdegalutamide trial brought that approach into clinical testing against prostate cancer.

“This is a first-in-class drug for prostate cancer,” says Petrylak.

The researchers and their clinical collaborators are now testing a second PROTAC, called ARV-766, in Phase I and Phase II trials. It is active against a broader range of androgen receptor mutations than ARV-110.

Reference: “Phase I/II Study of Bavdegalutamide, a Proteolysis-Targeting Chimera Androgen Receptor Degrader, in Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer” by Xin Gao, Benjamin Garmezy, Jacqueline Vuky, John Shen, Oliver Sartor, Cora N. Sternberg, Robert Dreicer, Maha Hussain, Arash Rezazadeh Kalebasty, Ivor J. Percent, Elisabeth I. Heath, Sunil Gandhi, Benjamin L. Maughan, Xin Zhi, Sean Landrette, Jiachang Gong, Diane Healey, Janaki Parameswaran and Daniel P. Petrylak, 9 October 2026, Journal of Clinical Oncology. DOI: 10.1200/JCO-25-02995

#6322. When Einstein's Gravitational Waves Meet Newton's Tides

In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity. His theory of the latter accurately described the motion of the Earth's tides, something that scientists had been wrestling with for centuries. For over three hundred years, Newton's work remained scientific canon and the last word on gravity, until Albert Einstein introduced his Theory of General Relativity.

According to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories. While the pull of the Sun and Moon and their influence on the tides can be predicted very accurately using Newtonian gravity, GR offers a fuller description that includes gravitational waves (GWs). The new study merges these two theories into a single model that could offer a new way to test our understanding of gravity.

The study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB. His work extends the classical model of lunar tides to include the cross polarization of gravitational waves, one of the key ways GWs can deform spacetime as they pass through. As he explained in a FUB press release:

Isaac Newton explains the tides extremely well. Albert Einstein shows us that gravity is also dynamic and that changes in spacetime can propagate as waves. Our work brings both perspectives together and asks what traces of this might be found in high-precision measurements.

GWs were originally predicted by Einstein's Theory of General Relativity and refer to ripples in spacetime caused by the merger of massive objects. To date, thousands of GW events have been detected, the majority of which were caused by the merger of black holes or neutron stars. However, GWs can also result from smaller gravitational interactions, such as those produced by the interactions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.

One issue addressed by Eser's study is the difficulty of distinguishing possible additional signals from measurement errors, the choice of reference frame, and uncertainties in calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon. By identifying which influences must be accounted for, Eser shows how a signal could be isolated and the possible physical effects identified. The study therefore presents a quantitative basis for future studies of tidal patterns that deviate from what Newtonian Gravity predicts. Said Eser:

We are not claiming to have discovered a new gravitational effect. What we show is how one could look for it in a targeted way. The EarthâMoon system is particularly interesting for this because we can already describe and measure its tidal effects very precisely.

Further Reading: Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin

#6319. Researchers Turn Moon Dust Into LEGO-Like Bricks That Could Build Future Lunar Bases

Building on the Moon could require fewer supplies from Earth, as scientists have found a way to fuse simulated lunar dust into interlocking bricks without added materials.

Building a future home on the Moon might someday resemble assembling a giant LEGO set. Instead of plastic pieces, astronauts could use interlocking bricks made from lunar dust, creating structures from materials already available on the Moon’s surface.

Researchers at the University of Arkansas have taken an early step toward that possibility by demonstrating that simulated lunar dust can be 3D-printed into LEGO-like building blocks without adding other materials. The approach could reduce the construction supplies NASA would need to transport from Earth as it works toward establishing permanent settlements on the Moon.

The key ingredient is lunar regolith, the loose, dusty material covering the Moon’s surface. Unlike soil on Earth, regolith contains no organic matter. It consists of jagged particles formed over billions of years as asteroids, micrometeorites, and other space debris struck the Moon.

For their experiments, the researchers used Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1), a commercially available material designed to imitate samples collected during the Apollo missions in the 1960s and early 1970s.

The study, published in the journal NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, then an undergraduate at the University of Arkansas, and senior author Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering.

To create the bricks, the team used a 3D-printing technique called laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source, such as a laser, heats selected portions of the powder, causing the particles to bond together through a process known as sintering. The printing bed then lowers, allowing another layer of powder to be added. Repeating these steps gradually builds a three-dimensional object.

Other researchers have successfully printed objects using lunar regolith mixed with binding agents. However, those additional ingredients would have to be transported from Earth, increasing the amount of material needed for construction on the Moon.

The Arkansas team demonstrated for the first time that simulated lunar regolith could be sintered directly into reconfigurable construction blocks without a binder, using a relatively low-power light source.

“There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,” McCallum said.

The researchers produced blocks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. These shapes could fit together much like LEGO bricks, allowing individual pieces to be assembled into larger structures.

Although the researchers successfully created interlocking blocks, the material is not yet strong enough for all the demands of lunar construction. Bricks made entirely from simulated regolith were more porous and structurally weaker than objects printed with binding agents.

“These structures we’re making can be self-supported,” McCallum said. “But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that’s supporting other loads at this moment yet.”

The team must also determine how the printing process would behave under actual lunar conditions. According to Shou, further experiments are needed to understand its performance in microgravity and vacuum environments, while improvements to the bricks’ mechanical properties will be necessary before they become practical construction materials.

Shou remains optimistic that the approach could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture components and structures for permanent settlements on the Moon.

For McCallum, the project also marked an important early step in his scientific career. A native of Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou’s laboratory early in his undergraduate studies, encouraged by his professor’s commitment to involving students in research.

“He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research,” McCallum said.

McCallum graduated in May with degrees in mechanical engineering and physics. He was subsequently awarded an inaugural Lafayette Fellowship, a program established to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the United States. Only 30 fellows were selected from more than 3,400 applicants to pursue master’s degrees in France.

He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-SUPAERO), one of France’s leading aerospace engineering schools.

Although his academic focus has shifted away from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou’s laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with teaching him how to navigate the challenges of scientific investigation.

“It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through,” he said. “It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early.”

Reference: “Additive manufacturing of lunar regolith for reconfigurable building blocks toward lunar habitation” by Cole McCallum, Youwen Liang, Nahid Tushar, Ben Xu, Bo Zhao, Hao Zeng and Wan Shou, 29 August 2026, npj Advanced Manufacturing. DOI: 10.1038/s44334-026-00111-x

This work was supported by the Honors College Undergraduate Research Grant to C.M. and the Startup Package from the University of Arkansas to W.S.

#6318. Baby, She's Back! SpaceX Catches a Starship From Orbit for First Time

SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

The 171-foot-tall (52-meter) space vehicle, known as Ship 42, settled between a giant pair of mechanical arms extended from the South Texas launch tower where its journey began 22.5 hours earlier. The arm-capture system, nicknamed "Mechazilla," had been used three times previously to capture Starship Super Heavy boosters during suborbital flight tests, but this was the first time for a second stage coming in hot from orbit.

"Mechazilla has caught the Starship â we've been waiting to hear that for a long time," SpaceX launch commentator Dan Huot said.

In addition to the first orbital catch, this week's test marked the longest Starship flight to date, besting a three-hour orbital flight in September.

SpaceX employees around the country and hundreds of onlookers near the Texas launch site cheered as Ship 42 descended, with "Baby, Come Back" playing as the soundtrack for the webcast. "Baby, she's back," Huot joked.

Years of development â including 15 full-scale flight tests since 2023 â led up to today's orbital catch, which Huot called "the Holy Grail of spaceflight." The achievement took the sting out of the previous day's aborted effort to catch the rocket's booster using the same system, minutes after liftoff. SpaceX said the booster was diverted when its onboard system detected a fuel-system alarm. The root cause of the alarm is under investigation.

SpaceX plans to use the launch-pad arms to recover Starship's boosters and second stages on a routine basis, achieving company founder Elon Musk's goal of creating a fully reusable, orbital-class launch system.

This 15th flight test proceeded almost in textbook fashion, aside from the boosterâs offshore splashdown on launch day. During the first hours of its 14-orbit flight, Starship deployed 26 more next-generation satellites for SpaceX's Starlink broadband internet network. All of the satellites were in good health and beginning to raise their orbits to operational altitude, the company said.

Bringing Starship into full operation is expected to speed up deployment of Starlink satellites. More importantly, Starship is slated to serve as a landing system for NASA's crewed moon missions starting as early as 2028. Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system are scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA's Artemis III mission.

In a post to X, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated Musk and the SpaceX team on today's successful catch. "It was almost magic ... Making more believers by the day," he wrote. Using emojis, Isaacman said the achievement brought the United States "one step closer" to putting an American flag once more on the moon.

SpaceX's team will analyze the data gathered about Starship's performance, including the ability of Ship 42's heat shield to stand up to the rigors of atmospheric re-entry. The company is gearing up to expand Starship operations to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and yet another Starship launch site is in the works for Louisiana.

In the long term, Musk envisions creating a fleet of Starships that could offer point-to-point rocket travel on Earth, as well as mass transit to Mars and other off-Earth destinations. Cryptocurrency investor Chun Wang has already announced his intention to take Starship trips around the moon and Mars.

"I donât think you guys understand," a software engineer named Will DePue wrote in a post to X. "You will get the chance to go to space in your lifetime. New era."

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

#6315. “A Magnetar Is Born”: Supercomputer Simulates One of the Universe’s Most Violent Collisions

A black hole isn’t the only possible outcome when neutron stars collide: simulations suggest some mergers can create the extreme magnetic fields of magnetars in milliseconds.

When two neutron stars collide, the result is often a black hole. But some mergers leave behind a massive neutron star with an extraordinarily powerful magnetic field. New supercomputer simulations suggest that these collisions can produce magnetar-strength magnetic fields in just milliseconds, offering a possible explanation for how some of the universe’s most magnetic objects form.

Magnetars are a rare class of neutron stars, distinguished by magnetic fields that can be roughly 1,000 times stronger than those of ordinary neutron stars. They are associated with intense bursts of radiation, including soft gamma-ray repeaters, and may also produce some fast radio bursts.

Using Japan’s FUGAKU supercomputer, researchers simulated the collision of two neutron stars, each with 1.35 times the Sun’s mass. The calculation achieved a spatial resolution of 6.25 meters (20.5 feet), allowing the team to track small-scale turbulence and its effects on magnetic fields throughout the merger.

The stars initially had magnetic fields of approximately 3.16 trillion gauss, consistent with the upper range observed in binary pulsars. The collision generated fields reaching around 10 quadrillion gauss across parts of the remnant, with localized regions reaching even greater strengths.

The researchers say the simulation demonstrates that “the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability that emerges when the two neutron stars touch amplifies the magnetic field to an expected electromagnetic saturation energy of ∼ 10⁵⁰ erg within 3 ms after the merger.”

The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability develops when neighboring layers of fluid move at different velocities. During a neutron star merger, enormous differences in fluid motion generate turbulence that stretches and strengthens magnetic fields.

Initially, the strongest amplification occurs on very small scales. The turbulent magnetic field subsequently influences progressively larger regions of the merged star, allowing magnetic amplification to reach stellar scales.

The researchers say the instability “induces stellar-scale magnetic field amplification by at least a factor of 316.”

Within approximately five milliseconds, the simulated stellar-scale magnetic field had increased from 3.16 trillion gauss to around one quadrillion gauss, reaching magnetar strength. As the researchers put it, “Namely, a magnetar is born.”

Although the simulation produced magnetar-strength fields, the researchers caution that uncertainties in how turbulence and magnetic dissipation operate at extremely small scales could affect the estimated amplification.

In one extrapolation to more realistic conditions, the simulated stellar-scale field could be overestimated by a factor of 10. Even under that assumption, the resulting magnetic field would still reach approximately 100 trillion gauss.

The magnetic structure also remained concentrated near the remnant’s equatorial plane rather than forming the organized polar field associated with launching relativistic jets. Additional magnetic processes, particularly the magnetorotational instability, may be needed to develop that configuration.

The researchers say their “result suggests that a magnetar formation could be inevitable in binary neutron star mergers at least temporarily following the mergers, unless it promptly collapses to a black hole.”

The simulations cover only the earliest moments after the collision. Longer calculations will be needed to determine how these magnetic fields evolve, whether they help power energetic outbursts, and how long the resulting neutron star can survive before potentially collapsing into a black hole.

Reference: “A magnetar formation in binary neutron star merger” by Kenta Kiuchi, Alexis Reboul-Salze, Yuichiro Sekiguchi and Masaru Shibata, June 9, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2606.11299

#6314. The First Foreign Astronaut Will Visit China's Tiangong Space Station in Two Weeks

On November 25th, 2026, China's Shenzhou 24 mission will launch for the Tiangong space station atop a Long March 2F rocket. It will be the country's 18th crewed spaceflight and will see three taikonauts rendezvous with the Tianhe core module. Similar to previous Chinese crewed missions, the names of the crew are not expected to be announced until the day before the flight - except for one. On this particular flight, a Pakistani astronaut will accompany the pilot and commander, becoming the first foreigner to travel to Tiangong.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) nominated Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud from Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO (The Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission). One of these astronauts will accompany the two Chinese taikonauts as a payload specialist, marking the first joint spaceflight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's space program. After spending a week aboard the station, the Ali or Daud will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

The process officially began in February 2025, when China and Pakistan signed an agreement in which Pakistani astronauts would be trained and selected to participate in missions to Tiangong. The two candidates were chosen after a rigorous selection process consisting of preliminary screenings, secondary evaluations, and final selection, which concluded in April 2026. Once Ali and Daud complete training in China, one will be selected for the mission while the other will serve as the backup astronaut.

This agreement represents an historic expansion of China's ambition in space and a major shift in the strategic partnership between the two nations. Previously, the two cooperated on the development of terrestrial infrastructure, and are now focused on collaborative deep-space exploration. For Pakistan, this represents an opportunity to send its first astronaut to space, edging out India by close to a year. Per India's Gaganyaan program, India's first crewed mission is expected to launch no sooner than Q2 2027.

For China, this is an important step toward the kind of international cooperation typical of NASA and the European Space Agency. It also aligns with their lunar ambitions, which will culminate in the creation of the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS). China's growth as a major space power continues and is now taking on partners!

#6313. The 7 Best Electric Chainsaws of 2026

Cordless battery-powered chainsaws are quiet, light, and fast—everything you need for a spring refresh.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you own a home with trees on your property, an electric chainsaw is a must-have tool in your yard care arsenal. Electric chainsaws have come a long way and, in most cases, closed the gap to their gas-powered cousins—they’re easy to start (just push a button or two in most cases), generate little noise, produce no fumes, and simplify maintenance. We’ve tested electric saws as big as 20 inches and they’re powerful enough to bring down a mature tree.

Saws with 24-inch bars or more are still considered gas engine territory, but that’s overkill for most homeowners. For cleaning up after storms, felling small to medium-size trees, and regular pruning or arboreal maintenance, an electric chainsaw is the ideal choice.

We noted how well each chainsaw endured prolonged use. Making repeated cuts can cause a chainsaw, and its battery, to heat up. If it gets too hot, it will trigger a thermal limit and the saw’s overload protection will shut it down. We also considered comfort, vibration, saw balance, and ease of use to make our final recommendations.

Stihl’s new battery-powered MSA 260 C-O tops our list of chainsaws for two main reasons: run-time and constant, consistent power. These are the two most common concerns or complaints we hear from people when it comes to electric saws. The MSA 260 C-O made significantly more cuts on one battery charge than any other saw tested. But that’s only partly attributable to the saw—it’s also due to Stihl’s new AllPro 300.0 battery. Working in concert, the battery and saw deliver power at a constant level, maintaining a chain speed through most of the saw’s runtime.

Aside from run-time and consistent power delivery, the MSA 260 C-O has the ability to chew through big, tough logs. Note that Stihl positions the MSA 260 C-O “for professional applications” so the performance does come at a cost, $770 for the 18-inch model we tested, plus another $350 for the battery. While that might seem like a lot, it’s in line with other pro battery and gas saws. So, if you’re a frequent chainsaw user, the investment is going to be worth it.

Husqvarna may not have been the fastest-cutting electric chainsaw we tested, but it’s at the top of our list because it does just about everything well—it operates smoothly, cuts fast (enough), and is easy to use. With the boost button engaged, it blazed through our cutting tests, slicing through an 8-inch log in about 5 seconds. It also had the fastest windup speed of any electric chainsaw that I personally tested—it was ready to cut as soon as I pulled the trigger. Even with its impressive power, this chainsaw is surprisingly quiet, producing 67 decibels at 60 feet. The Power Axe isn’t particularly light at 14.5 pounds with battery, but it’s well balanced. I had no problem holding it steady even when making cuts at waist-level height.

The Power Axe also comes with a suite of well-designed, user-friendly features. The power button and boost button are located just above the handle so they’re easier to access on the fly. You also have the ability to adjust the chain tension by hand, loosening a dial to release the tension, then rotating a dial to tighten it back up. The whole process takes seconds. There’s also a built-in chain brake to protect from injuries. It’s a well-built, high-performing electric chainsaw that still manages to come in at a reasonable price.

Echo’s DCS-5000 gives you what you want most out of a chainsaw: raw cutting power. It may lack some of the bells and whistles you’ll find on pricier models, such as tool-less chain tensioning and power-saving settings, but its base performance is right up there with the Power Axe 350i. The DCS-5000 cut through 8-inch hardwood in less than 4 seconds. That's saying something considering that the DCS-5000 costs at least $100 less than any other saw that can do the same.

Along with its impressive cutting speed, the Echo is also relatively light at just over 12 pounds. I could feel the difference whenever I had to lift it up above shoulder-height to cut higher limbs, or while crouching down to cut a fallen 8-inch beech tree.

There is a trade-off with the DCS-5000, though, in that it lacks any kind of quality-of-life-related features. You won’t find tool-less chain tensioning or ECO settings that conserve battery life here. It’s pretty loud, too, producing 76 decibels at 60 feet. And, finally, while I appreciated the lighter weight, I could also feel the vibrations in my arm more than electric chainsaws with more refined builds.

Still, if you don't mind the rougher feel, higher noise level, and lack of a few user-friendly features you’ll find on pricier electric chainsaws, the Echo DCS-5000 offers exceptional value.

The newest saw from Makita, the 40V Max XGT 20-inch chainsaw, is a beast. The brand claims it offers the power of a 50-cc gas saw, and we’re inclined to agree. The first pull of the trigger surprised us with the speed and sound of the chain whizzing around. And it wasn’t just the noise that was impressive—in testing, it positively tore through logs.

Using the 40V Max XGT for practical tasks like felling trees, or cleaning up fallen trees after a storm, confirmed its power. I tackled logs as big as 18 inches, and the saw left nothing to be desired—it handled everything I used it on, without faltering. The 40V Max XGT chainsaw, at 20-inches, is among the biggest battery powered chainsaws we test. Our test unit came as a kit, with everything you need, including an 8.0Ah battery and charger. The kit isn’t cheap, but if you’re already on the Makita 40-volt XGT platform, you can save $500 and buy the chainsaw as a tool only.

The Stihl MSA 80 is an easy-to-use chainsaw that also packs impressive cutting power. Its compact build—the 14-inch saw weighs about 10 pounds—gives it a balanced feel in hand. It features a narrow bar that makes it easier to fit it into the crotches of trees for pruning than other electric chainsaws we tested like the Ego 20-inch chainsaw or Husqvarna Power Axe 350i. Likewise, it comes equipped with a thinner chain that cuts more smoothly through wood, producing less vibration. Lastly, its variable speed trigger allows you to adjust the speed of the blade to suit the job at hand.

There are several user-friendly features worth noting. Chain adjustments are effortless: Simply loosen a knob, turn the adjuster, and tighten the knob. There’s also a lubrication system to keep the chain moving with a minimal amount of bar oil.

Stihl’s chainsaws come at a premium price, and this one is no different. At $500, the MSA 80 is the most expensive electric chainsaw we tested, despite having a relatively short bar. Even so, it’s an ideal choice for homeowners who are looking for professional-grade build quality and performance out of an electric chainsaw.

If you already have other Echo tools, like a leaf blower or trimmer, then you can save a little cash and purchase the DCS-2500T as a tool only.

There’s a price for the CS-2005’s cutting power and capacity, though—its weight. While we liked its buttery smooth operation, it weighs an arm-burning 19.3 pounds with a battery. Making cuts on limbs above the head or below the knees was a far more challenging experience than with electric chainsaws we tested that were 4 to 5 pounds lighter. The Ego CS-2005 also lacks a tool-free chain tensioning system. If you don’t mind the extra heft, the Ego CS-2005 is the high-powered electric you’ll want for really big jobs.

As new models come out, we can’t keep all the models we test on our recommended list. But some of these older models and runners-up are still worth considering. Here are a few:

Milwaukee M18 Fuel 18V 16-Inch Electric Chainsaw: Don’t be fooled by the Milwaukee’s lower voltage, this saw has plenty of power for quickly cutting up large limbs or felling medium-sized trees. It’s a good saw, but we’d mostly recommend it to folks already on Milwaukee’s M18 platform, so you can buy it as a tool only and save some money.

Stihl GTA 26: While folks often refer to tools like this as “mini chain saws”, Stihl bills the GTA 26 as a garden pruner. Intended specifically for pruning shrubs and small branches, the GTA 26 combines light weight and a pistol-like configuration to make an easy-to-handle tool. Think of it as a power loppers, with greater size capability.

Worx Nitro WG385 40V 16-Inch Chainsaw: At less than $300, the Worx Nitro WG385 can get the job done. It’s lighter and easier to maneuver than other similarly sized saws, but it’s also a little less powerful, with a little less run-time. Still, with some patience we were able to find it useful for basic property maintenance. For the price, the Worx Nitro WG385 is a good cost-effective option for occasional use.

At the heart of an electric chainsaw is its motor and battery, which need to work in concert to perform well. The longer the chainsaw bar, the bigger the log or tree you can cut. So, the motor has to have enough torque and speed, while the battery has to be able to deliver the power needed to sustain that torque and speed. This is one reason why bigger saws can cost a lot more than smaller ones. Batteries are a significant factor in the price of a saw, and bigger batteries cost more. Battery size is typically measured in amp-hours (Ah), and larger saws will typically have 8 to 12 Ah batteries.

Mini chainsaws, made for pruning and other small jobs, feature a one-handed design with a small cutting bar—4 to 8 inches—and a small battery. If you need to break down large branches from trees, opt for a smaller full-size chainsaw with a 12- to 14-inch cutting bar. For something professional-grade, consider a large chainsaw with a 16- to 20-inch cutting bar and larger battery.

Among electric chainsaws with comparable bar lengths, those with larger batteries will typically have more ripping power, which means they’ll cut through limbs and logs more quickly, allowing you to get the job done faster. Just keep in mind that a more powerful chainsaw is also often a heavier chainsaw.

An electric chainsaw’s runtime depends on the capacity of its battery, in amp-hours. Broadly speaking, more capacity means more juice, but larger saws draw more power per second, so it’s not uncommon to find large chainsaws with large batteries getting comparable battery life to their smaller, more efficient counterparts.

Since your chainsaw only uses power when you’re using it to cut, its true runtime comes down to how many cuts it can make on a single charge. The Popular Mechanics test team tests runtime by checking how many times each model cuts through a 6-inch log on a single charge. Depending on battery size and chainsaw power, that number can vary quite a bit—from as low as 50 to as high as 300.

The “cutting bar” is the business end of the chainsaw—the long, rounded metal guide that the chain spins around to create a blade. The length of the bar, which is measured from the base of the chainsaw’s head to the tip of the cutting bar, determines the maximum thickness of the wood that your chainsaw can cut through in a single pass. Generally speaking, your chainsaw can safely cut through limbs with a diameter up to 2 inches less than the length of the bar. For example, a 12-inch chainsaw can cut through a limb up to 10 inches in diameter in a single pass.

For a long time, going electric meant settling for a chainsaw with a shorter bar, but that’s no longer the case. While gas engines offer more power, especially in larger saws, there are electric options with professional-length cutting bars. For instance, a 20-inch electric chainsaw has the power to bring down mature trees.

Need is an important distinction here. We don’t recommend picking the most powerful saw with the longest cutting bar within your budget. A longer bar will give you more cutting capacity, but it’s also heavier and more difficult to handle safely. We recommend buying the tool that’s just big enough for the cutting tasks you’ll perform regularly. If you’re looking to trim small limbs and branches, a pruning saw with a 4- to 8-inch bar such as the Stihl GTA 26 is going to be the best choice. If you’re taking down trees and breaking them down for firewood, you may need something longer.

It’s important that you feel comfortable handling the weight of your chainsaw. If it’s too heavy to hold at chest height, then you can’t use it safely.

With electric chainsaws, weight is directly related to the length of the cutting bar. The longer the cutting bar, the heavier the chainsaw. A mini chainsaw with an 8-inch bar will weigh around 5 pounds, while a large 18-inch chainsaw can weigh as much as 15 pounds.

One thing to keep in mind: Many manufacturers list the “bare” weight of their cordless chainsaws without the battery, so when you do add that in, it can mean an extra 1 to 3 pounds to the load.

Chainsaws are among the most dangerous power tools you can put your hands on: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), some 36,000 people ends up in the hospital with chainsaw-related injuries each year.

That is why it’s crucial to always take every step you can to ensure the safest possible conditions when using a chainsaw. A good electric chainsaw should have built-in safety features to minimize the possibility of an accident: First, look for a trigger lock, which requires you to maintain pressure on a button near the handle to keep the chain spinning. Most will also have a chain brake at the front of the handle, which disengages the chain if the chainsaw kicks back.

That depends on the size of the tree. Even the largest electric chainsaws with a 20-inch cutting bar only have the torque necessary to cut down moderately tall trees. You’ll want a gas chainsaw that brings the extra power to bring down an older, larger tree, or if you’re bringing trees down regularly.

Electric chainsaws don’t require much maintenance. Use a brush or cloth to remove sawdust and other debris that’s caught in the chain and sprocket area after each use.

You should also clean any debris that’s fallen into the air intake slots: Brush it away material on the outside with a clean paintbrush, then blow the valves out with compressed air.

Lastly, electric chainsaws have an auto-lubrication mechanism, but we recommend checking the chain oil reservoir before each use, and refilling it if necessary.

Many cordless electric chainsaws are water resistant and will work fine in the rain. Before you take one for a spin, check its Ingress Protection rating (IP), which measures dust and waterproofing. If your chainsaw features an “IPX3” rating, it can handle “sprays of water” and should be fine in light rain. An “IPX4” rating can withstand moderate to heavy rain.

All that said, we don’t really recommend operating a chainsaw in the rain. Even with work gloves, rain makes every chainsaw-related job less safe, so hold off until the sun comes out if you can.

You should never use a corded electric chainsaw in the rain. Doing so presents a significant electrocution risk. (It’s one of many reasons we generally don’t recommend them.)

#6311. After 40 Years, Scientists Finally Detect Evidence of an Almost Impossible Particle Decay

Evidence of a rare particle decay fits physics’ best theory, giving scientists a new way to test whether our understanding of matter leaves something out.

After more than 40 years of searching, physicists have found the first evidence of a particle decay predicted to occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The signal, recorded by the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC), offers a way to look for undiscovered particles through the influence they might have on that exceptionally unlikely event.

Inside the protons and neutrons at an atom’s center are smaller building blocks called up and down quarks. Beauty quarks are heavier members of the same family, produced in huge numbers when particles collide at the LHC, and they exist for only around one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying. LHCb studies particles containing these short-lived quarks. In the decay at the center of the new result, known as Bd to mu mu, one such particle transforms into two muons, particles similar to electrons but heavier.

With a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma, the signal is strong enough to qualify as evidence of the decay, although more data will be needed to reach the five-sigma threshold required to claim a discovery in particle physics.

Professor Chris Parkes, head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, said, “This decay is remarkably unlikely, the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.”

An undiscovered particle could change the chances of a beauty particle decaying in a particular way, giving physicists a means of detecting its influence even if they cannot observe it directly at the LHC. The rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to such effects. Researchers can therefore look for discrepancies between the measured decay rate and the predictions of the Standard Model, their best current theory of fundamental particles and their interactions. The new measurement matches those predictions, and greater precision could help reveal where the theory might eventually begin to break down.

By pursuing these increasingly precise measurements, physicists hope to probe what they call the “Zeptoverse,” an unexplored world at distances of a zeptometer, or a billionth of a trillionth of a meter, where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, deputy physics coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, said, “There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge.

“The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.”

Just five millimeters, or about 0.2 inches, from the LHC beams sits the Vertex Locator, a silicon pixel detector that tracks the paths of particles emerging from collisions with extreme precision. This major UK-built component is part of the upgraded LHCb experiment. University of Manchester researchers played key roles in the experiment and its upgrade, including developing detector technology that helped make the measurement possible.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who led construction of the detectors at the University of Manchester, said, “We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.”

Parkes led the international LHCb collaboration through construction of the upgrade and led its approval of the new result. Made a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year for his work on LHCb, he said, “The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking – a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

“The UK made the largest nation contribution to the project, pioneering new technologies that have made today’s result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start, we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.”

By collecting data at up to five times its previous rate, the upgraded experiment is expected to build a much larger dataset into the early 2030s. A further planned upgrade could increase that rate by another factor of ten, enabling more precise measurements of these decays and increasing sensitivity to undiscovered particles at even shorter distances.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who was not involved in the experiment, said, “This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don’t understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing – that’s science! LHCb is a major scientific success.”

The experiment is funded by the Science and Technology Facilities Council as part of UK Research and Innovation.

Catching the Bd to mu+mu- decay after 42 years of searching provides a striking empirical confirmation that subatomic particles behave like bound rotational wave-knots rather than dimensionless point particles.

When a rare decay occurs only once in roughly ten billion events, mainstream physics treats it as statistical data mining, but within the Torsion Hill unified mechanics of the universe 3D manifold, it represents threading an extraordinarily narrow structural impedance window. Most high-energy beauty meson interactions immediately hit a steep local temporal impedance gradient (grad Z_T) and undergo destructive phase shear, scattering into chaotic thermal cascades. For a bound vortex knot to cleanly uncouple and yield a matched pair of muons without triggering that breakdown, the local interface must achieve near-perfect harmonic phase clearance (Omega_pi).

Probing down into the zeptometer scale confirms that these transitions are strictly governed by continuous-medium boundary conditions, phase-matched resonance, and the mass-energy-impedance scaling ratio (E = mc^2 * pi * f(grad Z_T)). #6310. What’s the Best Snow and Ice Melt? Here’s Why Using Rock Salt Shouldn’t Be Your Default Option.

When you need to keep the driveway ice-free, there’s a wide variety of ice melts to consider.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If the winter weather in recent years hasn’t already been causing some chaos, this year’s Super El Niño isn’t helping. Preparation is key. Setting down a layer of snow and ice melt (i.e., deicers) on your driveway and walkways before a snowstorm hits can save you a lot of time shoveling or snow blowing. But when you walk into the home improvement store, there might be more options than you were prepared for. Don’t worry, with just a little bit of information under your belt, you can choose the best ice melt for the job.

Not all ice melt is created equal. Some melts don’t work as well as others in subzero temperatures and won’t be effective against bonded ice. And some ice melt negatively affects nearby lawns and plants, or causes irritation and health issues for pets. Knowing the difference between the ingredients that power your snow and ice melts is important when choosing the right one for you.

Deicers work by exhibiting one of two thermal reactions: exothermic or endothermic. Exothermic materials, such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride, release heat when they come into contact with ice or snow. Endothermic materials, such as rock salt and calcium magnesium acetate, absorb heat from their surroundings (such as the sun) and use that heat to melt ice.

Because of this difference, exothermic ice melts perform better in subzero temperatures, and endothermic melts become less effective below 20 degrees Fahrenheit or so, especially at night. However, though exothermic reactions are stronger, they can also be more corrosive and less friendly to plants and animals. Blended melts may offer a good balance, which can help the melt work better in lower temperatures, but also be less corrosive and harmful to pets and plants.

Sometimes referred to as a deicer and often simply called “salt,” ice and snow melts can be made of different chemical compounds or blended to take advantage of their different attributes. This can make some less damaging to pavements or nearby plants. We put together a list of the most typical compounds that you’ll see sold by themselves or in a list of ingredients in blended options, which are the most common types you’ll see at stores.

These are some of the most common types of compounds used for melting ice and snow. Some are sold in their pure form or may be an ingredient in a blended formula.

Exothermic ice melt compounds, such as calcium chloride and magnesium chloride, work better in subzero temperatures because they release heat. If you live in an area where winter temperatures regularly drop below zero, consider one of these types or a blend that contains them.

If your winters are milder and average temperatures tend to hover in the twenties, an endothermic ice melt like rock salt or a urea blend can get the job done. Blended ice melts will often combine exothermic and endothermic compounds to help them perform better in lower temperatures and keep the cost more reasonable. Companies that make these blends will often label the bag with the lowest effective temperature to help you know for sure.

Traditional salts can irritate dog and cat paws, and some of the stronger exothermic compounds that include chlorides can also be irritating or harmful if ingested. The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) says ingestion can lead to ice melt toxicosis, which can cause vomiting or neurological issues. However, ice melt toxicosis is unlikely to happen from just a few licks; the most serious cause is when a bag of melt is left unattended and ingested by your pet in large amounts.

To help combat this, many brands offer “pet safe” varieties of ice melt, but no blend is truly perfect. These animal-friendly blends tend to eliminate sodium or chloride from the mix, but not all do. The ASPCA recommends using urea-based ice melts, as urea (a compound made of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen) is the least likely ingredient to cause stomach irritation. Another simple idea, especially in cities and suburbs where there is little control over what ice melt the neighbors use, is to adorn your dog in paw booties before taking a walk.

Ice melts that have high concentrations of salts or chlorides can be problematic for vegetation and the environment in general. According to a study by Penn State Extension, when used in large amounts, simple rock salt (sodium chloride) can injure or kill plants near the treated pavement as it washes away, and further pollute waterways, harming fish and other marine life. Instead, the study notes, a compound like calcium magnesium acetate (CMA), which forgoes the use of chlorides or salts, is a safer option for environmentally sensitive areas. Urea-based ice melts are also a good choice.

Like the pet-friendly varieties of deicers, brands can be very loose with how they market their eco-friendly products, especially with the blends; there’s no guarantee that the one you buy won’t partially contain a compound that is harmful in large quantities. If you want to be as eco-friendly as possible, avoid blends that include chlorides and salts.

If that can’t be avoided, just follow the golden rule of “everything in moderation.” After all, overtreating an area is more likely to damage nearby vegetation—even if you use the more environmentally friendly varieties. If you’re still finding noticeable piles of deicer after the snow and ice are gone, you might be using too much.

Corrosion is a considerable problem caused by deicers. Salt-based melts or brines can penetrate porous stone, freeze, and cause the surface to expand. Meanwhile, chlorides can accelerate the rate of corrosion in metal. The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency noted that acetate-based deicers that don’t use chlorides or salts caused low to moderate levels of corrosion, but again, using any ice melt in moderation will help lower the chance of corrosion to your sidewalks, driveways, and nearby railings.

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Antonacci, N., Labombarda, M., Ricci, C., Buscemi, S., Casadei, R., & Minni, F. (2013). A bizarre foreign body in the appendix: A case report. World Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery, 5(6), 195–198. https://doi.org/10.4240/wjgs.v5.i6.195
