#6306. A Lost Landmass Nearly the Size of North America Is Hiding Under the Sea—and It Could Rewrite Human History

A geographer calls it Aquaterra. For 120,000 years, early humans lived there—then the oceans swallowed it.

Several years ago, I travelled to North Carolina as part of a research trip for a story about the famous Lost Colony of Roanoke. Trying to leave no stone unturned, I explored the former colony’s dedicated National Historic Site, poured over archives of antique maps, and even took in a lavish outdoor stage production.

Ultimately, trying to wrangle all the many tendrils of that leviathan proved too unwieldy, and many of the ancillary elements have remained confined to my notebooks. Yet one moment from that trip has never been far from my mind, and it reshaped how I thought about our quest for answers about early human history.

It came about during a conversation with Dr. Eric Klingelhofer, a respected scholar and Vice President for Research with The First Colony Foundation. Dr. Klingelhofer had overseen several excavations that yielded remnants of Roanoke, but he was worried that many once-buried artifacts had already been claimed by a much more powerful force.

“Before my retirement,” he told me, “I attended a UNESCO-backed conference on Bonaire in the Dutch West Indies. These causes, rising sea levels and storm surges, plus coastal overdevelopment, endangered every island, as most prehistoric and early colonial sites lie close to the sea.” As we sat there on tranquil, federally protected land, it was hard for me to feel the urgency at the time, but he stressed that we were in a race against time. “At Fort Raleigh,”—the name the National Parks Service gave the National Historic Site—“coastal erosion has already swallowed up excavation units we had dug in 2007. The rate of loss is about twenty feet in twenty years—and it may be increasing.”

After our conversation, I walked along the island’s shoreline, struck by the thought that although I might be walking the same land as those colonists, the landscape wasn’t really the same. Their shoreline likely sat yards farther out than the one I strolled, and as the water swept that land away, it took with it our chance to learn more about the people who once stood there.

In the study of history, we too often focus on the preservation or replication of what was once on a certain parcel of land, taking it as a given that the land itself stayed constant. We spend all our time debating whether the proverbial Ship of Theseus is still the same after centuries of repairs, never stopping to question if the shoreline of Delos on which he landed still remains.

Yet, recent studies have emerged to remind us that even in the absence of human intervention, the world looked different to the peoples of the past than it does to us today.

The scale of this dilemma, the problem of our submerged history, is far greater than a single island in North Carolina, or a single colony from the 1500s. Our whole understanding of early humankind may be built on faulty ground, due specifically to how much of that ground is now underwater. But don’t let your thoughts drift to that Platonic idea of Atlantis; the proper term, as The Atlantic recently reminded us, is Aquaterra.

In 2014, the geographer Jerome E. Dobson mounted a case for the recognition of a global landmass he dubbed Aquaterra, a term he first proposed in 1999. In “Aquaterra Incognita,” Dobson argued that “all landmasses are defined by time as well as space,” and therefore, since “so little is known about the seacoast where a significant portion of humankind surely dwelled for the better part of 120,000 years,” we should properly recognize and name the 22.5-million-square-kilometer landmass that once hosted the earliest human civilizations.

When we think about the ice ages that have cycled across Earth’s history, we can easily picture the glaciers and ice sheets that formed, but we rarely consider where all that water came from. During an ice age, sea levels drop, exposing land that’s now underwater. As a result, the shorelines early humans knew looked very different from the ones we see today.

The lowlands these glaciers exposed were not bereft of life, either. The ecosystems they once supported varied, from grasslands to wetlands, forests to estuaries. They attracted wildlife, and later, early human civilizations. “Compare the most recent curve of sea level rise against the timeline of cultural innovations,” Dobson writes, “and you will find that much human progress occurred while seacoasts were still quite low.”

When the glaciers melted and sea levels rose again, naturally, early humans abandoned their soon-to-be-submerged settlements. But that doesn’t mean we should simply ignore what once stood there. “It would not change the timeline of human progress if, for instance, cities were found as low as -50 meters, since Jericho is known to have existed when sea levels were that low,” Dobson notes. What could revise that timeline, he notes, is “the possibility that precursors of major innovations may exist at even lower depths.”

“One intriguing possibility is pottery,” he proposes:

All this talk about “possibility,” of course, makes the benefits of recognizing Aquaterra seem entirely theoretical. Yet in just the last few years, the archeological world received a stirring reminder that the land we can see is not the only land there ever was, and that whole chapters of our history may have been claimed by the sea.

In 2021, Michael K. Faught and Morgan F. Smith published “The magnificent seven: Marine submerged precontact sites found by systematic geoarchaeology in the Americas.” The study documented not one or two but seven projects, in North America alone, that had found traces of precontact life now drowned beneath the continental shelf. Each of the seven projects worked “from the terrestrially known, to the submerged unknown.” Using methodical but varied mapping and modeling techniques, researchers predicted where people might once have lived, then searched for proof with underwater surveys, sediment cores, and even hands-on excavations.

One of the research efforts happened in the Gulf of Mexico’s paleo-Sabine River. Over the course of a decade, from 1976 to 1986, it turned up “charred wood and vegetation, nut hulls, seeds, fish scales, and bone from fish, reptiles, birds, and small mammals,” some of which dated back 9,000 years. Soon after, researchers in Belize found the drowned outlines of pole-and-thatch buildings, which turned out to be Classic-period Maya salt works now sitting underwater. Other research discussed in the study uncovered stone tools, campsites, and even a stone artifact more than 12,000 years old.

To truly understand human history, we can’t keep digging only in the land we can see. We also have to search for the land our ancestors knew, much of which now lies beneath the waves. That calls for a change in mindset and a rethinking of how archaeology works. As seas keep rising, how many more once-inhabited places will slip beneath the surface, taking with them secrets as recent as Roanoke’s? If we don’t change course now, the sites we have yet to excavate may be written off by tomorrow’s scholars as mere seafloor.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6300. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

P.K. Masonick et al. The repeated evolution of anti-bat bioacoustics in hawkmoths. Proceedings of the Royal Society B. 2026. doi: 10.1098/rspb.2026.2303

#6299. These 1,500-Year-Old Warriors Were Buried With Riches. Their Wounds Paint a Darker Picture.

The rare cemetery could finally shed light on a shadowy era after Rome’s collapse in what is now France.

Archaeologists with the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap) were excavating ahead of a residential construction project near Colmar, on the banks of the Ill River in eastern France. According to a translated statement, they found both a Gallo-Roman village occupied from the first to the third century C.E., and a fifth-century funerary complex containing 14 human burials and two horse burials.

The human burials included 11 adults or older adolescents and three children. Human bone fragments found west of the necropolis suggest that more burials may lie beyond the site’s boundaries. The burial pits were typically quadrangular or trapezoidal in shape and sized to fit the person buried inside. Some of the pits were also filled with artifacts.

Those artifacts caught the archaeologists’ attention. Two graves contained high-quality goods associated with warriors, including a sword partially preserved in a wooden scabbard, a single-edged knife, a shield, and a barbed javelin. The Inrap experts said the grave goods match those of Germanic chieftains, whose peoples allied with and joined the Roman army in the region near the Empire’s Rhine frontier during the fifth century.

The weapons and the clothing both featured decorative elements made of gold and silver and inlaid with garnets, further evidence of the high status of those buried.

Two graves associated with women also produced impressive finds, including silver-gilt bow brooches, silver bird-shaped brooches, glass-bead necklaces, belt buckles, and a bone comb. Even the horses received grave goods: harness equipment was buried with both animals.

The skeletons, however, told a grimmer story, with signs of injury and poor health found throughout the 14 burials. At least two of the deceased had fractures that were never set, and one of these likely left a man’s lower leg useless. Two other individuals had bone injuries likely caused by edged weapons. “The complete absence of perilesional bone remodeling suggests that death followed these violent acts rapidly,” the experts wrote.

The team was surprised to find so many injuries linked to violence in such a small sample of burials.

The fifth-century funerary complex was the excavation’s most striking discovery, but it wasn’t the only one. The team also uncovered part of the Gallo-Roman village’s core, including a residential district and a network of streets, showing that people lived there continuously from the first to the third century C.E.

Human activity at the site began in the middle of the first century C.E., and the site was most densely occupied from the second into the third century. Houses built of perishable materials stood on stone footings and were arranged along a street network that changed over time. Archaeologists also found hearths and wells, along with other structures that they said may have been used for industrial work.

After the village declined, a layer of silt covered the area. The silt shows only occasional use and little human activity through the fourth century, until the burials appeared in the fifth century.

Because evidence from this era is so rare, the funerary complex helps shed light on the poorly understood transition between the end of the Western Roman Empire and the Merovingian era in the Alsace region. “The exceptional nature of this find stems, in particular, from the scarcity of sites that document Germanic settlements during the specific chronological period in the region,” the statement reads. “These new findings will undoubtedly provide a fresh impetus for examining the region’s settlement dynamics, as well as the profound upheavals that shaped this territory during the second half of the fifth century.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

#6296. AI Surveillance Could Be Harming Your Health. Here’s How.

Doctors from Harvard and Johns Hopkins warn that mass surveillance is a health hazard—and AI is making it much worse.

When CEOs and scientists wax poetic about the potential benefits of AI, the technology’s impact on human health often rises to the top—and in many ways, they’re not wrong. Artificial intelligence’s ability to sift through massive datasets makes these algorithms ideal for spotting early-stage cancer or discovering novel drugs. The United Nations even notes that AI-powered disease surveillance could detect potential outbreaks quickly and prevent crises from spiraling into global pandemics.

However, like any tool, artificial intelligence can also be used for nefarious purposes, and a new perspective published in the New England Journal of Medicine highlights a particularly insidious one and its potential impacts on human health: mass surveillance. Debates over how governments and companies collect our personal data are usually framed as civil liberties or national security issues. But experts from Massachusetts General Hospital, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, and Harvard Medical School say that being watched can make us sick, and in the age of AI, things could get much, much worse.

The authors identify at least three ways surveillance harms health. First, knowing (or even believing) that you’re constantly being monitored can lead to hypervigilance and chronic “anticipatory stress,” which takes a toll on both physical and mental health. Second, surveillance can scare vulnerable people away from essential health behaviors. This includes groups with a reasonable fear of persecution, such as undocumented immigrants or people seeking reproductive or gender-affirming care, who may avoid pharmacies and clinics, hold back details from their doctors, or even skip buying groceries. Third, surveillance data can be used to hand out things that shape our health, like insurance, housing, and jobs, unequally.

“Historically, mass surveillance programs in the United States have most often been organized by government agencies and subject to democratic oversight,” the authors write. “AI-enabled surveillance, however, relies on data ecosystems that are controlled primarily by private companies.”

That’s a big distinction. The Fourth Amendment’s protections are limited when people voluntarily share information with third parties, even if they don’t realize they’re doing so. HIPAA also generally doesn’t cover data collected by consumer-facing tech companies. As a result, AI companies and other private actors can access and analyze vast amounts of personal data, and they could share it with the government without your knowledge or permission. Traditional surveillance usually needed human oversight. AI, by contrast, can continuously comb through social media, search results, financial transactions, geolocation records, and camera footage, then combine it all into increasingly powerful predictions.

This concern isn’t without real-world precedent. The Denver-based Palantir Technologies, founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, developed AI-enabled tools for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), including a system known as ImmigrationOS. ICE has used these tools to combine information from multiple government databases, including visa histories and Medicaid records, to target people for immigration enforcement. Another tool, called Enhanced Leads Identification and Targeting for Enforcement (ELITE), pulls names, photos, addresses, and race and ethnicity data from Medicaid records to map areas with people who could be detained, according to reporting in The BMJ. It can reportedly even generate a “confidence score” for whether someone might be at home.

For the authors, all this surveillance amounts to a public health problem. When data collected for health care or social services can be repurposed for surveillance, trust erodes, and people may stop using vital programs. That’s why they argue that AI-enabled mass surveillance should be considered an emerging “structural determinant of health,” which they define as a social, political, environmental, or economic condition that shapes how health and illness are distributed across a population.

“We believe medicine has an urgent responsibility to confront these developments,” the authors write. “Decisions about AI-enabled mass surveillance are being made with limited input from health experts, even though these systems have clear consequences for population health.” Health care technologies can contribute to the problem, too. Clinicians increasingly recommend wearables and smartphone apps that continuously collect patient data, which means the medical system may be feeding the same data streams that could be used for surveillance.

The courts offer another option. More than 20 state attorneys general have sued the federal government for sharing Medicaid data with ICE and Palantir, and the authors say health care institutions can support these lawsuits by publicly opposing troubling data-sharing deals. Clinicians can also help by documenting patients’ fears about how their data is used and any resulting changes in whether they seek care, which gives litigators and policymakers evidence to work with.

AI surveillance could still be a boon to public health. The same ability to rapidly pull together data from different sources that makes it dangerous could also help health officials spot and respond to threats more effectively. In the end, AI is just a tool, and it’s up to us how we use it. But the authors warn that we may not have long to decide. By the time AI surveillance’s effects become fully apparent, its infrastructure “may already be deeply embedded in everyday life.” As they put it, “The norms established today could determine whether AI-enabled surveillance becomes a tool in service to population health or a driver of avoidable health inequities and structural harm.”

#6294. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6293. A Viking Couple’s Grave May Reveal Who Really Settled This Strategic Island 1,100 Years Ago

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man were surprised to find not one but two of the island’s most significant Viking finds.

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man received double the surprise when they uncovered a 1,100-year-old double grave. It contained rare brooches typically worn by Scandinavian women and a sword that, according to one expert, would once have gleamed with a “bright silver” pommel. The site also produced intricately decorated trading weights, a Viking axe head, balance scales, and a ceremonial bronze ladle.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” Allison Fox said in a statement. Fox is curator for archaeology at Manx National Heritage, a museum and heritage trust on the Isle of Man, a self-governing British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland. “What makes it particularly exciting is the combination of finds, which gives us a rare opportunity to explore the lives of some of the island’s earliest Scandinavian settlers.”

Experts believe the metal detectorists, Daniel Crowe and Rhett Britton, came upon the double grave of a man and a woman who were buried with some of their finest possessions: three brooches for her and a sword for him. Fox said the date of the brooches suggests the grave may be the “earliest known female Viking Age burial” on the island. Together with the other finds, she said, the objects “help us build a picture of the people who lived here more than a thousand years ago, how they traded, and the connections they maintained across the Viking world.”

The find dates to around 900 C.E. That places it at the early end of the Viking Age on the Isle of Man, just as Scandinavian communities were becoming established there. Some of the objects are also the first of their kind found on the island.

Museum experts believe the Vikings first arrived on the island during the ninth century. Recognizing the strategic importance of its location in the Irish Sea, they established trading links before settling there. A rich Viking heritage remains across the island, and burials found in the past show evidence of pagan traditions. Viking influence still runs through Manx culture today. Tynwald, the island’s parliament, was founded during the Viking Age and is known as one of the world’s oldest continuous parliaments.

After making their discovery, Crowe and Britton didn’t try to clean the objects. Fox says this has allowed experts to fully appreciate the objects’ intricate details. She added that the brooches still have soil inside them, and the team is carefully excavating it in hopes of finding traces of textile.

Two of the brooches are a matching pair of oval “tortoise” brooches, the kind Scandinavian women wore to fasten their dresses at the shoulders. Both are covered in intricate interlocking animals, a hallmark of Viking art. According to Manx National Heritage, only one other pair like them has ever been found on the Isle of Man, and that was found by Daniel Crowe’s own father, John Crowe, along with fellow metal detectorist Craig Evans. The new pair is likely about 50 years older, which is why experts think this grave may be the island’s earliest known female Viking burial. The third brooch, decorated with spirals and a glass center, is the first of its kind found on the island.

The sword is the type a man would have carried, and it’s the 13th Viking sword found on the Isle of Man. Although the blade is badly corroded and parts of it are missing entirely, Fox said in a video from the heritage group that the pommel still shows “signs of the really intricate decorating that would have been on the pommel when it was buried.” X-ray analysis revealed traces of silver and copper wire inlaid into the iron, which makes it one of only three swords found on the island with such decoration.

“When this sword was buried,” she said, “this top part of the sword would have been really bright silver, a really high-status object.” In addition, traces of wood show that the sword’s handle was covered in wood rather than thread or horn.

Although 1,100 years in the ground caused much of the sword’s damage, experts believe the Vikings broke it on purpose as part of a burial ritual.

Because the brooches were found alongside the sword (items linked to a woman and a man, respectively), a double burial seems likely. Experts said, however, that they can’t be sure whether the grave goods came from one grave or from two graves placed close together.

Beyond the burial itself, the decorated lead weights and bronze balance scales found at the site highlight the Isle of Man’s role in Irish Sea trade. The weights are the first of their kind found on the island. One of them has a decorative bronze fitting, with artwork typical of Britain and Ireland, that may have been taken from another object.

The bronze ladle, another first for the island, was likely used in ceremonies.

Despite all the experts have gleaned from the discovery, there’s still much to be learned. “Although the original burial site has been disturbed,” Fox said, “further research may reveal much more about these objects and the people who owned them.”

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6291. The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These models deliver fast cleanup with minimal effort when there isn't enough accumulation to take out the snowblower. Here are our recommendations.

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was quickly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#6290. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have proposed a new tabletop device to detect the subtle way Earth's daily spin on its axis twists the space-time around it ‪—‬ an effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

If built, the sensor could measure the quantum effect known as frame dragging with the same precision as the best satellite experiments, but in minutes instead of years, the researchers proposed in a new study.

The research, published Sept. 17 in the journal Physical Review Letters, aimed to address a classic mismatch in physics. Picture a ring of clocks bolted to a spinning merry-go-round. You synchronize each clock with its neighbor around the ring. Then, you compare the last clock with the first. They don't match.

"It is impossible to synchronize that collection of clocks when you're in a rotating frame," Kai-Isaak Ellers, a physics graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) and first author of the study, told Live Science.

A photo of scientists working on NASA's Gravity Probe B in 2003. This device measured Earth's frame-dragging from space, confirming Einstein's predictions with an 18% margin of error.

Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a massive, spinning object drags the fabric of space-time along with it, just like a spoon twirling in honey. The effect is clearly visible around supermassive objects, like the Milky Way's central black hole. But around Earth, the effect is very faint.

So far, scientists have measured Earth's frame dragging only from orbit. They tracked how the twisting of space-time slowly shifts spinning gyroscopes or the paths of satellites. In 2011, NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite, which carried four gyroscopes, confirmed Einstein's prediction with a margin of error of about 18%. Satellites tracked with lasers have since done even better. In July, researchers reported in the journal Nature that the LARES-2 satellite had shrunk that margin of error to just 0.2%.

However, that took about three years of laser tracking. Researchers also had to account for the fact that Earth bulges at the equator and its mass is spread unevenly, which gives the planet’s gravity small irregularities that tug on satellites far more strongly than frame dragging does. To subtract those tugs, the team relied on detailed maps of Earth's gravity made by other satellites.

Measuring frame dragging more precisely is a way to stress-test general relativity. Several alternative theories of gravity predict a slightly different amount of twisting, and a lab-based measurement would also be free of the modeling assumptions that satellite experiments depend on, Ellers said.

The new device is a loop of superfluid helium-4 — helium chilled until it flows without friction and behaves like a single, giant quantum object. The loop is interrupted by a thin barrier riddled with tiny holes, called a Josephson junction. Superfluid helium can slip through the holes, but ordinary liquid helium cannot.

"That's where the quantum behavior comes from," said K. Birgitta Whaley, a quantum physicist at UC Berkeley and a co-author of the study.

As Earth spins and drags space-time, it nudges the quantum state of the helium flowing through the junction. That nudge shifts the frequency at which the helium sloshes back and forth in the loop, which the researchers could detect.

A visualization of Earth's uneven gravity field taken by NASA's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment in 2009. The lumpiness of our planet's gravitational field makes it harder to precisely measure relativistic effects.

Superfluid devices, many of them built at UC Berkeley, have detected Earth's rotation since the late 1990s. But the helium-4 versions built around a Josephson junction, like the new design, have worked within about a hundredth of a degree of 2.17 K (minus 455.76 Fahrenheit, or minus 270.98 Celsius), the temperature at which helium-4 becomes a superfluid. At that temperature, a lingering fraction of "normal" helium mixed in with the superfluid adds noise.

Instead, the team calculated how the device would behave at a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Below 0.7 K, the noise changed character, and the team found it drops sharply as the helium gets colder. One key finding in the new paper is the result of the team's thermal noise analysis, which showed how sensitive these devices could be at millikelvin temperatures, Elles said.

The catch is the barrier. Earlier helium-4 devices used holes about 90 nanometers wide. Working at these frigid temperatures demands much smaller holes, about 1 nanometer across ‪—‬ roughly the size of a helium atom. Keith Schwab, a physicist at Caltech and co-author of the study, and his collaborators are developing such materials, but they haven't been built into a working sensor yet.

If they can be, the researchers calculate that the device could measure frame dragging to 0.2% precision in about 35 minutes. If its vibrating membrane were made from the lowest-loss crystals, such as quartz or sapphire, that could drop to about one second, they said.

"This seems to be a very serendipitous discovery that at millikelvin, we can get this high sensitivity," Whaley told Live Science.

The signal corresponds to a time difference of about 10-35 seconds between helium flowing one way around the loop and the other — the same mismatch as the clocks on the metaphorical merry-go-round.

"The interesting thing about it is just how small it is," Whaley said. "It's not so far off from the Planck time," about 10-44 seconds, the shortest slice of time before the known laws of physics are expected to break down. This experiment is still a billion times too large to reach that limit, Whaley said. But future helium experiments could help explore whether time flows smoothly, like a ramp, or ticks forward in tiny, indivisible jumps, like the frames of a movie.

Ellers, K.-I., Christodoulou, M., Schwab, K. C., & Whaley, K. B. (2026). Quantum sensing of gravitational frame dragging with a superfluid ⁴He gyrometer. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121404. https://doi.org/10.1103/q3v9-rjm9
