#6288. A NASA Veteran Claims to Have Used Mind-Bending Physics to Conquer Gravity

Charles Buhler’s claim could change how spacecraft fly. But experiments show how much work it takes to establish that a mysterious push is real.

In April 2024, Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist who helped establish a laboratory at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, made a remarkable claim. His company, Exodus Propulsion Technologies, had built a device that could produce thrust without expelling propellant. He attributed the push to what he called a “New Force.”

As we reported in our earlier coverage, Buhler’s claim would have big consequences for spaceflight. That promise depends on whether researchers outside Exodus can reproduce the push and rule out an ordinary explanation.

One physicist has spent years investigating similar claims. Martin Tajmar, a professor and chair of space systems at Dresden University of Technology in Germany, has spent two decades measuring the forces produced by charged capacitors, including lopsided ones like the designs Buhler describes.

“It’s all negative,” he tells Popular Mechanics. Meaning, his tests found no evidence of that force within the limits of his equipment. He hasn’t tested Exodus’s hardware, but his experiments show what an independent test would need to account for.

A capacitor stores electric charge. Apply a high enough voltage to certain designs, and they can set the surrounding air moving, producing a push on the device itself. Tajmar calls this corona wind, “a discharge in air that drags air molecules with it.” In those cases, the device moves by pushing air backward, much as a fan does.

Tajmar’s team wanted to see whether a capacitor would still produce a push with almost all the air removed. For their 2024 study in Scientific Reports, they put the capacitor and its battery-powered electrical equipment together on a sensitive balance inside a vacuum chamber. At 10,000 volts, an asymmetric capacitor produced no clear sign of an unexplained force, even with instruments sensitive enough to detect a push measured in billionths of a newton.

Exodus hasn’t sent Tajmar a device, so he built his own capacitors for those experiments. He says his asymmetric design follows the principles in the company’s patent, though he doesn’t know the exact dimensions of its hardware.

“It’s Exodus who have to say why my asymmetric capacitor does not produce any thrust,” he says.

He believes his results challenge the company’s explanation, but he’d need its hardware to put its particular device through the same checks.

Keeping the battery and high-voltage equipment on the balance removes outside power cables that could interfere with the reading. Researchers also have to watch for electromagnetic forces or parts shifting as they heat up, either of which could look like thrust.

Tajmar also recommends swapping the device for an electrical dummy that draws power but should produce no thrust. If the balance still registers a push, something else in the setup is causing it. Researchers would need to track that down before treating the reading as evidence of a working drive.

Buhler has also said the devices can keep producing thrust after the power is switched off. Electrical charge can linger in insulating materials, leaving an electric field even after the supply is disconnected. Researchers would need to work out whether that leftover charge explains the reading and, if there really is a push, where it comes from.

In a short white paper, Exodus says other experimenters have reproduced the effect and argues that the device pushes against the vacuum itself, allowing momentum to be conserved. But it doesn’t include their laboratory reports. Without those details, readers can’t tell how the experiments were done or whether the researchers ruled out other causes of the push.

What leaving the propellant behind could change

Spacecraft have to bring along the propellant they’ll use to speed up, slow down or change course. That adds weight, which takes more propellant to move. The rocket equation puts numbers to that trade-off, showing how much a spacecraft can change its speed with the supply it carries.

If a drive could produce useful thrust without using up propellant, engineers could plan missions differently. A spacecraft could keep changing course as long as it had enough power and the drive kept working. Some of the weight now devoted to propellant tanks and their contents could go toward other equipment.

But the drive would bring its own baggage. It would need a power source and a way to get rid of waste heat, and all of that would have to travel with it. Engineers would need to find out whether the thrust was worth the weight of the complete system. Getting a reliable push in the lab would give them a reason to start working that out.

Light can give a spacecraft a push, too. When a laser sends light in one direction, the laser gets a tiny push in the other, because light carries momentum. Tajmar points out that this already offers a way to produce thrust without using up material propellant.

“If you just power a laser with the power that we use in our experiments, the thrust is also propellantless and actually already exists,” he says.

The catch is how much power it takes. To hold up a 1.2-ounce object, roughly the weight of the devices Buhler described, a laser would need to send about 100 million watts of light downward. A drive that produced a useful push with much less power would be worth engineers’ attention. Researchers would also have to explain what carries momentum in the opposite direction, as the light does for a laser.

“You have to test it in an independent laboratory. And then with a different method,” Tajmar says. He wants the results published so other experts can examine the work, including the equipment itself. Getting the same push on a different instrument would help show that the device deserves the credit.

Nobody needs to make the whole apparatus float. Even a small sideways push would warrant attention if it survived those checks and other researchers could reliably reproduce it. Then engineers could start asking whether it was strong enough to put to work aboard a spacecraft.

Buhler’s claim promises freedom from the propellant tank, which would change how we travel through space. The next move is closer to home. Put the drive in another lab, let someone else take the controls, and see whether the promise still has any push behind it.

#6287. Why do people keep stealing? Scientists uncover new clues

A study of repeat theft offenders suggests that difficulty learning from rewards may help explain why some people keep stealing.

People who repeatedly steal for profit may struggle to learn from rewards, a new study suggests.

In a game about finding the best payoff, offenders without kleptomania were slower to learn which choices paid off than people with no criminal record.

Yukiori Goto of the Graduate School of Informatics at Kyoto University in Japan led the research.

Among the co-authors are a clinician who treats kleptomania and a researcher at the Training Institute for Correctional Personnel of the Japanese Ministry of Justice.

The game tested only how people learn from rewards (not how they respond to punishment). Further, each person was tested once, so the study shows a difference between groups but cannot say what caused it.

According to Goto’s team, many people continue stealing even after being punished or sent to prison.

Some have kleptomania, a mental health condition that causes a strong urge to steal things, even when they have little or no value.

Others steal for money, out of need, or because of antisocial behavior. This is known as instrumental theft.

The study included 50 repeat theft offenders in Japan, most of whom had been jailed for shoplifting. Of these, 12 had kleptomania and were receiving treatment, while 38 did not have the condition.

Researchers compared both groups with 53 people who had no criminal record.

Each person played a computer game with four colored options on the screen. Each choice produced a payoff (a number from 1 to 100), and players were told to collect as much as they could.

However, the payoffs kept changing. The options started with average payoffs ranging from 20 to 80, and each payoff rose or fell from one round to the next.

Thus, the option that paid best at the start might not remain the best. A player had to keep deciding whether to make the same choice again or try another option.

The game ran for 160 rounds, and players had 1.5 seconds to choose or the payoff of that round was lost.

The game was shorter than in earlier research. Many participants, particularly the theft offenders, had dropped out of longer trial runs.

Compared with people who had no criminal record, the 38 offenders without kleptomania chose the best-paying option less often. The gap between their winnings and the best possible total was larger too.

Next, the choices of each person were fitted to a mathematical model of how people learn from rewards (a process known as reinforcement learning).

In the model, the learning rate describes how much each new payoff changes a player’s estimate of what an option is worth.

After age, sex, and smoking were accounted for, the offenders without kleptomania had a lower learning rate than the people with no criminal record.

By the team’s statistics, the data were about 650 times more likely with a real difference in learning rate between those two groups than without one.

“Given that instrumental theft is a profit-seeking behavior, reinforcement learning has been superficially believed to play a critical role, or even be abnormally enhanced in these individuals,” Goto said.

“Yet our findings have clearly demonstrated that recurrent instrumental theft involves neurobehavioral deficits.”

According to the authors, a person with a low learning rate gives little weight to recent results and is slow to change behavior when payoffs change.

Goto’s team hypothesized that slow learning could stop a person from coming to value stable rewards (such as holding a job). That person may then return to familiar behavior such as theft.

Results for the 12 offenders with kleptomania were inconclusive.

The learning rate in this group appeared higher than in the offenders without kleptomania.

However, the evidence was weak, as the data were only about twice as likely with a real difference between the two offender groups as without one.

The weak evidence may be explained by small group size, the authors wrote, and a larger sample might yet show a learning deficit.

Goto’s team suggested that kleptomania may involve an overwhelming urge to steal or a failure of self-control, rather than trouble learning the value of an action.

Brain signals were recorded from two of the groups as they played (the offenders without kleptomania and the people with no criminal record). The kleptomania group was not recorded, because of practical constraints at the testing sites.

Changes in blood oxygen were measured with near-infrared light at 10 points across the prefrontal cortex, a part of the brain that helps track what actions are worth.

In some parts of the prefrontal cortex, the oxygen signal tracked the value a player expected from the chosen option.

There was no reliable difference between the two groups in how closely the oxygen signal was tied to those values.

In two areas of the right prefrontal cortex, the groups did differ in their baseline oxygen signal, whatever was happening in the game.

Goto’s team suggested that such a baseline difference could add noise to learning signals without changing how the brain tracks value.

Criminal justice systems assume that offenders can adjust their behavior in response to severe consequences, Goto’s team wrote.

The game, which measured learning from rewards only, could not test that assumption.

According to the authors, learning from losses or punishment may work in entirely different ways in people with antisocial traits. The results cannot show how these offenders respond to legal penalties.

Why did these offenders learn more slowly? The researchers suggested two possible reasons: psychopathic or antisocial traits, or time spent in prison or other institutions.

Future studies could track offenders after release and test how they learn from punishment to see whether slow learning affects real-life stealing.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Psychology.

#6286. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6285. Young people worry about climate change, so what holds them back from taking action?

A survey of young Americans explores why climate worry can accompany both a willingness to act and a sense that taking action is pointless.

Worrying about climate change does not always translate into a willingness to act. A new study led by Portland State University suggests why.

Of the 1,603 young Americans who were surveyed, those most worried about the climate were the most willing to act on it.

Yet they were also the likeliest to feel that acting was useless, a state known as eco-paralysis.

But worry was not the strongest sign of eco-paralysis. Feeling annoyed by constant warnings about climate change was.

The study was led by Brianne Suldovsky, an associate professor of communication at Portland State University, together with colleagues at High Point University and the University of Arizona.

Because everyone answered the survey only once, the results can show which feelings tend to occur together, though not whether one of them causes another.

“We often assume that young people who are anxious about climate change will be motivated to do something about it,” Suldovsky said.

“Our findings suggest the relationship is much more complicated. Climate anxiety can motivate action, but it can also contribute to feelings of paralysis.”

The survey ran online for three weeks in late September and early October of 2024. Those who took it were aged between 13 and 22 and lived across the United States, with just under half of them younger than 18.

For most of it they were shown statements and asked to rate, from 1 to 5, how far they agreed with each.

There were nine statements about worry, one of which was “I feel anxious when I think about the consequences of climate change.”

They were also asked how willing they would be to do seven everyday things by themselves, such as recycling or turning the lights off when no one needs them.

Another seven activities involved broader political or collective action.

These included signing a petition, volunteering for a climate organization, and voting for a candidate who supports climate action.

A further 11 statements measured eco-paralysis, including “When I think about climate change, I feel so overwhelmed that I can’t do anything anymore.”

The more worried young people were, the more willing they said they were to act, and worry predicted that willingness better than anything else in the survey.

That was the case for the everyday steps and even more so for the group efforts.

Those who had given climate change more thought beforehand, and who rated it as more important to them personally, were more willing as well.

All of this is in line with what earlier studies of climate anxiety in teenagers and young adults have reported.

Worry also predicted eco-paralysis, though. The more worried a young person was, the more they agreed that their own efforts would not change anything.

Worry by itself could therefore not explain who wanted to act and who felt stuck.

The survey also measured a feeling which the researchers call climate contempt, using four statements that included “I am bored of hearing about climate change” and “I am annoyed by the constant publicity around climate change.”

Of everything that was analyzed, agreement with those four statements predicted eco-paralysis the most strongly, more so than worry did.

The young people who agreed with them more were also less willing either to take the everyday steps or to join the group efforts.

“Importantly, we found that climate contempt – or feeling annoyed about the panic over climate change – may be a key factor in understanding why some young people disengage from climate action altogether,” Suldovsky said.

Worry and annoyance were analyzed side by side, and each had its own link to eco-paralysis. The team did not test whether feeling both at once has any effect of its own.

Those who scored higher on worry tended to score somewhat lower on annoyance.

Asked where they learned about climate change, the young people said they had learned more from social media than from news outlets or from the people around them.

Yet how much they had learned from social media wasn’t tied to willingness to act, and it wasn’t tied to eco-paralysis.

It was different for news media. Those who had learned more from newspapers, TV, radio, online news or podcasts were more willing to join group efforts.

So were those who had learned more from family, friends, classmates and teachers, although that link was weaker. Neither of these sources was tied to the everyday steps such as recycling.

The survey asked only how much people had learned and not what they had learned. The authors noted that social media can carry false information about climate change as well as accurate information.

Close to half of U.S. teens described themselves as online almost constantly in a 2024 report from the Pew Research Center.

The study had several limits. Because it surveyed participants only once, researchers could not tell whether feelings influenced willingness to act or the reverse. It also measured intentions, not actual actions.

All participants had signed up for paid online surveys, so the findings may not reflect all young Americans.

Another concern was how contempt was measured. The questions focused on annoyance, boredom and surprise rather than hostility or resentment.

No climate messages were tested, leaving researchers unable to say which ones might cause annoyance.

Suldovsky’s team called for future experiments to compare climate messages and track what young people actually do, not just what they say they might do.

The full study was published in the journal Climate.

#6284. The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

Be prepared for unexpected power failures and off-the-grid camping trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

We evaluated eight power stations of varying sizes, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed their listed max output to see how well they could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using its AC adapter, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with more than five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

Bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts with 3,900-watt startup power and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

We hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-watt starting power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

The Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

A new and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

The Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

Performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

This power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

What is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

The S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

With the Bluetti Apex 300, the name of the game is flexibility. Alone, it delivers up to 3,840 watts of continuous power and handles up to an impressive 7,680 watts of surge power. Capacity is a solid 2,764.8 watt-hours for decent runtime, though it depends on the amount of power you intend to draw from it. If you happen to have 240-volt appliances or circuits, this model has you covered, too.

But everything on this power station is scalable. It’s possible to add up to six additional batteries for a very high capacity of 19,353.6 watt-hours, and connect up to two other Apex 300 units and run them in parallel. This expandability makes it a great entry-level home power station that expands into a larger backup system that delivers whole-home power.

The Apex 300 features four 120-volt outlets across the front, plus a 120-volt 30-amp outlet and a 120/240-volt 50-amp outlet on the side for powering devices individually, plugging into an RV, or delivering home power through a transfer switch.

One downside for me was the lack of direct DC outputs, e.g., USB-C ports. For that, you have to purchase an optional hub. There are also power inputs for a standard AC plug, a 30-amp connection, and two solar connections. The Apex 300 uses two inverters as opposed to one, giving you two banks of 120-volt, 1,920-watt output (two outlets in each bank). We easily ran two high-powered appliances at the same time, including a space heater and a toaster, with no issues at all.

This station is serious about solar recharging, too. There are two ports for connecting solar panels up to 1,200 watts each. Having the option of 2,400 watts of solar input is uncommon in a station of this size and price point. Plus, you can reach even higher input by pairing with a Bluetti SolarX 4K voltage regulator, which is designed for connection to larger solar arrays.

Most of the control options are accessed with the Bluetti Mobile app, and it’s one of the best we’ve seen. It’s easy to finely tune settings in ways that other companies don’t offer, such as adjusting the recharging level from as little as one amp to 50 amps.

If you’ve been eyeing power stations but aren’t sure if you want one more for portable power or more for home backup power, this is the model for you. It delivers a great amount of power for portable use, but lays the groundwork for building a more dedicated system in the future.

This is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

The unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans, and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The S5000 is the second power station in Anker's S-series, which features inverter efficiency technology that helps to reduce wasted energy when the inverter is idling or running lower-powered devices. We were impressed with how this technology performed in the S2000, and this model matched that performance.

We ran this through several tests, and the battery efficiency proved to be around 97 percent (the industry average is around 89 percent). For example, we left the AC inverter idling for 18 hours, and the battery remained at 100 percent capacity. Meanwhile, another station we idled at the same time lost 19 percent of its available power. That was impressive.

The next most impressive attribute about the S5000 is its size. It’s at least half the size of other power stations that feature 5,000 watt-hours of capacity and includes just as many outputs, including a 240-volt, 30-amp outlet. It also has both high- and low-powered DC inputs that enable up to 3,000 watts of solar power input if you have the panels to generate that. You can also recharge at up to 4,500 watts using a direct DC connection to Anker's 5500 Smart Tri-Fuel generator.

With only 4,500 watts of total output, we wouldn’t call this a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that), but the S5000 can deliver a decent amount to power an RV, run lights and appliances during an emergency, or even a couple of critical circuits.

During our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

This 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and new outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

We loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

As part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

The mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

We should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

In testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

Recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

The Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the important information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

All of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easiest to use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via Wi-Fi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel, via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge over a full 8 months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you plan to plug into it.

Some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds that you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048 watt-hour capacity, and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

Keep in mind that the usable watt hours are not the same as the watt hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

These days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

While all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Mid-size models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Large portable models can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

Portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large capacity power station that will back up critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn inputs off and on and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

Often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that they stay charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, this can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or run the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most new portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

That depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

Some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you plan on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

#6283. When to Visit Machu Picchu for Clear Views and Fewer Crowds

You may already have a clear picture of a trip to Machu Picchu long before you have a date to go in mind. On a first visit, you want time to take in the massive scale of the Inca city on its forested ridge above the Urubamba River, and then to walk among its stone walls. That picture, of course, depends on the weather. Here, where the Andes fall away toward the Amazon basin, a single bank of cloud can hide Waynapicchu, the peak behind the ruins, and with it the panorama you came to see.

The drier months improve the odds of a clear view, but draw more visitors with similar dreams to the same routes and entry hours. The weeks just after the rains offer greener slopes—and often thinner crowds—to anyone prepared to pack for showers. The best time to visit Machu Picchu comes down to matching the conditions to the type of visit you want, as well as confirming that your route is available before you commit to booking trains and rooms. Below are the questions that first-time visitors ask most, with advice from travel advisors and experts.

For a first visit, May and September—before and after the June-to-August rush, respectively—will have generally favorable walking weather, before the rains creep back in October. The two months aren’t interchangeable, especially if you hope to walk to the Sun Gate or the Inca Bridge. The 2026 route calendar opened those seasonal paths in September but not in May, so check the 2027 dates as soon as they’re published.

April brings greener slopes to anyone who can live with a little more water. “It’s also shoulder season so there aren’t many tourists yet,” says Alice Farkas, who leads marketing and communications at Aracari, a company based in Lima that plans private trips across South America. Kiernan Cochran, product manager at Andean, which plans trips throughout Peru, also favors April into early May. Even so, Cochran’s team books those weeks for travelers with much the same lead time as high season, since popular routes fill early.

When it comes to visiting Machu Picchu, daily timing might matter even more than which time of year you visit.

November through March offers significant savings on airfare and accommodations, though strategic planning remains essential. Permits for popular routes like Huayna Picchu still require three-month advance booking during these months (compared to six months of required lead time during peak season).

Mosquera makes a case for embracing the rainy season: "It's actually my favorite time. The site becomes magical with fewer crowds given that overtourism is one of Machu Picchu's greatest threats. The rain isn't nearly as disruptive as people imagine, as it mainly falls in the evenings, not all day. February is particularly special because the Inca Trail closes for maintenance, making the site even quieter." (Note: If you plan to arrive by trek, options will be more limited during these moments.)

The wet season transforms the landscape dramatically. Stone terraces flush vibrant green, hidden waterfalls emerge, and morning mist creates atmospheric reveals of the citadel. The timing also aligns perfectly with Peru's coastal summer. "More travelers are discovering this split-season strategy," says Mosquera. "You can explore misty ruins early in the trip, then travel down to Lima's world-class restaurants or Máncora's beaches where summer's in full swing." Temperatures at Machu Picchu remain moderate year-round, with rain typically following predictable afternoon patterns rather than all-day downpours.

The dry months from June through August draw the main crush of tourists, when the most desirable entry hours can sell out along with hotels and trains. Inti Raymi, the Inca Festival of the Sun, culminates in Cusco on June 24, and Peru’s Independence Day on July 28 brings another surge. In 2026, the daily cap was 4,500 visitors on ordinary dates and 5,600 on specified days, including June 19 through November 2, though that calendar doesn’t automatically carry over to 2027. Those places are also divided by route and hour, so your preferred route and entry time may be full even when the site has space overall.

Once each year’s tickets are released, Andean suggests booking sought-after routes about six months ahead in high season and at least three months ahead in low season.

Allow four or five nights in the region, as Cochran recommends, and begin in the Sacred Valley if your itinerary allows. Its Inca towns and terraces also mean the citadel isn’t your first encounter with the culture that built it. Cusco, where flights land for now, sits at roughly 11,150 feet. Heading straight down to the valley gives you a gentler start, and you can return to explore the city afterward. Cusco’s long-delayed replacement airport, Chinchero International, is under construction on the plateau above the Sacred Valley at about 12,340 feet, higher than the city itself. Its opening is targeted for late 2027, so most 2027 trips will still begin at the old one.

Ollantaytambo, at about 9,160 feet, is halfway between Cusco and Machu Picchu, and where travelers board the train to the latter. The town of ‘Ollanta’ has Inca-era streets and archaeological sites to explore, and is well worth a stop either going to or coming from Machu Picchu (the lovely El Albergue hotel sits just beside the train station).

From there, travelers catch the train to Aguas Calientes, also known as Machu Picchu Pueblo, which is the small town at the base of the ancient citadel. Spend the night prior to your Machu Picchu visit in Aguas Calientes for an early start up the mountain. Some allow just one day at Machu Picchu; others who want to appreciate the landmark from a few perspectives should budget two. You may, for instance, want to experience an upper terrace or a mountain climb alongside Classic Circuit 2, which is the standard walk through the Inca city (more on these routes below). If so, book that second route for another day. Either way, you can usually spend a full day at Machu Picchu and still catch a late afternoon/early evening train out, or bed down for another night in Aguas Calientes and depart the next morning.

Before buying anything sold simply as “Machu Picchu admission,” take a look at the official route maps, since the three circuits divide the site by elevation and access. For a single visit, Andean favors Classic Circuit 2. Its routes 2-A and 2-B each pair a viewpoint with a walk among the Inca buildings of the urban sector. Route 2-B takes its view from the lower terrace, a distinction worth knowing if you have a particular camera angle in mind.

For the upper-terrace panorama, choose Circuit 1’s route 1-B, which keeps you above the main streets, while route 1-A adds the climb up Machu Picchu Mountain which offers the classic view down onto the site. The Sun Gate and Inca Bridge carry seasonal tickets of their own. Circuit 3 covers the lower royal sector, including the Temple of the Sun. Its route 3-A adds the steep ascent of Waynapicchu (often spelled Huayna Picchu), which is the distinctive peak in the background of most Machu Picchu photos, and 3-B stays below. If Circuit 2 sells out, Andean suggests booking Circuits 1 and 3 separately to combine the panorama with a closer look at the ruins. Choose wisely before you arrive, since a ticket cannot be switched to another route at the gate.

Hikers face their own paperwork. Permits for the classic Inca Trail are limited and booked through authorized operators, and the shorter one-day trail from kilometer 104 of the rail line needs a permit and an operator, too. That day hike is Cochran’s own favorite—the final leg of the historic Inca route to the Sun Gate, without the multiday inn-to-inn or camping journey required. Ask what your hike covers before buying a separate admission.

Under the September 2026 rules, trail arrivals enter on a designated Circuit 3-B ticket, which matters if you also want Circuit 2 or the upper panorama. Heavy rain can also shut the kilometer 104 path outside the usual February maintenance period, which is something to keep in mind for any rainy season travel.

Your train booking does not include admission (treks are on a case-by-case basis; ask!), so buy entry through the Ministry of Culture’s Tu Boleto portal, where you choose your route first and your entry hour second. Enter each visitor’s details carefully, matching names and information to the same identification document they’ll present at the gate. The ticket fixes the holder’s name, date, time, and route; current rules allow no changes to the name or date after purchase.

The purchase process changed in September 2026, when the ministry began a 30-day trial of direct paid checkout in place of the earlier unpaid hold. Under the portal’s current purchase manual, you have 15 minutes from the start of an order to enter everyone’s details and pay. Have documents and payment ready, and follow the instructions on screen. Rail and admission are also released on separate timelines. PeruRail opened 2027 train sales on September 22, but Yuriko Aquino of PROMPERÚ, Peru’s tourism promotion agency, says the Ministry of Culture has yet to announce when 2027 admission will go on sale or what the daily visitor cap will be. If you buy rail first, read the fare’s change terms before you pay.

Within the overall cap, up to 1,000 tickets a day are held for in-person sale in Machu Picchu Pueblo, valid for entry the following day. If you’re counting on that uncertain fallback, budget a night in town. Whichever way you buy, a guide is recommended for a standard citadel visit, while Inca Trail hikers follow their operator’s separate requirements. Guides can be booked through your hotel or at the entrance to the site.

From Cusco, most travelers cross the Sacred Valley by road to Ollantaytambo and board the train there for the ride along the Urubamba to Machu Picchu Pueblo. From town, a separate shuttle bus climbs to the entrance in roughly half an hour. Check boarding points and total travel time before choosing a fare, since PeruRail’s January-to-April departures from Cusco involve a bus-and-train transfer.

For a first visit, Cochran favors a morning train from the Sacred Valley and an afternoon Circuit 2 entry, when her team generally finds the site less crowded; three or four hours is usually enough to take it in. Among the premium trains, she points to Belmond’s Hiram Bingham, PeruRail’s Vistadome Observatory, and IncaRail’s First Class.

Whichever train you choose, leave a cushion between arrival and admission. Peru’s tourism authority advises reaching the shuttle station about an hour before your gate slot, or setting out about two hours ahead if you plan to walk uphill. A train that pulls in just before your entry time leaves little margin for the bus queue and the gate check.

Down in Machu Picchu Pueblo are two fantastic Peruvian-owned options—Inkaterra Machu Picchu Pueblo Hotel, with scattered adobe casitas among orchids, and Sumaq Machu Picchu Hotel, which faces the Urubamba River. Both are close to the shuttle stop. Sanctuary Lodge, a Belmond Hotel, is the only property up on the mountain at the gates of Machu Picchu, which spares you the morning shuttle ascent, though hotel guests still enter on the same timed admission as everyone else.

#6282. Repairing damaged cells may not be enough to reverse aging

A new theory suggests the body’s signals may amplify cellular damage, helping explain why repairing cells alone might not reverse aging.

Aging is often described as a slow build-up of damage, but it is not a constant process. For many decades, the body declines only slowly, whereas in old age this decline speeds up sharply.

Some forms of cellular damage accumulate at a roughly steady rate in adulthood, yet the risk of death rises much faster. Why is that?

In a new paper, Pierre-Edouard Sottas of the xLongevity Center in Vevey, Switzerland, draws attention to the signals that pass between our cells and organs.

In his view, the effects of cell damage are not necessarily confined to the place where the damage occurs. They may be spread through the body by its own signaling network, and may even be amplified.

Further, if this is correct, simply repairing damaged cells may not be enough to reverse aging in old age.

This is only a theory for now. Sottas did not carry out any new experiments, but built his argument on previous research and a simple mathematical model.

So what is the real question for Sottas? An aging body, in his account, is more than the sum of the defects in its separate cells and tissues.

“The key question is what determines whether local dysfunction stays contained, is buffered, or becomes organism-level decline,” he wrote.

Earlier population analyses estimated that eliminating all cancer deaths would add only a few years to life expectancy, because the people spared would still die of other causes.

The risk of dying of those other causes rises steeply with age. This steep rise in the risk of death was first described in 1825, and is known as the Gompertz law.

Under this law, an adult’s risk of death does not increase by a fixed amount each year, but is multiplied instead. At the rate used by Sottas for humans, the risk doubles about every eight years.

As a result, deaths in late life are not spread evenly, but fall within a fairly narrow window of ages. According to Sottas’s calculation, the typical spread in the age at death is about 15 years.

Cell damage of several kinds, on the other hand, builds up in adults at a roughly constant rate.

Measurements show this for DNA mutations, for the shortening of telomeres (the protective caps on chromosomes) and for changes in the chemical tags on DNA.

On its own, a constant rate of cell damage is not enough to explain a risk of death that keeps doubling, Sottas wrote.

Sottas explains his idea using two terms: “load” and “gain.” Load is the damage that builds up inside cells. Gain is how much the body’s signals increase the effects of that damage.

His idea builds on a theory by Mikhail Blagosklonny, who suggested that the processes helping us grow when we’re young don’t fully switch off. As we age, they can start doing more harm than good.

Sottas believes something similar happens with the body’s immune, inflammatory and hormonal signals. When we’re young, they help protect and repair us.

But as we get older, these signals may keep spreading and making each other stronger.

Think of a microphone too close to a speaker. A small hum quickly turns into a loud screech. Sottas suggests aging signals may work in much the same way.

Cells that have stopped dividing for good (because of damage or stress) are known as senescent cells. In early life, this shutdown serves as a defense against cancer.

However, these cells are not inactive. They release molecules that promote inflammation, and they also release tiny membrane-wrapped packets, called extracellular vesicles, which carry proteins and genetic material.

These signals can reach other cells, nearby and in distant tissues. Those cells can then be pushed into the senescent state too, and start to send out signals of their own.

There are estimated to be 1.5 trillion vesicles entering human blood plasma every minute, which translates to tens of vesicles per day for every cell of the body.

A senescent cell can release vesicles at 10 to 100 times the rate of the non-senescent cells around it. Thus, only a small number of such cells is needed to supply a large share of the signal.

According to Sottas, the loop is held in check in a young body by systems of repair and clean-up.

As these systems weaken with age, senescent cells build up, and even a little new damage can then have an outsized effect on the whole body.

Sottas also addressed the case of the naked mole-rat, an exceptionally long-lived rodent, which he treated as a natural test of the theory.

The cells of the naked mole-rat are not spared from damage. In fact, more oxygen-related damage (to fats, DNA and proteins) has been reported in this animal than in mice, even at young ages. The chemical tags on its DNA also change with age.

If the pace of aging were set by damage alone, then the animal’s risk of death would be expected to rise sharply with age.

But this isn’t the case in the naked mole-rat. Across more than three decades of records, its risk of dying has hardly increased with age at all.

For Sottas, this suggests that the load is present in these animals without the gain. Even though the cells of the naked mole-rat suffer damage, this damage may never be amplified.

Why not? One possible reason comes from experiments on naked mole-rat cells. When these cells were pushed into the senescent state, they went on to die, which could prevent senescent cells from building up and their signals from persisting.

Sottas cited a study in which half the plasma (the liquid part of blood) of old mice was replaced with salt water and albumin, a blood protein. No young blood was added.

Afterward, muscle repair in the old mice improved, their livers had less fat and scarring, and more new nerve cells formed in the brain.

For Sottas, these findings support the idea that reducing circulating signals may improve tissue function in old mice.

Human evidence remains at an early stage. In a placebo-controlled trial of 42 healthy adults (over 50), a similar procedure called plasma exchange lowered estimates of biological age based on chemical tags on DNA.

These estimates do not establish that participants became healthier or would live longer.

Other treatments act on single cells, for example partial reprogramming, which resets a cell’s gene activity toward a younger state. In mice, this has improved retina, muscle and nerve function.

However, no study has documented the rejuvenation of several organs together (liver, kidney, blood vessels, immune system and brain) after such treatment.

According to Sottas, the repair of cells should work best as prevention in early life and may slow aging in midlife.

He proposes that lasting reversal in late life would require resetting the body’s signals.

In his paper, Sottas does not actually show that changing the body’s signals can reverse aging in humans. His model follows only four quantities, and the human evidence comes from two small studies.

Sottas was a co-author of one of them, a pilot that was completed by only 14 healthy volunteers. A comparison group was missing.

He is also affiliated with xLongevity, an organization active in longevity and rejuvenation. Sottas disclosed this as a conflict of interest.

Some damage may also remain even after the signals are reset. A reset might soften the effects of such damage (DNA mutations, shortened telomeres, stiffened collagen), but according to Sottas its full correction may require repairs inside cells.

Sottas has outlined six testable predictions, one of which is that shifts in the signals of the blood should appear before any improvement in the tissues.

The question that is still open is whether a reset of the body’s signals can produce a lasting improvement across many organs.

New methods to measure biological age, which go beyond the chemical tags on DNA, are needed to address this question, Sottas suggested.

The paper was published in the journal Aging.

The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

The unconformity is sharply evident in the transition between Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone and Proterozoic Brahma Schist in the Grand Canyon.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

Erosion during Neoproterozoic times, followed by sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times, formed the Great Unconformity. Bottom: Dynamic uplift was followed by subsidence for Laurentia ('LAU'), Baltica ('BAL') and North China ('NCH').

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

#6280. Tiny ocean animals reveal a hidden foundation of marine life

Tiny ocean animals depend on different food sources across the Pacific, revealing important differences in marine food chains.

Microscopic algae form the base of many ocean food chains, but bacteria also play a major role.

In the warm, nutrient-poor tropical Pacific, researchers found that roughly half of the food supporting tiny crustaceans called Calanus copepods could be traced back to bacteria.

Near the Arctic, in the Bering Strait and the southern Chukchi Sea, more than half was supplied instead by dinoflagellates, a group of algae.

Calanus is an important food of fish and seabirds, and a change in what feeds it can therefore be passed on to animals higher in the food web.

The study was led by Hyuntae Choi and Kyung-Hoon Shin of Hanyang University ERICA in South Korea; the co-authors include Brian Popp of the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa.

The copepods were collected on cruises between 2015 and 2020.

What the work provides is therefore a comparison among regions at particular moments; it is no record of change in a single place.

Copepods are small crustaceans that drift with ocean currents. They include Calanus, which feed by filtering tiny food particles from the water.

Adults were collected from two research ships, the Isabu and the icebreaker Araon, by means of nets pulled up from a depth of about 660 feet (200 meters).

From the tropical and subtropical Pacific, the sampling sites extended through the subarctic Pacific and the Bering Sea as far as the Bering Strait and the southern Chukchi Sea.

Copepod proteins were then broken down in the laboratory into their separate amino acids. Of these, the essential amino acids cannot be made by animals, which must get them from food.

Production of those amino acids by each source at the base of the food web yields its own mixture of carbon isotopes (slightly heavier and lighter forms of the same element).

Because passage up the food chain leaves the mixture almost unchanged, it serves as a fingerprint.

The proportion derived from each of six groups was then estimated with a statistical model; the groups included diatoms, dinoflagellates, two kinds of cyanobacteria (bacteria that use sunlight) and bacteria that feed on organic matter.

Such proportions refer to the origin of the food and not to what each copepod actually ate, since part of it may first have passed through other microbes.

The tropical Pacific is strongly layered: a warm surface layer mixes little with the nutrient-rich water below it. The condition is known as stratification, and relatively few algae grow there.

Satellite measurements of chlorophyll, the pigment with which algae capture sunlight, ranged there from 0.03 to 0.13 milligrams per cubic meter, against as much as 7.86 near the Bering Strait.

For these tropical waters, the model put about 31% of the copepods’ food base down to bacteria that feed on organic matter.

Cyanobacteria that turn nitrogen gas into a usable nutrient added about 20%, and algae about 47%.

Bacteria thus supplied roughly as much of the food base of tropical copepods as algae did.

Farther north, the share from algae increased with latitude, reaching about 74% in the southern Chukchi Sea.

The share of bacteria feeding on organic matter fell to about 16%, and that of nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria to about 7%.

The greater contribution from algae came mainly from dinoflagellates, single-celled organisms that use sunlight and of which some also eat other microbes.

In the tropics, dinoflagellates and diatoms contributed similar shares, about 19% and 18%. In the southern Chukchi Sea, dinoflagellates reached about 52%, whereas diatoms stayed near 15%.

The small share of diatoms is notable, because diatoms were the most common algae counted in the northern water samples (although at some sites dinoflagellates were equally or more numerous).

The ships reached these waters after the bloom of algae had ended, when nutrients were scarce and the sea ice had largely melted.

Dinoflagellates and other small algae tend to become more common under those conditions, the authors noted.

The researchers suggested that diatoms may be digested more slowly, or that copepods may choose other food. Across all sites, the dinoflagellate share increased with chlorophyll, a relationship shown by no other food source.

Nitrogen in the same amino acids was also used to estimate the number of feeding steps between the copepods and the bottom of their food web.

One estimate counts mainly the steps through animals. A second also counts steps through protists, single-celled grazers that eat bacteria and algae.

In the tropics, the second estimate exceeded the first by less than one step. At subarctic and Arctic sites, it exceeded the first by more than one step.

The authors wrote that the larger difference indicates more feeding on protists at higher latitudes during summer.

The difference between the estimates was also greater where the dinoflagellate share was higher.

The team therefore proposed that dinoflagellates able both to use sunlight and to eat microbes may be an important link between microbes and Calanus in the north.

Algae need nitrogen, which here came from two main sources: nitrate dissolved in seawater, or nitrogen gas turned by cyanobacteria into living tissue.

The two sources carry distinct nitrogen isotope signatures, which allowed the contribution of each to be estimated.

In the tropical Pacific, about 29% of the nitrogen in algae was estimated to come from nitrogen gas. Bacteria break down what the cyanobacteria make, and the nitrogen released is taken up by the algae.

In the Bering Strait and the southern Chukchi Sea, by contrast, nitrate supplied an estimated 91% of the algae’s nitrogen.

The authors linked the tropical pattern to stratification, which limits the amount of nitrate reaching the sunlit surface where algae grow.

“Importantly, our study shows how warming-driven changes in stratification and nutrient dynamics are reshaping planktonic food webs,” Shin said.

The study nevertheless compared different regions and did not follow a single region as it warmed.

Warm Pacific water flowing north through the Bering Strait in summer has sped up the loss of sea ice in the western Arctic Ocean, the authors noted.

Between 2015 and 2017, no year-to-year differences were found in the diets of copepods from the subarctic Pacific to the southern Chukchi Sea.

Summer surface water in the Bering Strait and the southern Chukchi Sea was, however, warmer in 2019 and 2020 than in 2016 through 2018.

An Arctic species, Calanus glacialis, also became less common there, while Pacific species increased.

The authors wrote that food-chain measurements from those warmer years may differ from the ones reported.

Not every copepod was identified to species, and tropical and northern waters were sampled in different months, so that seasonal changes could not be checked.

It also remains unclear whether dinoflagellates that eat other microbes carry the carbon pattern of an alga or that of their prey, an uncertainty that could blur the fingerprints.

The authors called for isotope measurements across more of the North Pacific and over more years, to see how these food chains vary as the ocean keeps warming.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.
