#6278. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6277. Crocodiles face a hidden threat that may weaken a vital survival response

Caimans with more mercury in their blood showed a weaker stress hormone response, raising concerns about how pollution affects their survival.

Mercury pollution may be weakening the stress response in crocodiles and their relatives.

Researchers studying smooth-fronted caimans in South American rainforests found that animals with more mercury in their blood had a weaker stress hormone response.

Gold mining is a major source of mercury pollution in South America. The findings suggest that mercury may interfere with a natural defense system that caimans and other crocodilians depend on to survive in the wild.

Jérémy Lemaire of the University of Vienna led the project with colleagues there and at the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna.

The researchers studied 20 adult and nearly adult caimans in French Guiana between November 2023 and June 2024.

“Given the overlap of crocodylian habitats with gold mining activities, this is a conservation concern that deserves immediate attention,” Lemaire said.

Since the late 1800s, atmospheric mercury has risen an estimated 300% to 500% above its natural level, mostly from burning fossil fuels.

Small-scale gold mining is a major contributor to this pollution. It produces 38% of the mercury released into the air worldwide, and more than 80% of mercury emissions in South America and sub-Saharan Africa combined.

Caimans live a long time and take in mercury mainly through their food. Over many years, it builds up in their bodies, which makes them a useful measure of how polluted their streams and forests are.

The authors describe mercury as an endocrine-disrupting chemical, meaning one that interferes with the body’s hormones.

Theirs is the first study to measure this hormone response in wild animals living in a tropical forest with high mercury levels, the team wrote.

The researchers studied caimans in different parts of the rainforest. One of the sites was the Nouragues nature reserve.

They caught the animals between 8 and 11 p.m. to account for the natural changes in stress hormone levels throughout the day.

Researchers caught each caiman with a snare pole. They taped its snout shut and laid a wet towel over its eyes, so every animal went through the same experience.

Then they drew blood four times. The first sample came within 3 to 5 minutes of capture to estimate baseline hormone levels. The rest came 15, 30, and 60 minutes after capture.

Red blood cells went to the mercury test. The liquid part of the blood went to a test for corticosterone, the main stress hormone in reptiles and birds.

Mercury in the caimans’ dried red blood cells ranged from about 0.3 to 2 parts per million. The team split the animals into three groups: four with low levels, nine in the middle, and seven with high levels.

At the first blood draw, resting hormone levels were about the same in all three groups. The groups differed only in the one-hour sample.

In the low and middle groups, hormone levels rose over the hour. In the high-mercury group, the levels didn’t change by a statistically significant amount at any point.

At 60 minutes, the high group’s levels were lower than those of both other groups. The high-mercury caimans started with similar hormone levels but showed a smaller increase after capture.

Across all 20 animals, the more mercury a caiman carried, the smaller the difference between its resting level and its level at one hour. Mercury levels accounted for about 40% of the variation in that difference.

The most contaminated caiman’s hormone increase was more than 100 times smaller than that of the least contaminated one.

“A fast, robust stress response is essential for survival in the wild,” Lemaire said.

“We show that even relatively low mercury burdens affect this response in caimans, potentially limiting their ability to cope with predators, extreme weather, human disturbance, and ultimately survive in the wild.”

Stress hormones work by attaching to a protein called the glucocorticoid receptor, which helps activate the body’s stress response.

Mercury can interfere with this process. Studies in male rats found that mercury made it harder for hormones to attach to the receptor.

Computer simulations also suggest that mercury can partly block the hormone’s binding site by attaching to an amino acid called cysteine.

Lemaire’s team found this same amino acid in the receptors of crocodilians and other vertebrates. This could help explain their findings, although they haven’t tested the effect directly in caiman cells.

The caimans had mercury levels similar to those found in other crocodilians worldwide.

Some slender-snouted crocodiles in Gabon, for example, have had blood mercury levels as high as 11 parts per million.

The researchers say the problem may extend beyond areas near gold mines. Even at the levels found in this study, mercury was linked to a weaker stress response.

More than a third of the 26 living crocodilian species are threatened with extinction, according to the IUCN.

Mercury pollution could put them at greater risk if it affects their ability to survive and reproduce.

The effects on wild populations could take years to become noticeable.

Since the late 1800s, crocodilians have gone through about five generations. In comparison, large land animals with generations lasting 5 to 10 years have gone through around 20.

Crocodilians take a long time to produce new generations, which can make changes in their populations difficult to detect.

Researchers still need to find out whether caimans with weaker stress responses are more likely to die or have fewer offspring.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

Archaeologists have found a 2,200-year-old golden bear in an Iron Age burial in Kazakhstan that may have held seven people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gold bear would have been worn on a headdress.

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan have discovered a unique gold bear figurine in a 2,200-year-old burial mound that looters had hit but failed to empty completely.

The sculpted bear stands on its hind limbs and holds a pot-like container between its front paws. The artifact would have been worn as part of a headdress, and holes at its base indicate that it could have been sewn onto the garment, according to a translated statement from the Kazakhstan government.

The 2,200-year-old gold bear is a unique find in Kazakhstan.

The gold bear was unearthed at an Early Iron Age burial mound at the Karagaily burial ground in the southern city of Almaty, along with a surprisingly high number of human bones for a single burial mound.

Although other gold-crafted animals have been found in the region, the newly unearthed bear is the first of its kind.

"The sculpted bear figurine is unique to Kazakhstan. No similar finds have been discovered previously," Lyazzat Sagyndykova, director of the Almaty Museums Association, which conducted the excavation, said in the statement. "This discovery allows us to trace cultural parallels across the whole of Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to Altai."

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan excavated a 2,200-year-old burial mound.

The figurine dates to the Saka period, named for a nomadic horseback-riding people from Iran who lived on the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin of what is now western China. Archaeologists have found comparable gold objects at other excavations in Kazakhstan, according to the statement. For example, a headdress element shaped like a small leopard previously came to light at the Almaty Kok-Kainar burial ground, which dates to the fourth century B.C. Also, the headdress of Kazakhstan's famous "Golden Man," a young Iron Age warrior buried in an extraordinarily lavish grave, also has a gold, sheep-shaped decorative element.

It's unclear which bear species the figurine depicts, but today Kazakhstan is home to two subspecies of brown bear: the Tien Shan or Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus), which lives in the Tien Shan Mountains in the southeast, and the East Siberian brown bear (Ursus arctos collaris) in the Altai Mountains in the east, according to a study published earlier this year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Preliminary analyses date the recently excavated site to the fourth to third centuries B.C., according to the statement. Based on the number of bones they excavated, experts suspect that the mound, which is around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and roughly 85 feet (26 m) wide, may have been the final resting place for four adults and three children.

Archaeologists found a surprising number of human bones in the burial mound.

"Of particular interest is the unusually large number of human remains in a single burial mound, as such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan," Marat Mugalovich Nurpeisov, a senior research fellow at the Almaty Museums Association, said in the statement. "As a rule, burial mounds of a comparable size were intended for the burial of one or two people."

Archaeologists also found pieces of Saka pottery, most of which had been strewn about after the burial had been looted in ancient times, according to the statement. The thieves left behind a 10-foot (3 m) looting pit.

"Research into the Karagaily burial ground is ongoing," Nurpeisov said in the statement. "To clarify the circumstances of the burial and determine the exact number of individuals interred, further analyses are planned, including the involvement of anthropologists."

After all of the investigations are finished, some of the artifacts will be put on display at the Almaty Museum, according to the statement.

#6274. How did barn owls reach the Americas? DNA offers an unexpected answer

Barn owls reached the Caribbean by crossing the Atlantic and spread from there to the mainland, while the islands' own giant owls died out.

A barn owl hunting over a Pennsylvania hayfield looks like it has always belonged there.

The common assumption was that barn owls arrived the way so many animals did, overland from Asia, then spread out to the islands offshore.

The DNA suggests the owls reached the Caribbean before spreading to the mainland.

The ancestors of every barn owl in the Western Hemisphere arrived first in the Caribbean, most likely by flying across the Atlantic from the Old World.

The oldest branches of the American barn owl’s family tree are still on the islands, along with the bones of its giant relatives, all of them now extinct.

Min Zhao led the work as a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History.

Collaborators included Jessica Oswald, now at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service‘s forensics laboratory in Oregon, and David Steadman, the museum’s curator emeritus of ornithology.

“Looking at their modern distributions, barn owls are widespread across continental America but not so much in the Caribbean. So, you would assume that the Caribbean barn owls came from the continent, right?” Zhao said.

“But actually, based on genetics, we found that the most divergent lineages are in the Caribbean.”

In an interview with Earth.com, Zhao said the finding is about the owls that people already know.

“For birdwatchers in the continental Americas, the barn owls they see today have ancestors that can be traced back to the Caribbean islands,” she noted.

The team read DNA from 42 owls for the main analysis.

A second analysis examined mitochondrial genomes from 68 owls, focusing on DNA inherited from mothers.

Most of the DNA came from the toe pads of stuffed museum specimens collected between 1876 and 1995, plus a few ribs and fresh tissues.

A century-old skin, it turns out, still holds enough DNA to place its owner on the family tree.

Specimens came from 11 museums, including the Field Museum in Chicago and Louisiana State University.

Fossil bones from the Bahamas, the Cayman Islands and Jamaica went in too, though radiocarbon dating showed none was older than about 220 years.

Together the samples covered all 11 recognized subspecies of the American barn owl and 15 of the 18 living barn owl species worldwide.

Dates on the family tree came from a molecular clock anchored by fossils, with Virginia Tech‘s Julie Allen among the co-authors.

The Western Hemisphere owls split from their Old World relatives about 5 million years ago, with a plausible range of 3.75 to 6.5 million.

Every branching after that happened in the past 2.6 million years.

Within the American barn owl family tree, the owls of Cuba, Jamaica, and the Cayman Islands form their own old branch. So do the owls of the Lesser Antilles.

The continental owls, by contrast, barely differ from one another across the mainland, which is what a recent, fast spread looks like.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most when the genetics pointed to the Caribbean, Zhao highlighted two barn owl subspecies in the Lesser Antilles.

Both are much darker than mainland barn owls and live on nearby islands, including Dominica and St. Vincent. Those similarities had led researchers to consider them close relatives.

“One of the biggest surprises was finding that the two barn owl subspecies in the Lesser Antilles represent two distinct evolutionary lineages and are not each other’s closest relatives, at least based on the genetic data we have so far,” Zhao said.

The Lesser Antilles “may harbor more evolutionary diversity than we previously thought,” Zhao said, and more genetic research is needed before the full picture there is known.

Reconstructing where each ancestor lived, the authors found the first foothold in the Americas was most likely the Greater Antilles.

From there owls reached the Lesser Antilles, then probably South America and then North America, with some traffic back out to the Bahamas and Bermuda.

Barn owls could perhaps have come by the Bering land bridge or by island-hopping across the North Atlantic.

However, Steadman grew up climbing a 35-foot-high (10.5-meter-high) silo to watch the barn owls that roosted on top. He noticed they left every year before the snow buried the voles they hunted.

“Barn owls are tropical and temperate. They can’t handle high latitudes where there’s snow. So, coming over to the Americas via Beringia or the North Atlantic via some blend of Iceland, Greenland and Canada never seemed realistic,” he said.

An ocean crossing has a witness of sorts. In 1722, the naturalist Mark Catesby wrote of an owl that appeared over his ship midway between Africa and America and tried to land on it.

Plants have made the trip: the sea lavenders spread from the Mediterranean to Atlantic islands and on to the Caribbean.

“Owls are good dispersers, and barn owls are probably the best,” Steadman said.

The findings from the Galápagos revealed another unexpected twist in the barn owls’ history.

An owl from Santa Cruz Island turned out to carry the earliest-diverging lineage of American barn owl anywhere.

This suggests its ancestors reached the Galápagos from the Caribbean before barn owls spread across the mainland.

A second owl, from San Cristóbal, belongs instead to the South American group, whose ancestors arrived much more recently.

San Cristóbal is the island closest to the mainland, heavily settled, and home to introduced mammals that an owl could hunt.

The first arrival came earlier in the Pleistocene and the second in the late Pleistocene or Holocene, Zhao said.

The dark owls live on western islands such as Santa Cruz and Isabela, and the much paler ones on eastern islands such as San Cristóbal.

“This means that the barn owls living in the Galápagos today may look like variations of the same bird, but they actually have two very different evolutionary histories,” she told Earth.com.

The Santa Cruz lineage differs enough in genes, plumage and bone to be its own species, the authors wrote, under the name Tyto punctatissima. It has already vanished from Floreana Island since people settled there in the 1800s.

The giant owls are the part the DNA couldn’t reach. The team tried five bones of the Hispaniolan giant barn owl and three of the Bahamian barn owl, Tyto pollens.

None yielded usable DNA. So whether the giants came from the same crossing or a separate one stays open.

In the Bahamas, Oswald also heard stories of the chickcharney, a legendary huge, owl-like creature that steals people away.

The real bird, Tyto pollens of Cuba and the Bahamas, stood roughly 3 feet (1 meter) tall.

Asked whether the giants met people, Zhao said that is quite likely. She pointed to Guadeloupe in the Lesser Antilles, where remains of another extinct giant barn owl species were found at an archaeological site.

“This suggests that humans and giant barn owls lived on the same island at the same time, and may even have encountered each other,” Zhao said.

The paper tallies the Caribbean’s lost barn owls, giants and a dwarf among them, alongside the hutias, rice rats and shrews they ate.

People reached the islands at least 6,000 years ago, hunted that prey and brought in new animals, and the specialist owls disappeared along with their food.

The Hispaniolan giant may have held on into the 1700s. No barn owl species is known to have gone extinct on a continent.

Whether the island giants were one lineage or several is the first open question, and better-preserved bones could help resolve it.

Within the two continental groups, the branches are short and some are weakly supported. The order in which owls spread across the mainland is therefore less certain than the big picture.

The common American barn owl keeps moving. It settled Hispaniola in the mid-1900s and nested in Puerto Rico for the first time in 2015. It has likely just reached San Cristóbal.

The authors wrote that it could outcompete the distinct island birds that remain, and they called for faster study of the Galápagos owls.

Common barn owls are themselves declining in parts of North America and Europe as small farms give way to monocultures and the birds face exposure to pesticides and rodenticides, the authors noted.

Steadman pointed to the little-known barn owls of the Lesser Antilles as the next target. They have barely been studied, he said, because no one considered them unique. Their genetics now say otherwise.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

#6272. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

W. Xin et al. Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252825

#6271. Picturing the outcome may help robots follow instructions

A new robot system uses predicted images to guide its movements, showing promise on tasks that require following detailed spoken instructions.

Robots that follow spoken instructions often turn words and camera images into movements.

A team in Seoul has built one that also pictures what the table should look like when the job is done, and uses that picture to choose its moves.

On four real tasks with a robot arm, it finished 78.4% of its attempts, a little ahead of comparison systems from NVIDIA and Physical Intelligence.

The system is called Dynin-Robotics. Hoeun Lee led the project in Jaeyoung Do’s AIDAS Lab at Seoul National University.

“This study is significant in that a single model jointly handles what a robot should do, how its surroundings will change after it moves, and what actions it should actually take,” Do said.

Most robot control systems of this kind take an instruction and a camera image and produce a stream of arm movements.

Dynin-Robotics does that too, but it treats words, images, video frames and robot movements as the same kind of data, a sequence of tokens. It learns four tasks on that one sequence.

The model produces the next movement. It predicts what the camera will see after that movement.

It predicts what the finished scene should look like. And it can watch a video of the robot working and write a sentence saying what the robot did.

Before any of that, the model was trained on about 1.33 million recorded sequences of robot movements drawn from 48 datasets in the Open X-Embodiment collection. It was then tuned separately for each job it was tested on.

The team first ran the model in a simulator on two tasks, picking a named fruit and placing a flower in a vase. The researchers then tested how well it handled rephrased instructions.

A direct request like “Insert the rose into the vase” became “Identify and carefully handle the flower linked to gestures of love, arrange it in the vase.”

A version trained on all four jobs handled those rephrased instructions better than a version trained only to produce movements.

Steering the moves with the predicted goal picture, and predicting the next scene alongside each move, helped further, but only together.

Either one on its own did worse than ignoring the pictures entirely.

Caveats like that run through the paper. The benefit of predicting the future, the authors wrote, depends on how those predictions are put to use.

The physical tests used a single Franka Research 3 arm in one workspace.

The four conditions were moving a named fruit, sorting colored cubes into matching boxes, stacking four cubes in any order, and stacking them in a spoken color order.

Averaged across the four, Dynin-Robotics scored 78.4%. Physical Intelligence’s π0.5 scored 76.9%, NVIDIA‘s Cosmos Policy 73.6% and its GR00T N1.6 model 73.0%. The 1.5-percentage-point gap over π0.5 was not spread evenly, though.

Cosmos Policy was the best of the group at moving fruit, at sorting and at free-order stacking.

Dynin-Robotics pulled ahead only when the instruction set the stacking order, where it succeeded 68.5% of the time against 64.0% for π0.5 and 42.0% for Cosmos Policy.

The authors read that as the unified model’s clearest advantage: tasks where the words carry a constraint the robot has to keep in mind.

The team also sped up the model’s own decision-making. A rewritten decoder produced movement commands up to 29.2 times faster than the original version.

That figure covers the model alone, not the camera, the network or the arm itself.

Everything physical here happened on one arm in one room, and the authors wrote as much.

The team said the system would need testing across a far wider range of objects, tasks and settings before it could work in a factory or a warehouse.

The team hopes to adapt the system for robots working in those settings.

The image predictions also showed a limitation.

On the standard measures of how close a predicted picture is to the real next frame, simply copying the previous frame still beats the model’s prediction.

The authors argue that whole-image scores miss the small changes caused by an action, and they list a direct test of those changes as unfinished work.

The model’s ability to describe what a robot did was judged by eye rather than scored. Longer predictions, other robot bodies and other kinds of sensors are the next steps the authors name.

Beyond that, the team has said it wants to build robot teams that split a goal into tasks and retry what fails.

The paper has not been published in a journal; it is posted as a preprint on arXiv ahead of its presentation at NeurIPS 2026.

#6270. The Universe May Be Twice as Old as We Think. A Rebellious Theory Says We Can Prove It.

A model built only on matter we can see still nails the Big Bang’s first elements—and doubles the universe’s estimated age.

We can all agree that the universe is more or less 13.8 billion years old, right? That figure comes largely from the European Space Agency’s Planck satellite, which mapped the cosmic microwave background (the leftover glow of the Big Bang), with results released in 2013 and finalized in 2018. Ground-based observations from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) in Chile later arrived at nearly the same number. Both fit the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). There’s just one problem: That age depends on the existence of dark matter and dark energy, neither of which has ever been directly detected.

What would happen if we tried to figure out the age of the universe with only tangible matter and energy? Physicists Rajendra Gupta and Nikolaos Samaras of the University of Ottawa are asking this exact question. Frustrated by theories built on invisible matter and on an expansion driven by energy no one has detected, Gupta and Samaras developed their own cosmological framework, called covarying coupling constants plus tired light (CCC+TL). In this model, only quantities measured in units of length change together over cosmic time, while dimensionless constants stay fixed. The researchers tested whether CCC+TL could reproduce Big Bang nucleosynthesis, the process that forged the universe’s first light elements in its earliest minutes. It could. The same model puts the age of the universe at 26.7 billion years, nearly twice the standard estimate.

“In this framework, only quantities with explicit length dimensionality covary through a universal scaling function, while dimensionless constants and dimensionless ratios remain invariant,” the researchers wrote in a study recently published in Universe, also adding that their model ensures “[Big Bang nucleosynthesis] predictions are preserved.”

In 1929, astronomer Edwin Hubble (namesake of the Hubble Space Telescope) found that the farther away a galaxy is, the more its light is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum. Most astronomers came to read this redshift as evidence that the universe is expanding. That same year, astronomer Fritz Zwicky proposed a different explanation, known as “tired light”: Light gradually loses energy as it crosses vast distances, so light from more distant galaxies arrives redder simply because it has traveled farther. Most cosmologists set tired light aside decades ago, but Gupta has revived a version of it as part of CCC+TL.

Gupta and Samaras are challenging the prevailing view. In ΛCDM, the hot plasma of the newborn universe expanded and cooled, and ordinary (baryonic) matter then gathered inside vast haloes of dark matter to form galaxies. Dark energy, meanwhile, is thought to be driving the universe’s accelerating expansion. CCC+TL abandons both of those hypotheses. Instead, the new theory modifies the standard equations for gravity and expansion, yet still reproduces the observed expansion of the universe and the amounts of hydrogen, helium, and other light elements formed in its first minutes. It can also reproduce galactic rotation curves, which measure how fast stars and gas orbit at different distances from a galaxy’s center.

Gupta has also argued, in earlier papers, that CCC+TL gets around the objections that sank tired light the first time, including time dilation. In an expanding universe, light from distant supernovae is stretched out in time, so the supernovae seem to brighten and fade more slowly than nearby ones. Simple tired-light models don’t provide an explanation for that phenomenon. Time dilation itself comes from Einstein: Because light always travels at the same speed, observers moving at different speeds experience time differently, and time passes more slowly for someone moving very fast. That’s why astronauts aboard the International Space Station, which circles Earth at about 17,500 mph (28,000 kph), age very slightly more slowly than people on the ground. Gupta says his new theory works better because the tired-light effect runs alongside cosmic expansion, instead of replacing it.

Dark matter and dark energy have been used to explain phenomena that would otherwise make no sense. CCC+TL tries to explain the same phenomena with modified gravitational effects instead. It also changes the cosmic timeline. In a 2023 paper, Gupta used CCC+TL to put the age of the universe at 26.7 billion years. That would give the first galaxies billions of years longer to form, which could explain surprisingly mature galaxies in the early universe and the Methuselah star, which some age estimates make older than the universe itself.

“A central requirement for any alternative cosmology is that it preserves the key empirical successes of standard Big Bang nucleosynthesis,” Samaras and Gupta wrote. They concluded that “the CCC+TL model is consistent with the [Big Bang]-predicted primordial helium and other light-element observations.”

The idea remains well outside the mainstream. Most cosmologists still see ΛCDM, for all its unknowns, as the best fit to a wide range of observations, from the cosmic microwave background to how galaxies are spread across the sky. CCC+TL will have to pass many more tests to win them over.

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6269. These Music City Airbnbs Exude All of Nashville’s Southern Charm

In the two decades I’ve lived in Nashville, I’ve seen a lot of changes. When I first moved, my friends and family would ask why I lived here; now, they’re asking when they can come visit. And as the Music City grows, so does the number of gorgeous places to stay. Travelers can choose from vacation rentals in any neighborhood for any group size, whether that be large bachelorette parties looking to hang out near the honky-tonks, or solo music lovers who want to catch a show at the Grand Ole Opry. Houses with vast yards are good options for folks with kids, dogs, and songwriter friends who want to pull out the guitar, and some even boast private pools that let you keep the summer heat at bay. Nashville, of course, is known for its street of honky-tonks, and securing a modern condo downtown with a bird’s-eye view of all the action offers a one-of-a-kind experience that you won’t soon forget. No matter what type of stay you’re after, there’s an excellent Nashville vacation rental worth holing up in. Read on for some of my favorite vacation rentals in the city I call home.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, editor stays, ratings, amenities, location, decor, and previous guest reviews.

There’s even a dedicated workspace if you have to check in with the office while on the road. It’s an oasis slightly away from all the noise and activity that downtown brings, but just a short drive from any late-night action you desire.

It’s the perfect spot for those who like to balance their big-city trips with a bit of solitude and relaxation after a long day. (If you're traveling with toddlers or infants, the home also offers a pack-and-play and children's books and toys.) There's also a full kitchen complete with a gorgeous Smeg fridge.

Location: Music RowThings to do nearby: Studio B; Vanderbilt University; Belmont University; restaurants, bars and shops in Hillsboro Village and Edgehill Village; Belcourt Theatre

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Nashville?

East Nashville and Wedgewood-Houston are two busy and buzzy neighborhoods with great dining scenes, music venues, and fun shopping. They’re also a quick Uber or bike ride to downtown, making it easy to experience it all. If you’re looking for something a bit quieter, check out the leafy Sylvan Park neighborhood. For something fit for families, head to Donelson, with easy access to parks and the Opryland attractions.

When is the best season to visit Nashville?

There’s no bad time to visit Nashville, but spring and fall offer more temperate weather, when it is easier to hike, bike, and paddle, or just stroll down Broadway without the steaminess of a southern summer collecting under your hat. Most people want to be in Music City during the warmer months to take advantage of outdoor concerts and street festivals, but if you come in winter, you’ll get to cheer on the NHL’s Nashville Predators and see the holiday magic of the five million lights at Gaylord Opryland.

In my opinion, a trip to Nashville should be about five days long, which offers you enough time to expand your vacation beyond Broadway and the honky-tonks. You’ll have enough time for a day or two in town—you can boot-scoot under the neon lights of Lower Broadway—and still have a few days for exploring the surrounding parks, greenways, museums, shops, and music venues away from the crowds.

#6268. Tadpoles are dying in waves in Brazil, and scientists have found a clue

Scientists linked recurring tadpole deaths in a Brazilian pond to ranavirus, with outbreaks more likely after weeks of low humidity.

Before January 2024, the only tadpole deaths recorded at a small pond in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest were isolated cases involving predators.

Since then deaths at the pond have occurred in repeated waves. Outbreaks were reported in three consecutive breeding seasons.

According to the research team, the cause was ranavirus. This virus is known to infect amphibians and reptiles as well as fish. Outbreaks were found to be more likely after periods in which the air had been dry for some weeks.

Most of the dead tadpoles (315 of 324) belonged to the monkey frog (Phyllomedusa distincta). This leaf frog is found only in the Atlantic Forest.

The authors reported that this was the first confirmed ranavirus die-off among wild native amphibians in the American tropics.

Researchers also recorded a sharp decline in egg-laying compared with counts from two decades earlier.

The authors believe the virus is the most likely explanation for the decline. A gap of more than 20 years in the egg counts makes a direct link difficult to establish.

The study was carried out by Aline Fonseca as part of her doctoral research at the Federal University of Paraná (UFPR).

Her colleagues included the owners of the reserve: Germano Woehl Jr. and Elza Nishimura Woehl of the Rã-Bugio Institute.

The work took place at the Rã-Bugio Sanctuary, a protected reserve of about 12 acres (4.75 hectares) in Guaramirim in the state of Santa Catarina.

The pond itself is fed by two springs. It is roughly two-thirds the size of a tennis court and has been kept free of fish so that frogs are able to breed in it.

Monkey frog tadpoles tend to hang upright at the surface of the water. As a result, dead tadpoles were relatively easy to find and count.

Three outbreak periods were recorded. The first ran from January to April 2024 and the second from November 2024 to January 2025. The third lasted from late November 2025 to March 2026.

Of the 324 dead tadpoles that were collected, 315 were monkey frogs and nine were Bischoff’s tree frogs (Boana bischoffi). Ranavirus DNA was detected in 287 of them (about 89%).

Redness and swelling were commonly observed in the infected tadpoles along with bleeding beneath the skin. Bleeding inside the eye was noted in some individuals.

The presence of a virus in a dead animal does not by itself establish the cause of death.

Liver tissue from 13 infected tadpoles was therefore also examined under a microscope and large areas of dead cells were found.

No sick tadpoles were observed in a second pond that lies about 1,500 feet (450 meters) away and is separated from the first by intact forest.

Measurements made at the affected pond during the first outbreak showed that water acidity was normal. No signs of contamination were detected.

On several occasions the discovery of a first dead tadpole was followed within a short time by many more.

Tadpoles that were dying were seen floating at the surface and were unable to swim down. In most cases, death followed within 30 minutes.

Tadpoles that hatched early or late in the breeding season survived better than those that hatched in the middle of it.

The pond was most crowded in the middle of the breeding season, when nearly all tadpoles died.

Most of the bodies that were recovered belonged to young tadpoles whose back legs had only begun to form.

However, older tadpoles carried about the same amount of virus. This suggests that heavier infection was not the reason the young made up most of the dead.

The authors believe timing is a more likely explanation. Most tadpoles in the pond were still young when the outbreaks occurred.

It is also possible that larger dead tadpoles were eaten by predators and scavengers before they could be counted.

Monkey frogs lay their eggs on leaves above the water.

The female folds each leaf around the clutch (a group of eggs). When the eggs hatch, the tadpoles drop into the pond below.

Between August 1999 and February 2004, the Woehls searched leaves, stems and tree trunks around the pond every morning during the breeding season.

Each new clutch was marked so that it would not be counted twice.

The same daily counts were repeated from August 2025 to February 2026 after the second outbreak season.

Egg-laying was estimated to have fallen by about 83% (with the likely decline lying between 70% and 90%).

Clutch counts were lower throughout the breeding season.

The decline therefore could not be explained by a change in the timing of laying.

The researchers suggest that fewer young frogs surviving to adulthood could help explain the decline in egg-laying.

Daily records from the three outbreak seasons were compared with weather data. Humidity (the amount of moisture in the air) was found to be the strongest predictor of deaths.

Temperature did not help to predict them. Rainfall added no further information once humidity had been taken into account.

When average humidity over the previous two weeks was 65%, the team’s model estimated a nearly 98% chance of finding dead tadpoles on a given day. When it was 90%, the estimate fell to about 7%.

“The virus is likely present in the environment at all times without causing disease, but low humidity may cause it to increase its own replication and trigger an outbreak,” Fonseca said.

As water levels fall the tadpoles are crowded into less space. This may make it easier for the virus to spread between them.

It has also been suggested by the authors that dry conditions may place the animals under stress and weaken their immune defenses.

Dry weeks may help to explain when outbreaks occurred.

But the researchers also had to consider whether longer-term changes in the weather could account for the decline in egg-laying.

For this reason, weather records covering the period from 1999 to 2026 were examined.

No clear long-term trend was detected in temperature or rainfall or humidity. Average temperature rose by about 0.27°F (0.15°C) per decade.

This increase was not statistically significant. The records therefore did not establish a clear warming trend.

Whether egg counts came from before or after the outbreaks explained the decline better than any of the weather measures. Adding weather data to that comparison improved it only slightly.

It should be noted that the weather data were not collected at the pond. They were taken from a global dataset in which each area measures about 7 by 6 miles (11 by 10 km).

No clutch counts were made between 2004 and 2025. As a result the point at which the decline began cannot be determined.

Although no signs of pollution were found at the reserve, other threats to the frogs cannot be ruled out.

Ranavirus is regarded by the authors as the strongest explanation for the fall in egg-laying. But it has not been shown to be the cause.

Six stretches of the virus’s genes were sequenced and were found to be identical in every sample analyzed. All of them matched the frog virus 3 group.

That group is known to infect amphibians and reptiles and fish on several continents. Because the match is so close, the origin of the outbreak is difficult to trace.

Ranavirus has previously killed wood frog tadpoles in North America. In South America most confirmed die-offs had until now involved bullfrogs raised on farms.

Frog virus 3 has caused repeated losses at farms in the Atlantic Forest region that raise American bullfrogs.

The authors suggest that wastewater from crowded farms could carry the virus into wild ponds. It has not been established that this occurred at the reserve.

The virus may have arrived in the forest recently, or it may have been present for many years.

Co-author Luís Felipe Toledo of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) has spent more than a decade studying chytrid fungus.

The fungus is another threat to amphibians. His group has found evidence of the fungus on Brazilian amphibians dating back to 1916.

“Perhaps the ranavirus has also been here for a long time. It remains to be seen what changed for it to become a threat,” Toledo said.

Climate forecasts for the Atlantic Forest indicate that droughts are likely to become more frequent and more severe.

The authors warn that if dry weeks do help to trigger these outbreaks then losses of this kind could occur more often and become more serious.

The UFPR team plans to collect samples from nearby areas in order to find out where else the virus is present. Toledo has also pointed to museum collections as a possible source of clues.

Testing preserved frogs could help to establish how long ranavirus has been in the region.

The study is published in the journal Biodiversity and Conservation.

Archaeologists have discovered the shoe of the first governor of the Danish West Indies, recovered from a 17th-century ship that was wrecked after one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark’s history.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Maritime archaeologists investigating a 17th-century shipwreck off the coast of Sweden have discovered a fancy shoe and two metal rings used as currency in the transatlantic slave trade. The items were lost during a mutiny on a slave ship in 1683, during which the governor of the Danish West Indies was thrown overboard.

The Danish frigate Havmanden (which translates to "Merman") was en route to St. Thomas, a Caribbean island that is now part of the U.S. Virgin Islands, with convicts and indentured servants aboard destined for work on the island with the Danish West India Company. The plan for the Havmanden, after dropping off the new colonists, was to sail to West Africa to buy enslaved Africans. But due to a shortage of food and water, several crewmembers and convicts aboard seized control of the ship near the Azores in the North Atlantic and began sailing it back to Copenhagen.

The mutineers shot the ship's captain and threw other officers ‪—‬ including Jørgen Iversen Dyppel, the first governor of the Danish West Indies ‪—‬ overboard in the English Channel. After the ship ran aground, the mutineers were tried for their crimes in Copenhagen and sentenced to death.

The story of the Havmanden is one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark's history, according to a Nov. 11 translated statement from the National Museum of Denmark. But now, underwater archaeologists are learning more about the fateful voyage from the wreck, which lies on the seabed just east of Gothenburg, Sweden.

Archaeological divers discovered the rear half of a man's "unusually fine" shoe in the wreckage, according to the statement.

"I see a great many shoes from shipwrecks, but I have never before seen a shoe of such high quality," Vivi Lena Andersen, director of the Rudersdal Museums in Denmark, said in the statement.

The sole has a high level of craftsmanship, Andersen said, which can be seen in the minuscule holes perforating the edge of the shoe. The regularity of the holes would have required tools and expertise that only the most skilled shoemakers had at the time. It was "undoubtedly an expensive and exclusive shoe that only the elite could afford to buy," Andersen said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Because the shoe was likely owned by an upper-class individual, experts think it could have belonged to Iversen, the Danish West Indies governor who was thrown overboard.

"The shoe testifies not only to Jørgen Iversen Dyppel's life and dramatic death, but also provides a personal point of entry into the larger story of the establishment of the Danish colonies in the West Indies and the widespread slave trade Denmark was a part of," Andreas Kallmeyer Bloch, a maritime archaeologist at the National Museum of Denmark's Center for Maritime and Underwater Cultural Heritage, said in the statement.

Additional clues to the Danish slave trade on board the Havmanden included two manillas, ring-shaped pieces of metal that were used as currency in West Africa. European merchants cast manillas from copper, brass or iron and traded them for enslaved people in West Africa, particularly along the coast of modern-day Nigeria. But manillas are rarely found in Scandinavia, according to the statement.

"The manillas add another layer to Havmanden's story and underscore the connection to the slave trade, which was a central part of Denmark's colonial activities in both the West Indies and on the west coast of Africa," Kallmeyer Bloch said.

Denmark continued to engage in the transatlantic slave trade for more than a century after the Havmanden sank. Although King Christian VII of Denmark-Norway banned the trade in 1792, slavery continued in the Danish West Indies until 1848, when hundreds of enslaved people revolted and were finally granted their freedom.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6265. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#6264. Webb captures a galaxy still reeling from an ancient collision

Webb’s infrared view of the Cartwheel Galaxy reveals how an ancient collision reshaped its structure and sparked waves of star formation.

Today’s Image of the Day features the Cartwheel Galaxy, where a bright ring of stars surrounds a glowing center and curved strands of dust stretch between them like spokes.

The striking shape emerged from a violent collision that disrupted a spiral galaxy hundreds of millions of years ago.

New stars now shine along the outer ring, while traces of the galaxy’s earlier structure remain woven through the scene.

The view comes from the James Webb Space Telescope, which combined observations from two infrared instruments to reveal stars and dust in extraordinary detail.

Released on August 2, 2022, the image also includes two smaller companion galaxies and a background scattered with more distant galaxies.

Located roughly 500 million light-years away in the constellation Sculptor, the Cartwheel belongs to an unusual class known as ring galaxies.

Its appearance differs sharply from the familiar spiral arms of our Milky Way.

Astronomers attribute that shape to a high-speed collision between a large spiral galaxy and a smaller galaxy.

The smaller galaxy responsible for the impact is outside this image, so neither of the two prominent companions should be mistaken for the intruder.

The encounter sent disturbances outward through the larger galaxy, producing a bright inner ring and a much broader outer ring.

NASA compares their expansion to ripples spreading across a pond after a stone hits the water.

Those enormous ripples have reshaped the galaxy over hundreds of millions of years. What appears to be a finished wheel is still undergoing change.

The outer ring marks a region where the collision’s effects continue to unfold. As it expands into surrounding gas, it triggers the formation of new stars.

NASA estimates that this outer structure has been expanding for about 440 million years.

Star formation and supernovas, the explosions of dying stars, help make it an especially active part of the galaxy.

The center has its own concentrations of activity. Hot dust fills the bright core, and its most luminous areas contain enormous clusters of young stars.

Together, these regions show how a galactic collision can do more than rearrange existing material.

It can also change where new generations of stars emerge, leaving a pattern that remains visible long after the original encounter.

Earlier observations, including images from the Hubble Space Telescope, had already revealed the Cartwheel’s unusual structure. But dust obscures parts of the galaxy when viewed in visible light.

Webb observes infrared wavelengths, allowing astronomers to examine stars that are harder to distinguish through that dusty veil.

Its Near-Infrared Camera, or NIRCam, reveals points of starlight and pockets of star formation.

It also helps distinguish the smoother distribution of older stars from the clumpier regions associated with younger populations.

The Mid-Infrared Instrument, known as MIRI, adds a different perspective by detecting emission from dust and revealing material rich in hydrocarbons and silicate compounds.

Combining the instruments brings the stellar populations and dusty structures into the same view.

Each contributes information that would be harder to recognize from the other instrument alone.

The image’s colors translate infrared observations into a form human eyes can see. They help separate different features rather than reproduce the view an astronaut would see through a window.

Blue points mark individual stars or regions of star formation.

Bright red strands trace glowing dust, including the curved spokes that connect the inner and outer portions of the galaxy.

Those spokes preserve something of the spiral galaxy that existed before the collision.

Despite the disruption, the Cartwheel retained rotating arms, linking its present appearance to its earlier form.

Similar glowing dust also appears in the companion spiral galaxy toward the upper left, giving viewers another structure to explore beyond the dominant ring.

The Cartwheel’s eventual shape remains uncertain.

Its expanding rings and surviving spiral features capture a galaxy in transition, with its past still visible inside the changes set in motion by the collision.

That makes the image more than a portrait of an unusual object.

Across its bright rim and dusty spokes, the Cartwheel records how one encounter can influence a galaxy for hundreds of millions of years.

The collision has passed. The galaxy is still responding.

#6263. Singapore Airlines Unveils the ‘Largest Double Bed in the Sky’ As Part of a $1.6 Billion Redesign

The airline announced the $1.6 billion redesign on Friday, November 6, with the first aircraft expected to enter service in the second half of 2027.

Singapore Airlines's new first class cabin

And the luxury doesn't stop there. The new suites will feature Italian Poltrona Frau leather upholstery, personal wardrobes, dedicated dining spaces, and 32-inch 4K entertainment screens. Passengers can also expect proper bedding, including cotton sheets, duvets, a choice of pillows, and mattress toppers from German bedding specialist Paradies.

The new business class seats also come with adjoining seats, offering the option to sleep alongside a traveling companion.

But what about those of us traveling farther back? Premium economy will benefit from additional personal space, adjustable leg rests, dedicated storage, and larger entertainment screens. Meanwhile, economy passengers can look forward to redesigned seats with more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The new economy class will feature more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The upgrades will be introduced gradually across Singapore Airlines's new Boeing 777-9 aircraft and 41 retrofitted Airbus A350-900 aircraft, including its ultra-long-range fleet. The latter will also receive first class cabins for the first time.

There's no confirmed date yet for when passengers will be able to try the new double beds, but one thing is certain: cuddling up at 35,000 feet has just become a little more appealing.

#6261. Rising seas could threaten coastal homes sooner than flood maps suggest

A study of Oʻahu finds that waves and erosion could threaten homes, roads, and sewage systems earlier than simple sea level rise maps suggest.

Most sea level rise maps assume that only land below the future ocean level will flood.

A new study of Oʻahu found that this approach misses 62% to 73% of the land at risk when sea levels rise by less than 4 feet (1.2 meters).

Anna Mikkelsen, a graduate student in the Department of Earth Sciences at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, led the study, which was carried out with colleagues at the university’s Climate Resilience Collaborative.

Waves and coastal erosion could threaten homes, roads, and sewage systems on the Hawaiian island long before rising water floods these areas.

The researchers used computer models to estimate exposure rather than actual damage. They assumed that no new defenses would be built and that no buildings or residents would move between 2022 and 2150.

Planners often use a method called passive flooding in regions where little data is available.

The model raises the sea surface and marks land below the projected water level.

Mikkelsen’s team combined two other hazards with passive flooding. The team used an erosion model to project shoreline retreat along 9,523 survey lines around the island.

A separate wave model estimated coastal flooding from the largest waves of a typical year.

The three hazard maps were placed over public records of buildings, land parcels, roads, schools, hospitals, parks, sewer mains, and cesspools.

The researchers repeated the comparison at 1-foot (0.3-meter) increments of sea level rise, up to 6 feet (1.8 meters).

The dates for each step came from federal sea level projections issued in 2022 for the Honolulu tide gauge.

Under the Intermediate scenario, the sea stands 3.8 feet (1.16 meters) above its 2000 level by 2100.

Under the Intermediate-High scenario, which assumes rapid loss of ice sheets, it stands 5.8 feet (1.78 meters) above that level.

The ocean already reaches some of the island’s buildings.

In 2022, 544 buildings housing about 2,700 residents lay within zones exposed to erosion, high tides, or yearly high waves.

Passive flood maps would have missed nearly all 544 buildings. Waves alone affected 84% of them, while erosion affected the remaining 16%.

Passive flood maps also miss most threatened cesspools. Of the 54 cesspools already lying inside a hazard zone, 82% are threatened by erosion and 98% are left off passive flood maps.

On Oʻahu, waves and erosion threaten coastal areas before permanent flooding does.

The higher waterline is expected to become the main hazard after 3 to 4 feet of sea level rise.

The team estimates that 74% of the affected buildings and 87% of the affected cesspools would still be left off a passive map even when the sea has been raised by 4 feet.

“This tells us that it is critical to use multiple hazard models, and that areas with little data, such as other Pacific Islands, that rely on simpler passive flood model estimates may be underestimating the risk to their coastal infrastructure,” said Mikkelsen.

Exposure increases gradually through the first 3 feet (0.9 meters) of sea level rise. It then roughly doubles over the next foot.

The models project that the number of affected buildings goes from about 5,900 to about 11,100 between 3 and 4 feet of rise. Affected residents go from about 27,800 to 58,100 on an island of roughly 1 million people.

The length of affected road grows from 57 miles (92 kilometers) to 130 miles (210 kilometers). Affected sewer mains grow from 38 miles (61 kilometers) to 94 miles (151 kilometers).

The timing depends on the scenario. Sea levels are projected to rise 3 feet by 2073 under the Intermediate-High scenario and 4 feet by 2102 under the Intermediate scenario.

“Sea-level rise will not come to O‘ahu as a slow, harmless rise in the water level,” said Chip Fletcher, the paper’s senior author and director of the Climate Resilience Collaborative.

“Waves and erosion are already damaging homes, roads and wastewater systems, and our results show a threshold, somewhere between 0.9 and 1.2 meters of rise, where scattered local problems become widespread infrastructure failure.”

Honolulu has the largest number of exposed buildings and residents, and low streets in parts of the city are already flooded by high tides.

Honolulu’s dense street network gives drivers other routes around flooded blocks. But many rural coastal communities depend on a single highway.

The models project that erosion will make about 650 feet (200 meters) of Kamehameha Highway impassable in Kaʻaʻawa on the east side.

The models project this loss at just 1 foot of sea level rise, expected around 2051 under the Intermediate scenario. No alternative route runs along that shore.

Residents who live north of Kaʻaʻawa now reach central Honolulu in about 35 minutes, and that travel time would be tripled by a detour around the rest of the island.

Farrington Highway carries as many as 40,000 vehicles a day along the west side, and no public alternative exists for it.

Impassable sections are projected by the models at 3 feet of rise and 15% of the highway is projected to be impassable at 4 feet.

Earlier studies of managed retreat in Hawaii put the cost of relocating a major road and its buried utilities at about $279,210 per meter in 2025 dollars.

The authors applied that figure to the 31 miles (50 kilometers) of major road exposed by 2100. The estimated cost came to nearly $14 billion.

Many households on Oʻahu are not connected to a sewer and send their wastewater into one of the island’s roughly 8,000 cesspools.

A cesspool is an unlined pit that releases untreated sewage into the surrounding soil. A 2017 state law requires all cesspools to be phased out by 2050.

The number of cesspools inside a hazard zone is projected by the models to rise from 54 in 2022 to 92 at 1 foot of sea level rise and to 738 at 4 feet.

Cesspools and septic systems already leak sewage into coastal waters around Oʻahu. This pollution damages coral reefs and increases the risk of waterborne illness.

“These pathways would increase as sea levels rise because the groundwater also rises, and these systems may become flooded or unable to function properly,” Mikkelsen said.

The central sewer network also faces risks. High tides already push contaminated water from the Ala Wai Canal through Honolulu’s storm drains and into its streets.

The models project that the number of affected sewage pump stations could rise from one today to 16 after 4 feet of sea level rise.

The main threat also varies from one coast to another.

In Honolulu, passive flooding and wave flooding account for most exposure. Erosion accounts for roughly half on the North Shore, while yearly high waves dominate along the Waiʻanae coast in the west.

A building was counted as affected whenever any part of its footprint was touched by a hazard zone.

This approach shows which buildings face flooding or erosion. It does not measure how badly each building might be damaged.

The models also left out rainfall, storms, sinking land, and rising groundwater.

Groundwater already floods some basements in Honolulu, but the maps do not show these buildings as affected until sea levels rise by 6 feet. For this reason, the authors say their estimates may be too low.

Another modeling assumption could overstate erosion risk.

The erosion model did not account for seawalls and other barriers that line 27% to 29% of Oʻahu’s sandy shoreline, so it may overstate erosion wherever those structures continue to hold.

The researchers also did not examine how the three hazards affect one another.

They ran each model independently, so the flood models retained the current shoreline even where the erosion model projected beach loss.

The University of Hawaiʻi has made every hazard layer public in its SOEST Climate Viewer. These results update estimates from a 2017 state report on sea level rise used by state and county planners.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research: Climate.

The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.
