#6243. 13 Travel Slippers That Are Comfier Than the Ones From Your Favorite Hotel

After a full day of sightseeing—or an even longer one spent in and out of airports—few things feel better than kicking off your shoes and sliding on a cozy pair of slippers. The complimentary slippers at a luxury hotel are always tempting to take home, but if we're honest, they rarely last beyond a few wears. Fortunately, plenty of more durable—and more comfortable—options exist, from plush, shearling slides and classic wool slip-ons to lightweight travel slippers that barely take up any room in your suitcase. Some have cushioned footbeds and rubber soles sturdy enough for a quick trip outside; others feature soft, suede soles better suited to padding around the house.

Whether you want a warm, fluffy pair by your bed or a foldable option for your next long-haul flight, there’s a slipper for everyone on this list. Read on for the very best pairs to pick up this season from Bombas, Cozy Earth, Ugg, and more.

⁠These lightweight, fuzzy slippers feature a soft, wool-like polyester upper, a breathable lining, and a memory foam footbed for a cushy feel underfoot. The nonslip soles are sturdy enough for quick trips outside to grab the mail or take out the trash, but they're best suited for indoor wear. Even better, they're machine washable, so you can easily keep them in pristine condition all season long. Available in five colors and backed by more than 10,000 Amazon reviews, they're an affordable option for wearing around the house or packing for a weekend away.

It's easy to see why this under-$25 Amazon find has racked up more than 23,000 five-star ratings. Not only are these slippers ridiculously soft (and just the right amount of over-the-top), but they're also pretty practical, thanks to the thick memory foam insole that retains its shape even after daily wear.

While your winter wardrobe likely contains a cashmere sweater or two, don’t sleep on these cashmere slides from Garnet Hill. Thanks to the slip-on slides’ sumptuous cashmere construction and breathable, thermal-insulating fibers, they’ll keep your feet warm and toasty—but not sweaty—all winter long. The padded footbed provides an extra layer of pillowy-soft comfort.

After a long day on your feet, you'll be glad to have these Quince slippers waiting by your bed. They have a soft suede leather upper and thick Australian shearling lining that feels plush against bare feet. And unlike some fuzzy slippers that leave your feet sweaty, the shearling material naturally wicks away moisture and regulates temperature, so you can wear them year-round.

The soft, moisture-wicking sheepskin wool lining of this classic shoe has made it an all-time favorite from the nostalgic Australian brand. The Scuff comes with a thin rubber sole that has just the right amount of support and stability for being on your feet in the kitchen or just puttering around the house on the weekend. Colors include the popular chestnut (shown above), dark gray, and black.

This luxury slide keeps your feet dry and cool, thanks to its moisture-wicking and temperature-regulating design. They're fluffy and warm, and so easy to slip on when you first wake up in the morning. Plus, they feature a slip-resistant sole, making them one of the sturdiest picks on the list.

One of the little luxuries of a hotel stay is slipping into the plush robes and slippers hanging in the closet. Now you can capture that vacation-level comfort at home with The Ritz-Carlton Frette slippers. Crafted from ultra-soft microfiber, they feel cozy and spa-like, while the nonslip soles make them practical for everyday wear around the house. The embroidered hotel logo adds a touch of opulence, and when they need a refresh, simply toss them in the wash.

These striped slippers from Parachute look like something you'd find at a cool boutique hotel. Made in Turkey from thick, absorbent cotton terry, they're soft underfoot and comfortable to slip on after a shower or while lounging at home. The stripes add a little more personality than your typical spa slippers, and the rubber soles grip slippery floors effortlessly. They're durable enough for everyday wear, too, though you may want to size up for a roomier fit.

Made with ultra-soft sheep fur and a plush shearling lining, these chic slippers provide plenty of warmth on chilly fall and winter mornings. As warm as they are, they're also naturally odor-resistant and breathable, so you don't have to worry about your feet getting too hot. They offer a grippy, durable outsole, so while they're best suited for lounging indoors, they can also be worn outside if necessary; you'll feel a little more secure wearing them out on the Airbnb's deck or down to the hotel lobby than in other pairs. They come recommended by commerce editor Meaghan Kenny, who regularly turns to them for extra warmth on cold weekend mornings at home.

Bombas has quite a few solid slippers from which to choose—including the Gripper Slipper that really blurs the line between sock and shoe. But the Sunday Slipper, with its super-soft faux fur and slip-on, slip-off capability, sits at the top of the heap when it comes to versatility. If you're stumped on what to gift someone for the holidays, the best-selling style is foolproof.

Birkenstock manufactures footwear of fabulous durability and quality, from the popular sandals and clogs that you can wear here, there, and everywhere to the more indoor-friendly Zermatt shearling slipper. Despite being supremely soft, the latex sole offers a boost of support, which is why they make such a great house shoe. They come in men's and women’s sizes, and you can pick between wide or narrow fits for optimal comfort.

The Ugg Tasman slipper might be the most recognizable slipper on this list, and it's popular for good reason: The closed-back design makes it a more practical alternative to the brand's classic Scuff slipper; the plush sheepskin lining and durable suede upper ensure coziness and durability; and the Fair Isle–inspired Tasman braid around the trim adds a hint of character.

L.L.Bean fans rave about these clog-like slippers for their arch support, heel cushioning, and playful patterns, featuring designs ranging from turtles to moose to ombré forest trees. They have a fleece lining and rubber anti-slip sole, and are roomy enough to wear your thickest socks underneath in colder months, making them our top pick for cold feet.

What are the best brands for travel slippers?

Bombas and EverFoams design lightweight slippers that are conveniently packable, while Ugg and Quince offer cozy shearling options that take up a bit more suitcase space. If you love the slippers you usually find at luxury hotels, The Ritz-Carlton also sells its signature Frette spa slippers online, so you can bring five-star comfort right to your home.

Slippers can be a welcome change from sneakers or boots on a long-haul flight, especially if you’re hoping to get some sleep. Choose a lightweight, packable pair with nonslip soles, but switch back to shoes when walking around the cabin or using the bathroom.

What should you look for in the best indoor slippers?

When shopping for indoor slippers, fit and material matter most: Wool and shearling provide warmth without trapping too much heat, while memory foam adds cushioning. Look for a soft, flexible sole with enough grip to keep you from slipping on hardwood or tile floors.

#6242. Does everyone carry disease-linked DNA variants? What nearly a million genomes revealed

The average human genome holds about 5 million variants, and one to three of them are already labeled as causing a genetic disease.

A DNA test may flag a variant linked to disease, but that result alone does not mean you will develop the condition.

The typical adult carries one to three rare variants already labeled as causing a genetic disease, plus about 50 more whose meaning is still uncertain.

Most of them do not cause disease in the person carrying them.

The counts come from the largest attempt so far to describe the average human genome.

Caroline Wright, a professor at the University of Exeter, led a team that read the full genomes of nearly a million adults in two large health studies.

The volunteers in UK Biobank and the All of Us program in the United States were not chosen because of any disease. Their DNA shows what ordinary variation looks like.

“Whole genome sequencing has become such an important tool in diagnosing genetic disease, and we’re increasingly moving towards genetic screening for predicting disease. Yet most people are unaware of just how much genetic variation is present in every genome. Actually, variation is the norm,” Wright said.

Scientists compare each person’s DNA with a reference genome, a standard copy of the 3.1 billion letters in human DNA.

A typical person differs from that standard at 4.3 million to 5.3 million spots, or roughly one letter in every 600 to 700.

People whose ancestry is genetically closest to African populations carry about a million more differences than everyone else.

The authors think that may be partly because the reference itself was built mostly from people of European ancestry, so it matches the DNA of people with African ancestry less well.

Most of those differences are single letters swapped, or a few letters added or dropped. The typical genome has 68 stretches longer than 10,000 letters that are either missing or present in extra copies.

Almost all of this variation is shared. In the typical genome, 98.4% of the variants are common, meaning they turn up in more than 1% of people from the same ancestry group.

Only about half a percent land in the parts of genes that spell out proteins.

Protein-coding variants can affect the proteins our bodies make.

A typical person has 21,000 to 26,000 of them, and the team predicts that about 48% change the protein in some way.

Even so, a computer score that flags protein changes likely to do harm picked out just 28 of the roughly 9,600 protein-altering variants in a typical genome.

Each person also carries about 229 variants predicted to break a gene outright, 165 of them with high confidence. That count is in line with earlier surveys of human variation, the authors wrote.

ClinVar, a public database at the U.S. National Institutes of Health, lists about 4 million variants, and around 300,000 of them are rated as causing or probably causing disease.

Eight to ten of those are in the average genome.

The team then narrowed the search to 4,262 genes with solid evidence of causing a single-gene disease and kept only rare variants. That leaves one to three disease-causing variants per person.

Most are in genes for recessive conditions, which need a broken copy from each parent before anyone gets sick.

One copy makes a carrier, and the average person may be a carrier for two to six such conditions.

Variants predicted to disrupt the gene for filaggrin, a skin protein linked to eczema, turn up in about 1 in 15 people of European ancestry in the study.

Not everyone who carries one gets eczema.

For genes associated with dominant conditions, in which one altered copy can cause disease, about 1 in 9 people carries a rare variant rated as disease-causing.

“Importantly, we found that everyone carries a small number of genetic variants linked to disease, although many of these will not actually cause disease in that individual,” Wright said.

“It is therefore crucial to consider context when interpreting findings from genetic testing, including symptoms or family history of disease as well as other clinical and environmental risk factors.”

Common diseases such as diabetes and heart disease usually involve many genetic variants alongside environmental and lifestyle factors.

Thousands of common variants each nudge the odds a little, and a polygenic risk score adds those nudges up to rank a person against everyone else.

Wright’s team used scores already calculated for 28 common diseases across UK Biobank. The average person ranked in the top 10% of risk for about three of them.

Among 450,209 participants of European ancestry, 102,831, or about 1 in 5 people, scored in the top 1% for at least one disease.

A high score for at least one condition is therefore relatively common. Participants of other ancestries landed in the top 1% even more often, about 1 in 3 people.

The authors read that as a flaw in the scores, which perform poorly outside the population they were built in, rather than as extra disease.

Run 100 such scores on one person, the authors calculate, and about 99% of people would land in the top 5% for at least one disease.

About 63% would be in the top 1%. Screening programs that run many scores at once, they wrote, carry significant potential for overdiagnosis.

Some variants come from neither parent. In 2,334 sets of two parents and an adult child, the child carried an average of 61 mutations found in neither parent, ranging from 30 to 113.

Typically only one of them fell inside a protein-coding stretch.

Three-quarters to four-fifths of those new mutations came from the father’s side.

Each year of a father’s age at the child’s birth added about 1.2 more of them, and each year of a mother’s age added about 0.4.

All three members of a trio had to be adults to join the studies, so the parents in this sample were young at the birth. That puts the average toward the low end of earlier estimates.

The volunteers came only from Britain and the United States, and 91.5% of the UK Biobank group was of European ancestry. So the figures say little about most of the world.

Sequencing read short fragments of DNA taken almost entirely from blood, which misses some kinds of variation and any change confined to other tissues.

Uncertainty is unevenly spread. People of European ancestry carried more variants with a known disease label, while everyone else carried more variants of unknown meaning.

The authors trace that gap partly to who has been sequenced so far, and it can affect who gets a diagnosis.

The largest open question is one the study did not try to answer.

The team did not assess whether participants had the diseases associated with their flagged variants, so it cannot say how often those variants were linked to illness.

Wright’s team is presenting the work at the American Society of Human Genetics annual meeting this week.

The authors call for genomes from more diverse populations, read with longer-range sequencing and from more than one tissue, and they urge caution as genetic screening of healthy people expands.

The full study was published in the journal Genome Medicine.

#6241. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

A common antibiotic may be linked to a higher risk of miscarriage and stillbirth when used early in pregnancy, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Taking doxycycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of pregnancy loss, a new study suggests.

The antibiotic is broad-spectrum, meaning it targets a wide range of bacteria. It's often used to treat acne, respiratory infections and sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia and syphilis. Doctors generally avoid prescribing the drug during the second and third trimesters because it belongs to a class of antibiotics that can bind to calcium in developing bones. Animal studies suggest that this may disrupt fetal bone development.

However, evidence on doxycycline's safety during early pregnancy has been mixed and limited. The new study, published Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, provides clearer evidence of a link between doxycycline use in the first trimester and pregnancy loss.

"I would advise physicians to carefully consider the benefit-risk balance when prescribing doxycycline to women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy," study first author Almut Winterstein, a pharmacist and drug-safety researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science in an email.

Using information from two U.S. insurance databases, the researchers analyzed 224,870 pregnancies in people ages 12 to 55. More than 218,230 of these patients were treated for respiratory tract infections, and over 6,630 were treated for acne, between conception and the end of the first trimester. About 4,385 of the women filled a prescription for doxycycline during that time frame, while the others received an alternative antibiotic.

Among women with respiratory infections, those prescribed doxycycline had a 40% to 54% higher risk of pregnancy loss, compared with those prescribed amoxicillin, another broad-spectrum antibiotic in a different class. The exact level of risk varied between the two databases.

The researchers also compared the doxycycline users against women prescribed macrolides, the class of antibiotics that includes azithromycin (or "Z-Pak"). Again, the doxycycline users saw a higher risk — 39% and 36% higher, respectively.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Among the patients treated for acne, doxycycline users had a 49% higher risk of pregnancy loss in one database than those given the antibiotic clindamycin. In the second database, though, the difference wasn't statistically significant. Winterstein said that may be because there were fewer patients included in that analysis.

Overall, doxycycline was associated with seven to 11 additional pregnancy losses per 100 pregnancies, compared with the other antibiotic options assessed, the researchers reported.

The researchers examined the risk associated with taking various antibiotics in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

It is not yet clear how the drug might contribute to pregnancy loss. Because the study was observational, it cannot prove that the antibiotic itself caused those losses, which included miscarriages and stillbirths. (Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of pregnancy, whereas stillbirth refers to pregnancy loss after the 20th week.)

Animal studies hint that doxycycline could interfere with early placental development, potentially making it harder for the placenta to support a growing pregnancy, Luke Grzeskowiak, an associate professor and clinical pharmacist at Flinders University in Australia who was not involved in the study, said in an email.

The study authors also noted in their report that the drug may have direct effects on the developing embryo. But these explanations remain hypothetical; the researchers have not established that either mechanism occurs in humans.

"Pregnancy loss affects around one in four pregnancies and can happen for many reasons," Grzeskowiak noted. Although doxycycline exposure may add to that risk, taking the antibiotic does not necessarily mean pregnancy loss will occur. The available data suggests that it is just one risk factor among many.

Because doxycycline may be prescribed before a pregnancy is recognized, doctors should consider the possibility of pregnancy when prescribing this drug to women of reproductive age, particularly those who are sexually active, Grzeskowiak suggested. That does not mean doctors should avoid prescribing the antibiotic to these women, he emphasized; rather, clinicians should consider pregnancy plans and medical history when choosing a treatment.

In some cases, doxycycline may still be the best option for a severe infection, Winterstein told Live Science, and that infection could itself put a pregnancy at risk. But for less-serious infections, safer alternatives may be available, she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6238. Water near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is changing color, and plastic may be the reason

Water near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch brightened in blue and green over 20 years, and microplastics are the likely cause, a study finds.

Satellites cannot see tiny pieces of plastic in the ocean, but they can see the color of the water. Over the last 20 years, the ocean near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch has actually changed color.

New research suggests that microscopic plastics are to blame. If this is true, scientists might soon be able to track invisible plastic pollution from space just by looking at the color of the sea.

Shea Cheatham, Daniel Koestner, and Børge Hamre of the University of Bergen in Norway carried out the study. They didn’t collect water samples. Instead, they compared three satellite records with computer simulations of how light travels through seawater.

Between Hawaii and California, clockwise surface currents carry floating plastic into an area called the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.

In the summer of 2015, The Ocean Cleanup, a nonprofit group, ran a survey in which boats towed nets in and around the patch 652 times. The group then tallied the catch piece by piece.

Using that survey, the group’s researchers estimated the patch’s area at about 620,000 square miles (1.6 million square kilometers) in a 2018 study. The group describes that area as twice the size of Texas.

The researchers put the number of plastic pieces at 1.8 trillion. They estimated that larger objects made up 92% of the weight, while microplastics made up 94% of the pieces.

But the plastic in the new study is too small to be in that count. Its pieces are no bigger than about a hundredth of an inch (0.3 millimeters), roughly the thickness of three sheets of printer paper.

Plastics that small are the most likely to enter the ocean’s food chain at its lowest level, the authors wrote.

These plastics are also hard to measure at sea, and cleaning them up on a large scale would be difficult, if not impossible.

The color of the ocean depends on what’s in the water. Microscopic algae called phytoplankton absorb some colors of light far more than others.

Plastic behaves differently. In earlier lab work, Koestner and his colleagues measured how water with microplastics mixed in absorbs and scatters light.

The plastic absorbed light fairly evenly across colors. It also scattered a lot of light back the way it came.

In the team’s simulations, seawater with these particles in it looked brighter from above. Blue-green light increased the most.

When the amount of phytoplankton or other natural material changes, blue light tends to get brighter while green gets dimmer, or the other way around. Plastic should brighten both at once.

The team analyzed three records of ocean color. Each ran from August 2002 through September 2022.

One came from an instrument on NASA’s Aqua satellite. The other two, from the European Space Agency and the Copernicus Marine Service, combine readings from several satellite sensors.

Large parts of the ocean have changed color in recent decades, often because of shifts in ocean life. So the team compared the patch with the water around it.

In all three records, areas in and near the patch grew brighter in both blue and green light. Together, those colors make cyan.

The cyan areas were shifted west and north of the patch’s densest part. That may be because wind pushes large floating objects, while microplastics travel with the water, the authors wrote.

Elsewhere, the three records didn’t always match. Farther south, the NASA record showed much more brightening in red light than the other two.

Two likely causes, the authors wrote, are an aging NASA instrument and differences in how the records were processed.

The European Space Agency record showed the fewest areas of clear change. Even so, it showed cyan in and near the patch.

How much plastic would it take to change the ocean’s color enough for a satellite to detect? The team ran 1,100 simulations to find out.

By their calculation, it would take about 5 milligrams of small microplastics in a cube of seawater 3.3 feet (1 meter) on each side.

At that level, the plastic brightened the simulated water more than satellite readings normally vary from one pixel to the next.

Suppose plastic alone caused the change in the brightest area on the patch’s western edge. In that area, a cube of water that size would have gained 11 to 25 milligrams of plastic over 20 years, depending on the satellite record.

The authors called those amounts reasonable. Net surveys by The Ocean Cleanup suggest that larger microplastics may reach similar concentrations near the surface.

In 2018, the group’s researchers also reported that the amount of plastic in the patch appeared to be rising exponentially, and more quickly than in nearby waters.

A color that fits plastic isn’t proof of plastic, the authors wrote, so they tested what natural changes could do alone.

The team simulated 500 versions of the ocean in which only natural material varied: phytoplankton, other natural particles, and colored material dissolved in the water.

In 500 more versions, the amount of microplastics varied too.

Then they compared the versions two at a time and sorted every case of brightening by its color: blue, cyan, green, or red.

With only natural material varying, 3% of the brightening cases were cyan. With microplastics added, 13% were cyan.

In the simulations, adding plastic made a cyan change more than four times as likely.

Without plastic, cyan appeared only when phytoplankton shifted from mostly larger kinds to mostly smaller ones, usually with less living material overall. With plastic, much smaller natural changes were enough.

Blooms of plankton called coccolithophores can brighten seawater too. But these plankton haven’t historically been active here, and their blooms would likely turn the water greener than the satellites recorded.

Mineral dust can brighten the ocean as well. But a dust record at Station ALOHA, north of Hawaii, appears to show no significant change between 1980 and 2025.

The study can’t say for certain that plastic is the cause. The satellites recorded color, and more than one thing in seawater can change it.

In one plausible scenario, the authors wrote, moderate changes in ocean life and a buildup of microplastics are both adding to the brightening.

Plastic could also be acting indirectly, they wrote. Chemical pollutants that come with plastic could be disrupting ocean life, and that disruption could change the water’s color.

Scientists haven’t directly measured how much plastic this small is in the patch.

The team also built its simulated seawater to match a measurement from the South Pacific. No complete set of light measurements exists for the patch’s own region.

Researchers will need to measure light and particles directly, at different depths near the patch, to check the result.

If those measurements confirm the pattern, satellites that already record ocean color could help scientists monitor where small microplastics are building up.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

#6237. These 9 Hotels for Broadway Lovers Put You in the Heart of NYC’s Theater District

As a Californian who discovered the wonderful world of Broadway by borrowing CDs from my local library, it was only fitting that the first trip I ever planned by myself was to New York City—and the entire itinerary revolved around collecting Playbills. Now, after living in the area for more than two decades, I’m that unlikely New Yorker who still claims Times Square as her favorite and most-frequented neighborhood. I just love the Theater District—where else can you find 41 venues featuring the world's best live theater all within a single mile?

In this age of event tourism, Broadway has remained a constant. And seeing a show is about more than just the storyline of a play or the numbers in a musical—it’s an experience that you’re a part of. Over my 20 years as an entertainment editor and journalist, I’ve interviewed numerous Broadway stars, and they always say they feed off of, and are fueled by, audience reactions. You’re not just a passive viewer; your presence drives the show. It's something special to take part in.

If you've got a Broadway trip in your future, chances are you're going to need a hotel that will help you maximize your experience. The list below features properties with themed suites, theater lore, and locations just steps from the Great White Way. Read on for the best places to stay in NYC for a show-stopping Broadway getaway.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Palace Theatre, 3-minute walk to James Earl Jones Theatre and Lunt-Fontanne TheatreWhy we love it: Right across from Palace Theatre, pre- and post-show prix-fixe menus, Studio 54 history

These days, Studio 54 is one of Broadway’s most popular stages (currently home to The Rocky Horror Show ), but back in 1977, Ian Schrager opened it as a nightclub, and it has since come to epitomize celebrity culture for a generation. Schrager brought that same visionary spirit when he opened the 452-room Times Square Edition in 2019, just across the street from the Palace Theatre. One of my favorite spots in Times Square is the hotel's Terrace and Outdoor Garden, a lush dining oasis that offers three-course Broadway Express prix-fixe menus both pre- and post-show. For those looking for an upgraded theater experience, the Edition's Showstopping Stay package—which can be booked up to 10 days in advance—includes two premium tickets to select shows, dinner with Champagne, theater-themed amenities, and house-made snacks.

Closest theaters: 9-minute walk to Studio 54, 10-minute walk to Vivian Beaumont Theater, 11-minute walk to Broadway TheatreWhy we love it: Central Park views, Broadway VIP Experience

Though a few blocks north of the Theater District thrills, the Mandarin Oriental is still less than a 15-minute walk to most theaters—yet it feels a world apart. It overlooks Central Park in one direction, and its 75-foot lap pool has views of the Hudson River. Guests are pampered with a true five-star experience every step of the way, whether it’s raising a glass at The Bar speakeasy or lounging around at celeb-favorite MO Lounge. You can also rub shoulders with the stars via the hotel's Broadway VIP Experience package, which includes an hour-long meet-and-greet with a Broadway cast member over bites and Champagne at the lounge. Also included are orchestra tickets (choose from 13 shows, including Hamilton and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child) and show merch, as well as add-ons like a theater transfer in a Mercedes, a 90-minute guided tour of the Museum of Broadway, or even acting lessons or a private concert with a stage star.

Closest theaters: 3-minute walk to Belasco Theatre, 4-minute walk to Hudson Theatre, 5-minute walk to Stephen Sondheim TheatreWhy we love it: Official partner of the Tony Awards, recently refreshed, early check-in option

If hotels could earn Tonys, the Sofitel New York would be a clear winner. As a longtime partner of Broadway’s iconic awards show, many a theater star has walked through its doors. That includes George Clooney during his Broadway debut in Good Night, and Good Luck, Jonathan Groff during his turn as Bobby Darin in Just in Time, and Mia Farrow while she was in The Roommate. Just last year, the property underwent a full makeover, reimagining its 398 rooms and suites (some with Empire State Building views), as well as its lobby, fitness center, and dining options (including Social 45 Bar & Bistro), drawing on the Art Deco glamour of Paris and New York. While an exclusive Broadway package is currently in the works, the Sofitel does currently offer The Ultimate Manhattan Luxury Staycation experience, which includes a welcome drink, dining credit, signature pastries, and early check-in at noon, perfect for squeezing in an extra Wednesday or weekend matinee.

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to Eugene O’Neill Theatre, Walter Kerr, and Longacre TheatreWhy we love it: Quiet, designed by a Tony-winning scenic designer, curated theater mementos

Despite being footsteps away from several Broadway theaters, Civilian Hotel manages to create a cozy boutique experience, starting with an entrance just around the corner from Eighth Avenue. One step inside, and you feel like you’ve earned a backstage pass— hotelier Jason Pomeranc teamed up with scenic designer David Rockwell (Hairspray, Legally Blonde, Elf) on a classic theater theme featuring everything from marquee-inspired lighting to dramatic curtains. Even its 203 guest rooms channel vintage dressing room vibes. Rockwell's goal was to create a space for NYC’s creatives—performers, designers, directors, producers, and writers—that paid homage to classic Broadway. Stop by the Blue Vault tasting room and lounge to spot some theater relics, and the Olio Collection rooftop bar for more than 250 pieces of theater-inspired art.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Palace Theatre, 3-minute walk to Marquis TheatreWhy we love it: Location across from TKTS booth, buzzy Sky Lobby

When it comes to Theater District locations, you can't find much better than the 661-room Tempo by Hilton New York Times Square. Making its debut in the dense area in August 2023, it snagged a prime spot right across from Duffy Square’s TKTS booth, the bright red discount ticket outlet that sells last-minute show tickets for up to 50% off (psst, check here for today’s offers). Even closer is the Palace Theatre, currently home to the musical The Lost Boys, which the property has partnered with on a themed suite, bookable through September 14, 2027. Inside the suite, you'll find an ’80s seaside feel mimicking the musical’s world of Santa Carla.

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to Eugene O’Neill Theatre, Walter Kerr, and Ambassador Theatre; half a dozen more a 3-minute walk awayWhy we love it: Vacation vibes at its Bar Sprezzatura, daily complimentary wine in the Living Room Lobby during Evening Social Hour, Roundabout Theatre Company partnership

The first time I stepped off the elevator into Kimpton Theta New York’s Bar Sprezzatura, I immediately craved an Aperol spritz. That’s how much I was transported to the Italian Riviera. The contrast between the lively Midtown streets below (the bar sits on the 15th floor) and the laid-back rooftop bar made me fall in love with the 364-key property instantly, and with multiple two- and three-bedroom suites, it's perfect for families and groups looking to book a foodie-friendly Broadway bonding trip. This November, the hotel launched the Roundabout Theatre Co. x Kimpton Theta package, giving guests 20% off tickets to Roundabout Theatre Co. shows (currently The Rocky Horror Show and Imaginary Invalid) plus pre- or post-show drinks at the bar.

Closest theaters: Attached to Marquis Theatre, 1-minute walk to Minskoff Theatre, 2-minute walk to Richard Rodgers TheatreWhy we love it: Ideal for Marquis Theatre shows, home to NYC’s only rotating restaurant, Broadway Bound Dining Package

For a mega-sized hotel smack dab in the middle of Times Square, the Marriott Marquis still has a sense of character. When I first moved to the area 23 years ago, I used to frequent its eight-floor Broadway Lounge, looking out at Times Square and marveling that I had finally “made it." Nowadays, I still pop in for a dose of nostalgia, gazing up at the 36-floor atrium’s elevators leading to the hotel's 1,900 rooms—a constant in a world that’s changed so much since it opened in 1985. But that throwback feel comes with a new spring in its step, most notably at its 48th-floor spinning restaurant, The View, reimagined by Danny Meyer in 2024. (Note: TodayTix members get free bubbly and bar snacks here, depending on their tier.) But what makes the property so unique for theater fans is that it’s the only hotel ever built with a Broadway theater inside—yes, the Marquis Theatre is literally on the third floor. Also special: The Broadway Bound Dining Package includes the chance to mingle with a theater star!

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to the Nederlander Theatre, New Amsterdam Theatre, and Lyric TheatreWhy we love it: Themed rooms, located on 42nd Street, close to other attractions

Now here’s a hotel that reflects both “A Whole New World” and “The Circle of Life.” Through its partnership with Disney’s two long-running musicals, Hilton New York Times Square guests can go all in with themed rooms curated by Broadway designer Devin Sparkles Design. Aladdin's Times Square Palace Suite is decked out just like Agrabah, down to a genie lamp, Moroccan magic carpets, and Jasmine-inspired silks. Over in The Lion King’s Royal Suite, it’s all about the wonders of the Serengeti Pridelands, with hand-painted Rafiki-like patterns and bird puppets flying from the ceiling. Both include wake-up calls from each musical’s most iconic characters—the Genie and Rafiki—as well as themed drinks. But perhaps the most valuable part of the package, especially for those driving in? Parking in Times Square.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Hudson Theatre, Belasco Theatre, and Lyceum Theatre

Why we love it: Passageway running between Hudson Theatre’s entrance and stage door, June 2026 refresh

Ever since my first Broadway trip to NYC in 2002, I’ve been stage-dooring shows. The Hudson Theatre shows can be tricky for this, as the theater’s entrance is on 44th Street, but its stage door is on 45th. It wasn’t until I discovered that the Millennium Hotel had a secret passageway—which is also the entrance to the hotel—that I started snagging spots close enough to get autographs (including from Daniel Radcliffe during Merrily We Roll Along). That said, I've always been jealous of those actually staying at the 751-room property, with a trio of theaters literally at their doorstep. Those eager to dive even deeper into the Theater District's history will love that the property is just across the street from the Museum of Broadway.

Is it expensive to see a show on Broadway?

Yes, price tags can be high—the year-to-date average per ticket for 2026 is $122.67. But there are also plenty of ways to find discounts through lotteries, TodayTix, Theatr, and the TKTS Booth. I’ve only paid more than $100 five times in my life—and never more than $200. (That’s why I haven’t been to a movie in nearly a decade, but have seen nearly 40 shows in the last year!)

What show should I see on Broadway this winter?

For last-minute trips, hot tickets right now include Bowen Yang’s record-breaking run in Cole Escola’s Oh, Mary! (Lyceum Theatre), plus A Few Good Men (Vivian Beaumont Theatre), Much Ado About Nothing (Winter Garden), Other Desert Cities (Hudson Theatre), and School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play (Samuel J. Friedman). And of course there are long-running hits like Wicked (Gershwin Theatre), Hamilton (Richard Rodgers Theatre), Harry Potter and the Cursed Child (Lyric Theatre), The Great Gatsby (Broadway Theatre), and Disney’s The Lion King (Minskoff Theatre).

Are there any shows I should plan a 2027 trip around?

As we’re standing on the precipice of one of the most anticipated Broadway seasons, there’s no better time to plan a theater getaway. Coming soon are Dolly: A True Original Musical (opening December 7 at St. James Theatre), the Julia Roberts and Paul Rudd–led Small Mouth Sounds (February 10 at Ethel Barrymore Theatre), Jonathan Groff’s The Amish Project (February 10 at Broadhurst Theatre), Dirty Dancing (February 12 at Lena Thorne Theatre), Evita on Broadway (February 27 at Winter Garden Theatre), Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Warriors (March 9 at Lunt-Fontanne Theatre), Purple Rain (March 12 at Majestic Theatre), The Sound of Music (March 23 at Vivian Beaumont Theatre), Damn Yankees (March 24 at Marquis Theatre), and the one I’m most thrilled about, the West End transfer Paddington: The Musical (March 30 at Al Hirschfield Theatre)—I already have my ticket for the first preview!

#6236. Archaeologists found a rare gold bear hiding inside an ancient grave in Kazakhstan that was raided by robbers thousands of years ago

A small gold bear from the 4th-3rd century B.C. was found in a looted Saka mound in Almaty, with remains of perhaps seven people.

Earlier this year, staff of the Almaty Museums Association dug into a Saka burial mound at Karagaily, in the city’s Nauryzbay district. They found a small gold bear and a lot of human bones.

Somebody had been there first. Robbers in antiquity left a 10-foot (3 meter) pit in the mound.

On November 5 the Almaty city administration published the result and called the bear figurine unique for Kazakhstan. The date it gave is preliminary, and nobody yet knows how many people lay in the grave.

Karagaily is a cemetery of the Early Iron Age, and the mound dug this year was an emergency job done with the support of the city administration. It is 25 to 26 meters wide, or roughly 82 to 85 feet, and about 8 feet (2.5 meters) high.

Based on its knowledge of the cemetery, the team put the mound in the 4th or 3rd century B.C., the time of the Saka, nomadic peoples of the Central Asian steppe. Broken Saka pots came out of the dig too.

Meanwhile, Marat Nurpeisov, senior researcher at the association, said the work at Karagaily has not finished.

The statement calls the object “presumably” a small cast figurine of a bear. In the photos the city released, it stands on its hind legs on a scrap of thin gold sheet, and rows of short notches cover its back and flanks.

Because the sheet has holes in it, the excavators think somebody stitched it to a headdress. They point to two Kazakh parallels for animals worn on the head.

The first is the gold argali, a wild mountain sheep, that topped the hat of the Golden Man, the young man buried in a suit with more than 4,000 gold pieces and dug up near Almaty in 1969. Kok-Kainar cemetery gave the second in 2014, a small snow leopard that had also been part of a headdress.

Lyazzat Sagyndykova, who directs the association, was blunt about the bear. In the statement, translated here from Russian, she said the sculptural figurine of a bear “is unique for Kazakhstan.”

She also said the find lets researchers trace cultural parallels across Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to the Altai, though the statement names no objects from either end of that range.

Altogether, excavators think four adults and three children may have gone into this one mound. However, the administration is careful to say nobody has established the exact number.

Nurpeisov said mounds of comparable size were usually meant for one or two people, and that such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan.

Anthropologists will join the work, along with other tests, to find out how many bodies there were and how they came to be there.

Kinship is one thing those tests could look at, although the Almaty statement never mentions DNA. In a study of 85 people from 20 Scythian-era sites on the steppe, elite burials turned out about eleven times more likely to be relatives of each other than of lower-status people at the same sites.

Only in 2022 did the association get its special license to excavate, and it began work inside the city that same year.

In Alatau district it found an untouched burial of a Saka warrior, dated between the 5th and 2nd centuries B.C., with pieces of a sword inlaid with gold, animal-style gold ornaments and silver.

Another Alatau mound in 2024 gave up bits of human bone, bronze fasteners and nails. Italian and French specialists meanwhile ran geophysical surveys with the museum staff at the park called the Saka Mounds of Boralday. That site has 52 mounds over about 430 hectares (1,060 acres) northwest of Almaty.

Last year the team came across an old robbers’ tunnel in a further Early Iron Age mound and recorded how it was built and what the damage was.

Digs forced by development have paid off in other countries. Infrastructure work in southeastern Bulgaria led to a Thracian warrior buried beside his horse with a gilded silver wreath.

At Tepe Chalow in northeastern Iran a teenage girl’s Bronze Age tomb held 34 objects, gold rings and earrings among them.

Everything official so far comes from that one city statement, which is not a scientific paper. It gives no height or weight for the figure.

It does not say where in the mound the bear was lying or how the robbers came to miss it.

“Unique” is the association’s own word. The date, too, comes from the cemetery as a whole and not from a laboratory result on this mound.

Once the research is over, the association intends to put the best pieces on show at the Almaty Museum. Robbers left a 10-foot hole at Karagaily, and the bear is headed for a glass case.

The information was obtained from the Almaty city administration.

#6235. The 6 Best Inflatable Hot Tubs for Backyard Relaxation

Bliss out with one of these affordable inflatable hot tubs for the ultimate at-home spa experience.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Nothing beats a warm, bubbly soak under the stars, but not everyone has the space—or budget—to install a permanent hot tub in their backyard. That’s where inflatable hot tubs come into play.

They cost less than their hard-sided counterparts—some four-person models are under $500, if you can believe it—and are easy to store in the off-season. Another plus: inflatable hot tubs come with everything you need to get them up and running, so you just fill them with water and crank up the temperature.

Whether you’re looking for a small option for two or a larger model to soak with friends and family, read on for our best inflatable hot tub recommendations and the essentials to consider before you shop.

Looking for more ways to upgrade your backyard? Check out our stories on the best outdoor sectionals, cantilever umbrellas, and smokeless fire pits.

We scoured user reviews and chose options across sizes, styles, and price points, from value-packed to high-end. We spent a lot of time weighing different hot tub models—both permanent and inflatable—so we used our expertise to recommend only durable, comfortable options. As mentioned above, there are plenty of features to consider when shopping for an inflatable hot tub, and we highlighted the most notable ones for each model we cover.

The Intex PureSpace Plus gives you the jet count and water capacity of pricier six-person inflatables for less. It holds 290 gallons and lists a six-person capacity, though four adults is more realistic if everyone wants ample legroom. The 170 air jets run along the walls and floor for a full-body massage, but they’re fixed, so you can’t aim them at a sore spot.

The tub can inflate in a few minutes with the included hose, no tools needed. Heating is slow, though, with the pump reaching a 104-degree Fahrenheit maximum over several hours, so start it in the morning if you want to relax by dinner time. A built-in hard-water treatment system softens the water as it fills, which slows the mineral scale that otherwise builds up inside the heater and pump.

A multicolor LED light is great for nighttime soaks, and two spare filter cartridges and a floating chlorine dispenser keep the water clear. It also includes a ground cloth and insulated cover to help retain heat between uses. Two removable headrests are included, so you can really relax after a long day.

The Miami is built for two people who want a hot tub without much fuss or yard space. It’s round, 71 inches across, holds 177, and fits two adults comfortably or four if everyone doesn’t mind a snugger fit.

The insulated EnergySense cover and liner retain heat, and Coleman rates the tub 40 percent more energy-efficient than comparable inflatables, so it uses less power over a season of use. A Freeze Shield feature turns the heater on automatically when the water temperature nears freezing, so the pump and liner won’t ice up. A power-saving timer also lets you schedule heating for when you’ll actually use it.

The 120 air jets are spaced around the seating area, so the bubbles reach your back and legs. Setup needs no tools, and the box includes the heater pump, a ChemConnect chemical dispenser, a Type VI filter cartridge, and the insulated cover. The one compromise is size. At 26 inches tall with a 52-inch interior, it’s shallower and snugger than some of the six-person tubs on this list.

For large groups, you can’t go wrong with this Bestway inflatable hot tub, designed for up to eight adults. What I love most about this model is that the pump doesn’t hang off the side—it’s integrated, built directly into the liner. A control panel extends above the rim, so you don’t need to get out of the tub to change the temperature or massage system. It’s a big improvement over models with exterior pumps that have hard-to-reach control panels on top. And, if you’re sitting on the opposite side of the tub and want to make an adjustment, you can do so through the brand’s app.

Another plus is this hot tub’s energy-efficient design, with insulated walls and an included cover, plus the three-layer material is said to be durable enough to withstand punctures. The hot tub features 190 jets, a 380-gallon capacity, and a power-saving timer.

Made of laminate PVC and polyester mesh, this 222-gallon hot tub seats four people—perfect for a backyard gathering. This hot tub is similar to the 6- to 8-person model we wrote about above, just smaller and without some of the higher-end features, including an upgraded pump.

The 4- to 6-person model has 140 high-powered jets, an all-in-one heater and filtration system, and a pump mounted high off the ground for easy access to the digital panel.

There’s also a floating chlorine dispenser to regulate the amount of chemicals in the water, plus two filter cartridges and a carrying bag. The insulated cover and thermal ground cloth help keep your hot tub warm when you aren’t using it, so you can spend less money heating it every time.

The Intex PureSpa Greystone Deluxe is designed to hold its heat when the weather turns cold. The cover is filled with high-density thermal foam instead of air, and Intex rates it up to 50 percent more efficient at retaining heat, so the heater cycles on less often. The heater covers 50 to 104 degrees Fahrenheit, and the Intex Link app lets you schedule heating ahead of time, so the water is ready when you get home from work.

The control panel is wireless. You can take it off its dock and adjust the temperature, jets, or multicolor LED light without fully climbing out. The blower heats the air before it reaches 140 bubble jets, so running the jets doesn’t cool the water as much. The square shell is 69 inches on each side and holds 120 gallons, and Intex rates it for four people. It also has a built-in hard-water treatment system to reduce mineral buildup and extend the life of the heater and pump.

With a name like Palm Springs, it’s no surprise this Coleman inflatable hot tub performs better in milder climates. Coleman says the tub can’t run when the air drops below 39 degrees Fahrenheit, so it suits patios in states where it doesn’t snow for much of the year.

Its EnergySense cover traps heat, and Coleman rates it 40 percent more efficient than covers on similar inflatables. Free Shield turns the heater on automatically if the water nears freezing, protecting the pump during an unexpected cold snap.

The tub is 77 inches across and holds 242 gallons, with 140 AirJet bubble jets in a ring around the floor. The DuraPlus walls have three layers and stretch 56 percent further than PVC before tearing, so a stray branch or a dog’s claw is less likely to cause a leak.

Budget aside, if you’re in the market for a hot tub, first nail down how many people you’ll need to accommodate. Most options comfortably fit four to six people, including our best overall pick, the Intex PureSpa Plus 6-Person Inflatable Hot Tub.

Larger models seat eight or more adults, and extra-small hot tubs are ideal for two. Square inflatable hot tubs generally offer more room to stretch out, but they’re typically harder to find than round models.

Most inflatable hot tubs are made of PVC and vinyl, and the best models have three-layer outer walls (often labeled as TriTech) to prevent punctures.

It may surprise you that more jets aren’t always better. It’s more important to consider jet placement, whether they’re adjustable, and whether they vary in size and function.

All inflatable hot tubs typically include a pump, heater, filtration system, and cover, and many also come with ground cloths, extra filter cartridges, chlorine regulators, and carrying bags. Nice-to-have extras include cup holders, multicolor LED lights, and removable headrests.

#6234. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6233. Students helped astronomers track a rare alien comet that contains strange chemicals

Students helped the Webb Telescope locate a rare interstellar comet, revealing record-high heavy hydrogen levels that prove it was born in an incredibly cold, unknown star system.

School groups in Upminster, Bridgend, Alcarràs and Zagreb were among the observers who sent in position measurements of an interstellar comet in the weeks before the Webb Telescope observed it on December 22, 2025.

Those positions helped astronomers refine the predicted location of 3I/ATLAS before beginning their study. Webb then discovered that the comet contained methane with a higher share of heavy hydrogen than had ever been measured in the solar system.

Nathan X. Roth and 17 co-authors put the ratio at 3.18 percent. They link it to a very cold birthplace, but the paper names no star system.

The paper credits Comet Chasers, a school outreach program led by Helen Usher, with supporting position measurements, and lists the schools among the observers. The program reaches telescopes in the Las Cumbres Observatory network.

The target had been known for less than six months. The ATLAS survey telescope in Río Hurtado, Chile, reported the object on July 1, 2025, according to NASA. It was the third known visitor from outside the solar system, and it passed closest to the sun around October 30.

Roth, of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and American University, did the spectral modeling and led the writing. Martin Cordiner, also at Goddard, calibrated the Webb data.

Webb observed the comet under General Observer program 5094 with its Near-Infrared Spectrograph. On December 22, the telescope took a single 642-second exposure starting at 03:36 Universal Time.

The key data came the next day. Five exposures of 700 seconds each began at 08:07 Universal Time and covered wavelengths where methane emits strongly.

The comet was then about 223 million miles (360 million kilometers) from the sun and 167 million miles (269 million kilometers) from Webb. Roth’s team extracted light from a small circle reaching about 610 miles (980 kilometers) from the nucleus.

Lines from ordinary methane were up to 100 times stronger than those from the heavy form. Methanol, formaldehyde and ethane also emit at nearby wavelengths.

The team used NASA’s Planetary Spectrum Generator to model those gases and subtract them from the spectrum.

They removed ordinary methane next, masked its line positions and fitted what remained. They fitted the spectral baseline together with the gas emission, using low-order polynomials.

Deuterium is a form of hydrogen with a neutron in its nucleus. In the molecule CH3D, one deuterium atom replaces one of the four hydrogen atoms in methane.

The measured ratio was 3.18 percent, with an uncertainty of 0.30 points. The authors wrote that it “exceeds any other value for methane measured in the Solar System,” a list that includes Venus, the giant planets, Titan and the dwarf planets Eris and Makemake.

Carbon monoxide was the most abundant molecule in the gas around the comet on December 23. Water usually leads closer to the sun. Methane escapes ice very easily, so the authors concluded that this shift should not have changed the ratio they derived.

A second Webb instrument looked at the comet that same month. The Mid-Infrared Instrument observed the comet on December 15 and 16 and again on December 27.

That’s when Webb directly detected methane gas on an interstellar visitor for the first time, according to NASA. Other Webb work on the same comet found water ice mixed with dust in very small grains.

Only one other comet has a secure detection of this molecule. The European Space Agency’s Rosetta spacecraft measured it directly at comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, and the 3I/ATLAS ratio is about 13 times higher.

Telescope searches at a few bright comets produced only upper limits, between 0.5 and 1 percent. The Webb spectrum therefore counts as a rare remote detection of CH3D in any comet’s atmosphere.

Methane is not the only enriched gas in this object. The earlier analysis of the same Webb observations put the heavy hydrogen ratio in its water at 0.98 percent, according to a paper in Nature, and a separate team reported water far richer in deuterium than comets near the sun.

The methane ratio is roughly three times the water ratio. Comet 67P shows the same direction of difference, and regions where stars form show organic molecules more enriched than water by up to a factor of 10. Around the young star V883 Orionis, astronomers have also reported heavy water older than the sun.

Roth and his colleagues wrote that the result fits ices formed in a cold interstellar or protostellar setting with few heavy elements and strong cosmic ray exposure.

Low temperatures keep deuterium attached to reactive ions, and a shortage of carbon monoxide leaves those ions alive for longer.

Cosmic rays add more of the ions that start this chemistry. Models of planet-forming disks that include X-rays give methane ratios of only about 0.2 to 0.6 percent, so the team argued that the ices were inherited from an earlier stage.

Cordiner’s team had estimated that the comet could have formed as long as 10 to 12 billion years ago, according to ESA/Webb.

“This was a unique opportunity to study an ancient object from the distant Galaxy,” Cordiner said in that release. Webb’s carbon and deuterium readings hint at a distant origin for the object.

Few published models list a heavy methane ratio at all, and none of those predicts more than 1 percent. The authors noted that astrochemical models have not yet tested deuterium chemistry with low heavy element levels and strong cosmic rays together.

The comparison also rests on two comets. Methane’s ratio is still unconstrained in sources outside the solar system, so the team estimated it from a small ring-shaped hydrocarbon called cyclopropenylidene. Those indirect values may reach at least 4 to 7 percent and offer tentative support only.

Two of the five background exposures failed because of background star problems, and the team worked without subtracting background light.

This article uses the journal figures. A preprint of the study lists 3.33 percent and a factor of 14, while the journal version gives 3.18 percent and a factor of 13.

The paper does not name a home star for 3I/ATLAS. It does name the schools in Upminster, Bridgend, Alcarràs and Zagreb.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

The paper’s acknowledgments thank optical observers whose position measurements helped refine the comet’s ephemeris, the table of its predicted positions.

They then name the schools, which include Coopers’ Company and Coborn School in Upminster, St Mary’s Catholic Primary School in Bridgend, Institut d’Alcarràs in Catalonia and Jelkovec High School in Zagreb.

J. M. Perez Redondo and students A. Matea, L. Guillamet, A. Montoy and A. Martin took part from the Catalan school.

Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

#6228. Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”
